technique: CSS2D label overlay on orbiting 3D objects with layer-based label toggling
description: A 3D globe or product model slowly rotates with crisp HTML labels anchored to specific points in 3D space, following the object as it moves. Suits interactive data visualizations, educational science or geography sites, product configurators, or dashboard widgets where users need to identify parts of a 3D object with toggleable annotation layers.
usageNote: In React or Next.js, initialize both WebGLRenderer and CSS2DRenderer inside a useEffect with a canvas ref; append the CSS2DRenderer's domElement as an absolutely-positioned sibling div over the canvas. Attach OrbitControls to the CSS2DRenderer domElement. Replace local planet textures with any publicly hosted or bundled image URLs (e.g., /public/textures/ in Next.js or imported via Vite asset handling). Clean up both renderers, controls, and the timer in the useEffect return. In react-three-fiber, use the @react-three/drei Html component as a drop-in replacement for CSS2DObject.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer plus a second CSS2DRenderer overlay; both must be resized together on window resize. CSS labels are real DOM elements so they scale with page font size and support CSS styling, but adding hundreds of labels will degrade DOM performance. Mobile is supported but touch events must be routed through the CSS2DRenderer domElement for OrbitControls to work correctly.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to resize both renderers on window resize causes label misalignment. Not positioning the CSS2DRenderer domElement as absolute/top:0 causes layout shifts. Attaching OrbitControls to the WebGLRenderer domElement instead of the CSS2DRenderer domElement breaks mouse interaction because the label layer sits on top. Forgetting to dispose textures and geometries on unmount causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container ref breaks embedded or partial-page layouts.
accessibilityNotes: CSS2D labels are real DOM elements and can be read by screen readers; ensure label divs have appropriate ARIA roles or are inside a labelled region. Add a prefers-reduced-motion media query to pause or slow the orbital animation. Provide a static fallback image for users without WebGL support. Ensure sufficient color contrast on label text against the 3D background.

technique: mixed CSS3D and WebGL renderer with interactive iframe embedded in 3D scene
description: A navigable 3D room containing a live HTML iframe embedded in a floating framed panel, orbitable by the user. Ideal for portfolio sites, product showcases, or interactive presentations where a live web experience (video, app, widget) needs to appear as a physical 3D exhibit.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, wrap all renderer and scene setup inside a useEffect with a ref for the mount container. Create both CSS3DRenderer and WebGLRenderer, append their domElements to the ref container (not document.body). Return a cleanup function that cancels the animation loop, removes event listeners, and disposes renderers. Replace the iframe src with any valid absolute URL or same-origin path. In Next.js ensure the component is client-only ('use client') since it accesses the DOM.
constraints: Requires a browser that supports both CSS 3D transforms and WebGL. The iframe content must be same-origin or CORS-permissive for full interactivity; cross-origin iframes render but cannot be scripted. Performance is moderate: two renderers run in sync each frame. Not recommended for mobile devices with low GPU/CSS compositing budgets or when many 3D objects are also in the scene.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to sync both renderers on window resize will misalign the CSS3D and WebGL layers. Appending renderer DOM elements to document.body instead of a scoped container breaks React unmounting and cleanup. Not disabling iframe pointer events during orbit causes accidental iframe interaction while dragging. Failing to set alpha:true on the WebGL renderer breaks the visual stacking order between the two layers.
accessibilityNotes: The iframe content should itself be accessible with proper ARIA and keyboard support. Provide a static screenshot or direct link to the embedded content as a fallback for users who cannot or prefer not to interact with the 3D scene. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by skipping OrbitControls damping animation or auto-rotation if added. Screen readers cannot navigate the 3D container meaningfully, so ensure the embedded content is reachable via a normal link.

technique: interactive 3D molecular structure viewer with CSS3D sprites and bond cylinders
description: Renders interactive 3D molecular structures using CSS3D sprites for atoms (colored balls) and DOM elements for bonds, with trackball orbit controls. Suits science education platforms, pharmaceutical product pages, chemistry learning apps, or any site needing a visually rich interactive molecular or network visualization.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a ref'd container div; instantiate CSS3DRenderer targeting that div, not document.body. PDB model files must be self-hosted — replace 'models/pdb/' paths with your own CDN or public folder URLs (e.g. '/public/models/pdb/' in Next.js). The ball sprite texture must also be self-hosted; replace 'textures/sprites/ball.png' with a public asset path. Dispose all CSS3D objects and remove event listeners in the useEffect cleanup. React-three-fiber does not support CSS3DRenderer natively, so stick with imperative useEffect pattern.
constraints: Requires CSS3DRenderer layered over a WebGL renderer (or standalone); CSS3D elements do not depth-sort correctly with WebGL geometry so mixing with complex WebGL scenes is difficult. Performance degrades with large molecules (e.g. Diamond PDB) due to many DOM elements. Mobile support is limited — trackball controls are not touch-optimized and many DOM nodes reduce scroll performance. Not suitable for scenes needing accurate z-depth blending with other 3D objects.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to remove old CSS3D DOM elements before loading a new molecule causes unbounded DOM growth. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks in embedded or panel layouts — use container.clientWidth/clientHeight instead. Not calling controls.dispose() and removing the resize listener on unmount causes memory leaks. Failing to negate the bounding box offset leads to off-center molecules.
accessibilityNotes: Pure visual; no screen reader information about the molecule. Add an aria-label or visually-hidden text describing the molecule name and type. Provide a prefers-reduced-motion media query that disables auto-rotation and stops animation. Offer a static image or 2D SVG fallback for users who cannot load WebGL or CSS3D. Keyboard navigation for switching molecules should be preserved in the GUI controls.

technique: CSS3D planes in orthographic 3D space with orbit controls and HTML color panels
description: Renders colored semi-transparent HTML div panels arranged as walls and a floor in an orthographic 3D scene, overlaid on a WebGL wireframe layer. Suits product configurators, room/space visualizers, interactive floor plan previews, or admin dashboards that need a 3D spatial layout with real DOM elements (text, images, video) embedded in planes.
usageNote: Wrap the init and animate calls inside a useEffect hook with a ref-attached container div; append both renderer.domElement (WebGL) and renderer2.domElement (CSS3DRenderer) to that container div rather than document.body. Clean up by calling renderer.dispose() and removing DOM elements in the useEffect return. In react-three-fiber this pattern is harder to use directly because CSS3DRenderer is outside R3F's render pipeline—vanilla three.js inside useEffect is the recommended approach. Replace the lil-gui panel with React state and controlled inputs for a production UI.
constraints: Requires both WebGLRenderer and CSS3DRenderer running in tandem, which means two DOM layers must be z-stacked; CSS3D elements are real DOM nodes so they respect browser CSS but cannot be captured by WebGL post-processing. Orthographic camera means no perspective foreshortening—good for architectural/diagrammatic views, bad for immersive 3D scenes. OrbitControls minZoom/maxZoom limits are set; adapt for mobile pinch-zoom. Performance is low-cost for a small number of planes but scales poorly with many CSS3D objects.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to append CSS3DRenderer on top of WebGLRenderer with position:absolute will break layering. Not updating both camera projection matrix and both renderer sizes on window resize causes misalignment between the WebGL wireframe and CSS3D panels. Binding OrbitControls to the WebGL canvas instead of the CSS3DRenderer domElement blocks mouse interaction with the CSS layer. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of the container element's dimensions breaks embedded/partial-page use. Forgetting to remove event listeners and dispose the renderer on component unmount causes memory leaks.
accessibilityNotes: CSS3D div panels are real DOM elements and can contain accessible text, ARIA labels, and focusable controls—leverage this advantage over pure WebGL. Add prefers-reduced-motion media query to disable auto-rotation or orbit animation. Provide a static flat layout fallback (e.g. a CSS grid of the same colored panels) for users with motion disabled or when WebGL is unavailable. Keyboard navigation of the 3D space is not provided by default; consider adding keyboard shortcuts for camera reset or panel focus.

technique: CSS3D multi-layout morphing card grid with animated transitions between table, sphere, helix, and flat-grid arrangements
description: A large collection of styled HTML cards (each showing a name, symbol, and value) that can smoothly tween between four distinct 3D spatial layouts — a flat grid, a sphere, a helix, and a periodic-table arrangement — with full trackball rotation. Ideal for product catalogs, team directories, portfolio showcases, or any dataset that benefits from a dramatic, explorable 3D presentation.
usageNote: Wrap initialization in a useEffect with a ref-attached container div; instantiate CSS3DRenderer and append its domElement to that ref instead of document.body. Overlay the WebGL renderer canvas behind the CSS3D renderer layer. In Next.js, guard with typeof window !== 'undefined' and dynamic import with ssr:false. Replace the hardcoded dataset array with props or fetched data. Clean up by calling renderer.dispose() and controls.dispose() in the useEffect return. TWEEN.update() must be called inside the animation loop.
constraints: Requires CSS3DRenderer, which composites HTML elements in 3D via CSS transforms — not compatible with WebGL post-processing or standard three.js materials on the cards. Performance degrades with more than ~200 cards on mid-range mobile GPUs due to DOM compositing cost. Desktop-first; on mobile, trackball controls are touch-compatible but frame rate may drop. No local assets needed.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to append both the CSS3DRenderer domElement and the WebGL canvas in the correct z-order (CSS3D must be on top). Not calling TWEEN.update(time) in the animation loop causing transitions to never run. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions for responsive sizing. Failing to remove event listeners and dispose controls on component unmount causing memory leaks. Not setting pointer-events: none on the WebGL canvas overlay, which blocks interaction with the CSS3D cards.
accessibilityNotes: Cards are real HTML DOM elements so they are technically readable by screen readers, but the 3D spatial arrangement conveys no semantic meaning — provide a plain list or table fallback. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by skipping or drastically shortening TWEEN animations (check matchMedia). Add keyboard navigation to cycle between layouts as an alternative to mouse-only controls. Ensure sufficient color contrast on card text against card backgrounds.

technique: CSS3D panels composited with WebGL wireframes in 3D space with trackball navigation
description: Randomly positioned and rotated colored HTML div panels float in 3D space, each backed by a matching wireframe plane, creating a layered mixed-renderer environment navigable via trackball drag. Suits interactive data dashboards, portfolio showcases, or spatial UI explorers where real HTML content panels need to exist in 3D space.
usageNote: Wrap all init logic in a useEffect hook with cleanup (dispose controls, remove DOM elements). Create two canvas/div refs: one for the WebGLRenderer canvas and one for the CSS3DRenderer overlay div, ensuring the CSS3DRenderer div is position:absolute overlaid on top. In React 18+ use a single useEffect to avoid double-mount issues. Replace lil-gui with a React state panel if needed. No local assets to replace.
constraints: Requires CSS3DRenderer layered over WebGLRenderer, meaning the WebGL canvas must sit behind the CSS layer — transparent WebGL background or careful z-index management is required. CSS3D does not support real 3D occlusion between HTML and WebGL objects. Mobile support is limited by trackball controls (no touch-optimized defaults) and CSS 3D transform performance on low-end devices. Not suitable for scenes needing true HTML-behind-geometry occlusion.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to append both renderer DOM elements and set CSS3DRenderer to position:absolute will break layering. Not syncing both renderers to the same camera causes misalignment between wireframes and HTML panels. Failing to call controls.update() each frame breaks trackball. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container ref will cause sizing bugs in partial-page layouts.
accessibilityNotes: Rotating 3D HTML panels can cause vestibular discomfort; wrap animation in a prefers-reduced-motion media query and pause or disable rotation for affected users. Provide a static flat-layout fallback for screen readers since CSS3D-transformed elements may be inaccessible or read out of order. Add aria-hidden to the 3D container and expose content through a separate accessible DOM structure.

technique: CSS3D billboard sprite swarm with animated formation transitions
description: 512 billboard sprite particles animate between four distinct 3D formations—a wave plane, a cube grid, a random scatter, and a sphere—using smooth exponential easing tweens. Ideal for hero sections, product launch pages, data visualization intros, or brand experiences that want a dramatic, kinetic particle display with interactive 3D camera control.
usageNote: Wrap the init and animate logic inside a useEffect with a ref to a container div; return a cleanup that calls renderer.dispose() and removes the DOM element. Replace 'textures/sprite.png' with any hosted PNG (CDN URL or imported asset via Next.js public folder). In React-three-fiber this pattern is harder to port because CSS3DRenderer must overlay the WebGL canvas as a sibling DOM element—manual DOM management in a useEffect is simpler than using R3F here. Ensure the TWEEN update loop and TrackballControls are tied to the same requestAnimationFrame loop.
constraints: CSS3DRenderer composites real DOM elements rather than WebGL geometry, so it must be layered over the WebGL canvas using absolute positioning and pointer-events CSS. Performance degrades on mobile with 512 DOM sprites—consider reducing particlesTotal to 128–256 on small screens. Requires a GPU-composited CSS transform pipeline; older Android browsers may stutter. TrackballControls require a non-passive pointer-event target.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to append the CSS3DRenderer domElement as a sibling to the WebGL canvas with matching absolute positioning causes sprites to be invisible. Not cloning the image element for each sprite causes all objects to reference the same node, breaking layout. Omitting TWEEN.update() in the animation loop stops all transitions. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element dimensions breaks embedded or partial-page use cases.
accessibilityNotes: Respect prefers-reduced-motion by skipping or freezing TWEEN transitions and stopping the formation cycling; offer a static screenshot or CSS background as a fallback. The particle field conveys no semantic information, so add an aria-hidden='true' attribute to the container and provide meaningful text content outside it. Keyboard users cannot interact with the 3D scene meaningfully; ensure no critical site content is embedded inside the canvas layer.

technique: 3D CSS cube of embedded iframe video panels with trackball rotation
description: Four YouTube video iframes are positioned as the faces of a 3D cube that the user can freely rotate and spin in all directions. Ideal for media showcase pages, video portfolio sections, or interactive content hubs where multiple video channels or campaigns need dramatic spatial presentation.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, initialize the CSS3DRenderer and TrackballControls inside a useEffect with a ref-attached container div; return a cleanup function that calls controls.dispose() and removes the renderer DOM element. Replace hardcoded YouTube video IDs with props or CMS-sourced data. Because CSS3DRenderer requires a separate DOM overlay, position it absolutely over a WebGL canvas if mixing renderers, or use it standalone. No local assets to replace.
constraints: CSS3DRenderer composites real DOM elements in 3D space — it does not render to a WebGL canvas, so it cannot be composited with post-processing effects. Iframes are heavy; four simultaneous YouTube embeds may cause performance issues on low-end or mobile devices. Requires a browser that supports CSS 3D transforms. Not suitable for contexts where iframe embedding is blocked (CSP restrictions, YouTube embed policies).
antiPatterns: Forgetting to add a pointer-events blocker div during camera drag will cause iframe elements to intercept mouse events and break rotation. Not disposing TrackballControls on component unmount leaks event listeners. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using a container ref breaks layout in partial-viewport use cases. Mixing CSS3DRenderer with WebGLRenderer without careful z-index and positioning causes rendering order conflicts.
accessibilityNotes: Rotating 3D content can trigger vestibular disorders; honor prefers-reduced-motion by disabling auto-rotation and limiting user-initiated spin speed. Provide a static flat grid of the same video embeds as a fallback. Iframes should have meaningful title attributes for screen readers. Keyboard navigation for the 3D rotation is not supported out of the box and must be added manually.

technique: first-person capsule character controller with octree spatial collision and projectile physics
description: A first-person 3D environment where the user walks, jumps, and throws bouncing balls that collide with geometry using an octree for fast spatial queries. Suits interactive product showcases, virtual tours, gamified onboarding experiences, or browser-based mini-games embedded in a website.
usageNote: Wrap the renderer setup, animation loop, and event listeners in a React useEffect with a canvas ref (or a react-three-fiber Canvas + useFrame). Clean up by calling renderer.dispose(), removing event listeners, and cancelling the animation loop in the useEffect return. Replace the GLTFLoader asset path with a URL served from /public or a CDN (e.g. useLoader(GLTFLoader, '/models/scene.glb') in R3F). The Octree must be rebuilt after the GLTF loads.
constraints: Requires WebGL with shadow map support; VSM shadows and the octree traversal are CPU/GPU intensive so performance degrades on low-end mobile GPUs. The pointer lock API is not available on iOS Safari, making mouse-look non-functional there. Best suited for desktop-first experiences; add a virtual joystick fallback for touch devices.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to remove pointer lock and keyboard event listeners on component unmount causes memory leaks and stale closures. Not rebuilding the Octree after dynamically loading or changing scene geometry will break all collisions. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of the container element's dimensions breaks embedded (non-fullscreen) layouts. Neglecting to dispose sphere geometries and materials when the component unmounts leaks GPU memory.
accessibilityNotes: Pointer lock and WASD controls are inaccessible to keyboard-only and screen reader users; provide an alternative static panorama or image fallback, and honour prefers-reduced-motion by disabling the animation loop or replacing it with a static render. Add an accessible skip/exit button since pointer lock traps input focus. Ensure UI controls (GUI panel) are reachable without a mouse.

technique: synchronized multi-object animation group with shared keyframe state (rotation, color, opacity cycling)
description: A 5×5 grid of cubes all rotate, shift color (red→green→blue), and fade in and out in perfect unison using a shared animation group. Suits hero sections, loading screens, or data visualization backdrops where rhythmic, synchronized 3D elements reinforce brand identity.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, mount inside a useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer targeting the ref element, store the AnimationMixer and RAF id, and clean up with renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame on unmount. With react-three-fiber, use useAnimations or manually drive mixer.update(delta) inside useFrame. No local assets are referenced, so no path replacements are needed.
constraints: WebGL required; no WebGPU fallback. Performance is light (25 meshes sharing one geometry and one material), so mobile is fine. The AnimationObjectGroup pattern scales well to hundreds of objects without per-object mixer overhead. Not suitable for objects that need independent animation states.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call mixer.stopAllAction() and mixer.uncacheRoot() on cleanup causes memory leaks. Not disposing the shared geometry and material when unmounting leaves GPU memory allocated. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using the container element dimensions breaks embedded or partial-page use. Failing to update camera.aspect on resize distorts the scene.
accessibilityNotes: Wrap the canvas in a region with aria-hidden='true' since it is decorative. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or stopping clipAction and mixer updates when the media query matches. Provide a static fallback image or CSS gradient for environments where WebGL is unavailable.

technique: keyframe-animated 3D object with position, scale, rotation, color, and opacity tracks
description: A white cube cycles through smooth keyframe animations — sliding across the scene, scaling up and down, rotating on its axis, and flashing through red, green, and blue while fading in and out. Suits hero sections, product teasers, or interactive onboarding screens that need an eye-catching animated 3D element without external model assets.
usageNote: In React or Next.js, wrap the init logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer with that canvas element instead of appending to document.body, store the animation loop ID and call renderer.dispose() plus cancelAnimationFrame on cleanup. For react-three-fiber, use useFrame with an AnimationMixer ref updated each frame. No local assets are referenced, so no path replacement is needed — all geometry and keyframe data is generated procedurally.
constraints: Very low GPU cost; runs on virtually all WebGL-capable devices including mid-range mobile. Requires WebGL renderer (not WebGPU). The Stats panel import is optional and should be removed for production. Suited for looping ambient animations, not for high-density scenes.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call mixer.stopAllAction() and mixer.uncacheClip() on unmount causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight breaks layout in embedded or portal contexts — always derive dimensions from the container element. Omitting the resize listener causes distorted aspect ratio after viewport changes. Using Euler interpolation instead of quaternion tracks causes gimbal lock artifacts.
accessibilityNotes: Wrap the canvas in a region with aria-hidden='true' since it is purely decorative. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or stopping the AnimationMixer when the media query matches, and providing a static image or CSS fallback. Ensure surrounding text content is accessible independently of the animation.

technique: drag-to-select box selection in 3D scene
description: A 3D viewport filled with randomly placed, colored, and scaled boxes that can be rubber-band selected by clicking and dragging a rectangular marquee. Selected objects highlight in white emissive glow. Suits 3D asset editors, spatial data explorers, product configurators, warehouse or layout planners, and any tool requiring multi-object selection in a 3D canvas.
usageNote: In React or Next.js, wrap all setup in a useEffect with a canvas ref and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes event listeners. Instantiate SelectionBox and SelectionHelper inside the same useEffect after the renderer is created. In react-three-fiber, use useThree to access camera and scene, and attach pointer event listeners via the canvas element ref rather than document to avoid conflicts. No local assets are referenced, so no path substitution is needed.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer; not suitable for CSS2D or SVG renderers. Performs well up to ~500–1000 meshes; beyond that, frustum culling checks in SelectionBox may become expensive. Touch support is partial—pointermove-based selection works on touch but drawing a marquee is unnatural on mobile. Desktop-first pattern.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to remove pointerdown/pointermove/pointerup listeners on document when the component unmounts, causing memory leaks and stale closures. Not disposing shared BoxGeometry and individual MeshLambertMaterial instances on teardown. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of measuring the container element, which breaks when the canvas does not fill the viewport. Attaching events to document instead of the renderer's canvas can intercept events from other UI elements.
accessibilityNotes: The interaction is entirely pointer-driven with no keyboard equivalent for box selection; provide a fallback click-to-select or checkbox list for keyboard users. Add aria-label to the canvas element describing the selectable scene. Screen readers cannot perceive selected objects; expose selection state via a live region (aria-live) announcing the count of selected items. For reduced-motion preferences, the scene itself is static so no animation reduction is needed, but the selection highlight flash could be softened.

technique: interactive 3D model viewer with arcball orbit controls
description: A fully-lit, PBR-rendered 3D object that users can drag to rotate freely in any direction using intuitive arcball (trackball-style) interaction, with smooth momentum and damping. Ideal for product configurators, portfolio showcases, 3D asset previews, or any site section that needs interactive 360-degree model inspection.
usageNote: Wrap the renderer setup, scene, camera, and ArcballControls instantiation inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js. Return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and controls.dispose(). Replace OBJLoader paths with URLs served from /public or a CDN (e.g. /models/myProduct.obj); replace the HDR path with a publicly hosted equirectangular HDR. In react-three-fiber, use @react-three/drei's <OrbitControls> or a custom <primitive> wrapping ArcballControls via useThree.
constraints: Requires WebGL 1 or 2. HDR environment loading adds a noticeable initial network cost; lazy-load or compress to a smaller resolution for mobile. Arcball controls are touch-compatible but complex multi-touch gestures may conflict on low-end Android. GUI overlay (lil-gui) is dev-facing and should be removed in production builds.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call controls.dispose() and renderer.dispose() on component unmount causing memory leaks; not removing the resize and keydown event listeners on cleanup; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of measuring the parent container; leaving the lil-gui debug panel visible in production; not setting renderer.setPixelRatio capped at 2 for performance on high-DPI mobile screens.
accessibilityNotes: 3D rotation controls are not keyboard or screen-reader accessible by default; provide a static rendered image fallback behind a prefers-reduced-motion media query. Add aria-label to the canvas element describing the model. Expose keyboard shortcuts (already partially present via ctrl+c/v state copy) and document them visually. Consider a pause/freeze button for users who experience motion sickness from continuous inertia spin.

technique: interactive 3D drag-and-drop object manipulation with group selection
description: A 3D scene filled with randomly colored, sized, and rotated boxes that users can click and drag freely in space, with shift-click to group-select multiple objects and move them together. Suits interactive product configurators, 3D mood boards, spatial planning tools, gamified onboarding experiences, or creative sandbox sections of a web app.
usageNote: Wrap initialization in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; attach the renderer to the ref instead of document.body. Install drei's DragControls or import directly from three/addons. Clean up by calling controls.dispose() and renderer.dispose() in the useEffect return. Replace the 200 random boxes with your own mesh data (product models, cards, icons as sprites). In react-three-fiber, use @react-three/drei's DragControls component for a declarative approach.
constraints: Rendering 200 shadow-casting meshes is moderately expensive; reduce mesh count or disable shadows on mobile. Requires WebGL (not WebGPU). DragControls conflicts with OrbitControls if both are active simultaneously — disable OrbitControls on drag start. Touch support exists but requires toggling touch mode via keydown (M key), which is desktop-centric and needs reworking for mobile UX.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose geometry and materials when objects are removed, causing memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions, which breaks embedded or partial-page layouts. Not removing event listeners (resize, click, keydown) on component unmount in React. Leaving shadow maps at full resolution on low-end devices. Forgetting to update controls.objects array when the draggable set changes dynamically.
accessibilityNotes: Purely pointer/touch driven with no keyboard navigation for individual objects beyond the shift-select modifier; add ARIA live regions or a companion list UI for screen reader users to understand and manipulate the scene content. Provide a reduced-motion fallback (e.g. a static screenshot or simplified 2D list) when prefers-reduced-motion is set. The M-key touch toggle has no visible affordance — add a UI button for mobile users.

technique: interactive 3D Earth globe with fly-through camera controls and film grain post-processing
description: A photorealistic rotating Earth with cloud layer, moon, and star field rendered in deep space, navigable via first-person fly controls with cinematic film grain overlay. Ideal for space-tech homepages, satellite or aerospace product sites, science education platforms, or dramatic hero sections requiring an immersive space environment.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref: instantiate the WebGPURenderer targeting the ref element, attach FlyControls to it, and run the animation loop inside the effect; clean up with renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame on unmount. Replace all local texture paths (earth_atmos_2048.jpg, earth_specular_2048.jpg, earth_normal_2048.jpg, earth_clouds_1024.png, moon_1024.jpg) with CDN-hosted or /public directory URLs. With react-three-fiber, note that WebGPU renderer support requires using the @react-three/fiber experimental WebGPU branch or a custom renderer prop.
constraints: Requires WebGPU renderer (Chrome 113+, no Safari/Firefox stable support as of 2024); not suitable for mobile devices or low-end GPUs. High texture memory footprint (~8 MB in textures). FlyControls require pointer lock / continuous input, making it unsuitable for passive scroll-driven hero sections without modification. TSL (Three Shading Language) post-processing adds a non-trivial compile step.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call controls.dispose() and renderer.dispose() on unmount causes memory leaks; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks in contained layouts — use the parent container's getBoundingClientRect instead; omitting the resize observer means the camera aspect ratio and renderer size go stale on layout changes; not setting renderer.setPixelRatio can cause blurry output on HiDPI screens; assuming WebGPU availability without a fallback will silently crash on unsupported browsers.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static full-bleed Earth photograph as a CSS background-image fallback for browsers lacking WebGPU or for users with prefers-reduced-motion: stop the animation loop and render a single static frame instead. FlyControls keyboard bindings (WASD) are non-obvious; document them or disable them for decorative-only use. Add aria-hidden='true' to the canvas and supply a visually hidden description of the scene for screen readers.

technique: top-down map navigation with pan, zoom, and orbit controls over instanced 3D city blocks
description: A bird's-eye view of a procedurally generated cityscape of box-shaped buildings that the user can pan, zoom, and orbit using mouse or touch. Suits dashboards, GIS viewers, urban planning tools, real estate platforms, or any site needing an interactive 3D map-style interface.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, wrap the entire init and animate logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref: pass the ref's current element to WebGLRenderer instead of appending to document.body, and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes event listeners. In react-three-fiber, replace MapControls imperatively with the MapControls component from @react-three/drei. No local assets are used, so no path replacement is needed.
constraints: Requires WebGL support; instanced mesh of 500 boxes is lightweight and mobile-friendly. The maxPolarAngle cap prevents going below the ground plane, which is intentional for map-style navigation. Not suitable for purely 2D interfaces or environments where WebGL is unavailable.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call controls.update() inside the animation loop when damping is enabled (causes no smooth deceleration). Not removing the resize event listener on component unmount causing memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of measuring the container element, which breaks embedded/partial-page usage. Failing to call renderer.dispose() and mesh.dispose() on teardown.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static screenshot or image fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion or no WebGL support. The 3D scene is not keyboard-navigable by default; add custom keyboard pan/zoom handlers for accessibility. Include an aria-label on the canvas element describing the interactive map. Screen readers will not perceive 3D content, so pair with a text-based data table or description if content is meaningful.

technique: interactive orbit-controlled 3D scene with inertial camera navigation
description: A freely explorable 3D environment where the user can rotate, zoom, and pan around a scene using mouse drag, scroll, and keyboard, with smooth inertial damping. Ideal for product configurators, architectural walkthroughs, data visualisation dashboards, or any site section requiring interactive 3D exploration.
usageNote: In React or Next.js, wrap initialisation in a useEffect hook with a ref attached to a <canvas> or container div; pass the ref's current element to the WebGLRenderer constructor instead of appending to document.body. Return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose(), controls.dispose(), and cancels the animation loop. With react-three-fiber, replace OrbitControls with @react-three/drei's <OrbitControls> component and configure via props. No local asset paths need replacing in this snippet.
constraints: Requires WebGL 1 or 2; works on all modern desktop and mobile browsers. Mobile touch orbit is supported natively by OrbitControls. enableDamping requires a continuous animation loop; do not use the commented-out static render path with damping enabled. Performance is low-cost due to instanced geometry, but spawning many independent meshes instead of InstancedMesh would degrade frame rate quickly.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call controls.dispose() on unmount causes event listener leaks. Not calling onWindowResize on container resize (only window resize) breaks aspect ratio in embedded canvases. Removing the controls.update() call from the animation loop breaks damping. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of the container element's dimensions breaks layouts where the canvas is not full-screen.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static fallback image or screenshot for users with prefers-reduced-motion enabled by skipping the animation loop and rendering a single frame. Keyboard orbit is enabled via controls.listenToKeyEvents(window) but the canvas element itself should have tabindex='0' and an aria-label describing the 3D scene. Screen readers cannot interpret the 3D content; pair it with a descriptive text alternative or ARIA live region for meaningful content.

technique: first-person pointer-lock navigation with WASD movement and jump physics
description: A fully navigable first-person 3D environment with mouse-look camera control, WASD walking, spacebar jumping, and gravity-based collision detection. Ideal for virtual showrooms, architectural walkthroughs, game-like product experiences, virtual event spaces, or interactive museum exhibits embedded in a website.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer targeting the ref element instead of document.body, attach PointerLockControls to the canvas ref or its parent div, and clean up the animation loop and event listeners on unmount. In react-three-fiber, use @react-three/drei's PointerLockControls component and handle WASD state with useEffect keyboard listeners. No local asset paths to replace in this example.
constraints: Requires WebGL. Pointer Lock API is not supported on iOS Safari, making this unsuitable as the primary navigation on mobile; a fallback touch joystick or alternative view must be provided. High geometry count (500 boxes + large floor) makes this moderate-to-high GPU cost; reduce object count for lower-end devices. Desktop-first pattern.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to remove keydown/keyup event listeners on component unmount causing memory leaks; not calling controls.dispose() on cleanup; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the parent container's dimensions for embedded viewports; leaving the animation loop running after the component unmounts; failing to handle the pointer lock 'unlock' event to restore the overlay UI.
accessibilityNotes: Pointer lock completely hides the cursor and traps keyboard input, which is highly disruptive for screen reader users and keyboard-only navigation; always present a visible, focusable 'Click to enter' overlay and an explicit 'Press Escape to exit' instruction. Provide a reduced-motion or static screenshot fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion. Screen readers cannot access 3D content; include ARIA-described alternative text or a text-based description of the virtual space.

technique: free-rotate 3D scene with trackball camera controls and dual camera modes
description: A fog-filled 3D space scattered with hundreds of geometric shapes that the user can freely rotate, pan, and zoom in any direction using trackball-style drag controls. Ideal for interactive 3D product explorers, data visualization dashboards, CAD-style viewers, or immersive portfolio pieces where unconstrained camera navigation is required.
usageNote: Port into React using a useEffect hook that initializes the renderer on a canvas ref and returns a cleanup function calling controls.dispose() and renderer.dispose(). In react-three-fiber, use the <TrackballControls> component from @react-three/drei instead. Replace instanced cone geometry with your own models or data-driven geometry. No local asset paths are referenced, so no substitution is needed.
constraints: Requires WebGL. TrackballControls allows full 360-degree rotation (no gimbal lock), making it more suitable for desktop use; mobile pinch-zoom and multi-touch roll work but feel less precise on small screens. Instanced rendering of 500 meshes is GPU-efficient but overall scene complexity should still be profiled on mid-range mobile GPUs.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call controls.handleResize() on window resize breaks zoom and pan calculations. Not disposing controls before recreating them when switching camera types causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the canvas container dimensions breaks embedded usage. Omitting controls.update() in the animation loop stops trackball interpolation from working.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static screenshot or poster image as a fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion enabled or when WebGL is unavailable. The interactive 3D canvas is not navigable by keyboard by default; add aria-label and role='img' to the canvas element, and consider providing a separate keyboard-driven camera interface for accessibility compliance. Screen readers will not interpret 3D content.

technique: interactive 3D object transform gizmo with translate/rotate/scale controls
description: A 3D object sits in a grid-floored scene with an overlay gizmo allowing the user to drag handles to move, rotate, or scale it in real time. Ideal for web-based 3D editors, configurators, scene builders, or any tool that lets end users position and manipulate objects in a 3D viewport.
usageNote: Wrap initialization in a useEffect with a canvas ref; assign renderer.domElement to the ref instead of appending to document.body. Clean up with renderer.dispose() and control.dispose() on unmount. With react-three-fiber, use the @react-three/drei TransformControls component which wraps this addon cleanly. Replace 'textures/crate.gif' with any hosted texture URL or a Next.js public-folder path such as '/textures/crate.gif', or swap the material entirely for a plain MeshStandardMaterial color.
constraints: Requires WebGL; TransformControls is not mobile-friendly out of the box as it relies on mouse drag interactions and keyboard shortcuts for mode switching. Performance cost is low for a single object but scales with scene complexity. OrbitControls and TransformControls must share input focus carefully via the dragging-changed event to avoid conflicts.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to disable OrbitControls while dragging the transform gizmo causes both to fight for pointer events. Not calling control.dispose() and orbit.dispose() on unmount leaks event listeners. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks inside fixed-size containers — use the parent element's offsetWidth/offsetHeight instead. Forgetting to call control.attach(mesh) after adding the mesh to the scene results in a visible but non-functional gizmo.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard shortcuts (W/E/R for mode, Q for space toggle, Shift for snapping) are the primary interaction mode but are undocumented in the UI — add visible legends or a help panel. No screen-reader-accessible alternative exists for 3D manipulation; provide a numeric input fallback (position/rotation/scale fields) for accessibility. Add a prefers-reduced-motion check to disable orbit animation auto-updates if continuous rendering is used.

technique: 3D mesh viewer with DRACO compressed geometry export
description: An interactive 3D model viewer with orbit controls and a one-click export button that downloads the displayed mesh as a highly compressed Draco (.drc) file. Suits tools like 3D asset editors, CAD web apps, product configurators, or any platform that lets users create or customize geometry and then save it in a bandwidth-efficient format.
usageNote: Wrap the renderer initialization inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js, attaching the renderer to the ref element instead of document.body. Clean up with renderer.dispose() in the useEffect return. The DRACOExporter is a pure computation utility and works the same way; trigger exportFile via a button onClick handler. No local assets are referenced so no path replacement is needed. In react-three-fiber, use the useThree hook to access gl and scene, then call DRACOExporter.parseAsync(mesh) from a button handler.
constraints: Requires WebGL support; works on all modern desktops and mid-to-high-end mobile browsers. DRACO export is CPU-intensive for very high-polygon meshes and may block the main thread briefly — consider offloading to a Web Worker for production. The DRACOExporter requires the Draco WASM encoder libraries to be available; ensure they are served correctly alongside your build.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose geometry and material when the component unmounts, causing GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container element's dimensions. Not providing the Draco encoder WASM files, which silently breaks export. Triggering export synchronously before the mesh is fully defined. Omitting the animation loop cancellation on unmount.
accessibilityNotes: The 3D canvas is not screen-reader accessible; add an aria-label or visually hidden description of the scene content. The export button should be a real <button> element with a descriptive label like 'Export model as Draco file'. For reduced-motion preferences, the scene is already static (no animation loop movement), so no additional fallback is needed. Provide a static thumbnail or screenshot as a fallback for environments where WebGL is unavailable.

technique: HDR/EXR texture export from WebGL render target or data texture
description: Renders an HDR equirectangular environment as a 360-degree panoramic backdrop with orbit controls, then exports the scene or a procedural normal-map texture as a high-dynamic-range EXR file. Suits creative tools, photography platforms, 3D asset pipelines, or any site that needs to let users capture and download HDR imagery from the browser.
usageNote: Wrap the renderer setup in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js. Replace the HDR asset path with a URL from your public folder or a CDN (e.g. '/textures/environment.hdr'). The EXRExporter and download logic can live in a button onClick handler outside the render loop. For react-three-fiber, use useThree() to get the renderer and gl.domElement, and trigger export via a Zustand/context action.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 for HalfFloatType render targets; not suitable for very low-end mobile GPUs. Exporting large render targets (1024×512+) is CPU-intensive during EXR encoding and can block the main thread briefly. The HDR loader and EXRExporter add meaningful bundle weight (~50KB+). FloatType textures double memory vs HalfFloat.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.setRenderTarget(null) after rendering to the offscreen target will break the main display. Not cloning the camera before adjusting aspect for export distorts the live view. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using a container ref breaks layout in embedded components. Not revoking the object URL after download leaks memory.
accessibilityNotes: The interactive 360 panorama has no keyboard navigation by default; add keyboard event listeners to OrbitControls or expose azimuth/elevation inputs. Provide a visible static fallback image of the environment for users with WebGL disabled or who prefer reduced motion. The export button should be a proper <button> element with an aria-label describing the action.

technique: interactive 3D model slicer and G-code exporter with orbit controls and settings GUI
description: A 3D viewport displaying geometric primitives (cube, cylinder, cone, sphere, torus) on a grid plane with a settings panel for printer, filament, and slicing parameters, plus one-click G-code file export. Suits a browser-based 3D printing preparation tool, CAD/fabrication SaaS product, or maker-focused web app where users need to visualize and export models for FDM printers.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref: initialize the renderer targeting the ref element, store controls and animation frame ID for cleanup. In Next.js, use dynamic import with ssr:false since three.js and the CDN-loaded Polyslice library require the browser environment. Replace the CDN Polyslice import with a local npm install (@jgphilpott/polyslice) if bundling is preferred. The lil-gui panel should be appended to a specific container div rather than document.body to avoid z-index conflicts.
constraints: Requires WebGL and a stable CDN connection for the Polyslice library; slicing large meshes is CPU-intensive and may block the main thread — consider a Web Worker for production use. Not suitable for mobile due to GUI complexity and orbit control UX. Desktop-first pattern. Exporting large models may generate very large G-code files that strain browser memory.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose geometry and material when switching shapes leads to GPU memory leaks. Not handling CDN load failure for Polyslice gracefully will silently break export. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of reading from the container element breaks layout in embedded or split-pane UIs. Omitting the animation loop cleanup (cancelAnimationFrame) in React causes ghost renderers after component unmount.
accessibilityNotes: The canvas provides no screen reader content; add an aria-label and a visually hidden description of the current model and export action. All controls are in the lil-gui overlay which is not keyboard-navigable by default — consider supplementing with native HTML controls for the key actions (shape selection, export button). No reduced-motion concern since the scene is static unless the user orbits; disable auto-rotation if any is added.

technique: in-browser 3D scene to glTF/GLB file export with configurable options
description: A utility scene that lets users export Three.js 3D objects and scenes to standard glTF or GLB files directly from the browser, with controls for texture size, visibility filtering, and binary vs JSON output. Ideal for web-based 3D editors, configurators, or asset pipeline tools where users need to download or save composed 3D content.
usageNote: Wrap renderer setup and export logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref for React/Next.js. The GLTFExporter and file-download pattern (creating a hidden anchor element) is framework-agnostic and can be extracted into a standalone utility function. Replace local texture paths (textures/uv_grid_opengl.jpg, textures/hardwood2_diffuse.jpg) with paths relative to the Next.js /public directory or with imported asset URLs. Replace model paths (models/gltf/ShaderBall.glb) similarly. For react-three-fiber, keep exporter logic outside the R3F render tree and invoke it imperatively via a ref or zustand action.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer with access to texture utilities for KTX2 and compressed texture export. GLB binary export can be memory-intensive for large scenes with high-resolution textures — not suitable for low-memory mobile devices. KTX2Loader requires a transcoder WASM binary served from a public path. Not suitable as a passive visual display; it is a functional tool component.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose the GLTFExporter and revoke object URLs after download, causing memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight without a resize observer. Not handling the async nature of KTX2 transcoding before export. Attempting to export scenes before textures are fully loaded. Neglecting to set the correct colorSpace on loaded textures, which causes incorrect color output in exported files.
accessibilityNotes: The export trigger should be a clearly labelled button with aria-label describing the action (e.g. 'Export scene as GLB'). Provide visible feedback (spinner or status message) during export since it can be slow for large scenes. The download is browser-native and screen-reader accessible if the anchor element has a descriptive download attribute. No motion is involved, so reduced-motion concerns are minimal.

technique: normal-mapped surface export to glTF/GLB with OpenGL vs DirectX convention comparison
description: Two side-by-side flat planes rendered with normal maps under directional lighting, demonstrating surface detail shading without geometry complexity. Suits a 3D asset editor, configurator tool, or content pipeline tool where users need to preview and export textured meshes with correct normal map conventions.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, wrap renderer creation in a useEffect with a canvas ref and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose(). For react-three-fiber, use <mesh> with <meshStandardMaterial normalMap={...}> and the useGLTF or custom exporter hook. Replace the local texture paths (textures/NormalMapOpenGL.png, textures/NormalMapDirectX.png) with paths served from your /public directory or a CDN URL, loaded via THREE.TextureLoader or useTexture in R3F.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer with standard material support; normal maps require a GPU capable of per-fragment lighting. Mobile support is generally fine but performance depends on texture resolution. The GLTFExporter export-to-download flow requires Blob and URL.createObjectURL support, which is unavailable in SSR environments — gate the export logic behind a browser check. Does not require animation loop; renders on demand via OrbitControls change event.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to handle the UV convention difference between three.js (bottom-left origin) and glTF (top-left origin) will produce incorrect normals on export. Not calling texture.dispose() and geometry.dispose() on component unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container ref breaks layout in non-fullscreen contexts. Ignoring the normalScale.y sign inversion when switching between OpenGL and DirectX normal maps causes inverted lighting.
accessibilityNotes: The 3D canvas has no inherent keyboard or screen reader support; add an aria-label describing the preview and provide a static screenshot fallback via a <noscript> or CSS background image. The export button must be a real <button> element with a descriptive label. No animation loop is running so reduced-motion concerns are minimal, but OrbitControls interaction should be suppressible for users who experience motion sickness from camera movement.

technique: KTX2 texture export from WebGL render target or data texture
description: A 360-degree HDR environment viewer with an orbit-controlled camera that can export the current view or a procedurally generated normal map as a compressed KTX2 texture file. Suited for web-based 3D asset pipelines, texture authoring tools, or CMS platforms where users need to capture and download GPU-ready compressed textures.
usageNote: Wrap the renderer, scene, and animation loop inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js, returning a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose(). Replace the HDR asset path with a URL from your own CDN or public folder (e.g. /public/textures/venice_sunset_1k.hdr in Next.js). The KTX2Exporter and HDRLoader imports work fine in ESM environments with an import map or bundler aliases. The export button can be wired to a React onClick handler calling the async exportFile logic directly.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 for KTX2 export support; not suitable for environments that only support WebGL1 or Canvas2D. HDR environment loading adds a network cost; serve the .hdr file from a fast CDN. Mobile support is limited by GPU memory for large render targets and the file download trigger may not work reliably on iOS Safari. The KTX2 export is async and can block the main thread briefly for large textures.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.setRenderTarget(null) after capturing the render target will break subsequent frame rendering. Not cloning the camera and adjusting aspect ratio before exporting to the render target produces distorted output. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container ref breaks layout in React. Not revoking the object URL after download leaks memory. Omitting renderer.dispose() and texture.dispose() on component unmount causes GPU memory leaks.
accessibilityNotes: The 3D scene has no keyboard or screen reader equivalents; provide a visible text description of the tool's purpose. The export button should be a real <button> element with an aria-label. For reduced-motion users, the orbit controls animation loop can be paused and camera updates made only on explicit user input events. Ensure the GUI panel has sufficient color contrast and is keyboard navigable.

technique: interactive 3D geometry viewer with OBJ file export
description: A real-time 3D viewport displaying user-selectable geometry (triangle, cube, cylinder, point cloud) that can be orbited and then exported as a downloadable .obj file. Suits product configurators, 3D asset preview tools, or any web app where users need to inspect and download 3D models.
usageNote: Wrap initialization in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; mount the renderer to the ref instead of document.body. Tear down renderer, controls, and GUI in the cleanup function. OBJExporter and OrbitControls are addons importable via an import map or bundler alias. No local assets are referenced, so no path replacements are needed. In react-three-fiber, use useThree for camera/renderer access and a custom hook for the export button.
constraints: Requires WebGL support; performs well on mobile and desktop for simple geometry counts. Not suited for exporting very high-polygon scenes (millions of triangles) as OBJ serialization is synchronous and will block the main thread. GUI panel (lil-gui) is desktop-first and may need custom mobile UI replacement.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose geometries when swapping shapes causes GPU memory leaks — the example does this correctly but adapters often omit it. Do not hardcode window.innerWidth/innerHeight; use the container element's dimensions instead. Failing to remove the event listener for resize on unmount will cause stale callbacks. Do not skip the animation loop teardown when the component unmounts.
accessibilityNotes: The 3D canvas has no keyboard navigation or screen reader labels by default; add an aria-label and role='img' to the canvas element. The export button should be a real <button> element outside the canvas for screen reader access rather than relying solely on the GUI panel. No reduced-motion concern as the scene is static until the user interacts.

technique: 3D mesh viewer with PLY file export (ASCII and binary formats)
description: An interactive 3D viewer showing a vertex-colored mesh on a grid floor with orbit controls, plus buttons to download the mesh as a PLY file in ASCII or binary format. Suits tool-based web apps, 3D editors, CAD viewers, configurators, or any site that needs to let users export geometry they've created or customized in the browser.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref: initialize the renderer targeting the ref element, run the animation loop, and return a cleanup function that cancels the animation frame and disposes renderer. For react-three-fiber, use useThree to access the scene and trigger exporter.parse() from a button's onClick handler. The PLY export logic is self-contained and needs no local asset paths—just pass the target mesh reference to PLYExporter.parse().
constraints: WebGL renderer required; no WebGPU variant. PLY export is CPU-bound and may be slow for high-poly meshes (>500k vertices) on mobile. Binary export produces smaller files and is preferred for large meshes. OrbitControls require pointer events, which work on touch but may feel less precise on mobile.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose geometry, material, and renderer on component unmount causing memory leaks. Not updating camera.aspect and renderer.setSize on window resize. Creating a new PLYExporter or anchor element on every export call instead of reusing them. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of measuring the container element.
accessibilityNotes: The 3D canvas is not navigable by keyboard or screen reader; add an aria-hidden attribute to the canvas and provide a visible text label or tooltip explaining the export buttons. Export buttons should be real <button> elements outside the canvas with descriptive aria-labels. For reduced-motion, the scene is essentially static (orbit is user-driven), so no special motion reduction is needed beyond stopping any auto-rotation if added.

technique: 3D model viewer with STL file export (ASCII and binary)
description: A lit 3D scene with an orbitable mesh and one-click download buttons to export the geometry as an STL file in either ASCII or binary format. Ideal for e-commerce product customizers, 3D printing prep tools, CAD-adjacent web apps, or any site that lets users build or configure a 3D object and then download it for fabrication.
usageNote: Wrap initialization in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; pass the ref to WebGLRenderer instead of appending to document.body. Move exporter, scene, camera, renderer, and controls into useRef slots so they persist across renders. Clean up with renderer.dispose() in the useEffect return. The export buttons can be wired to onClick handlers on regular HTML/JSX buttons outside the canvas instead of using lil-gui. No local assets are needed.
constraints: Requires WebGL. Export works on all modern browsers via Blob/URL.createObjectURL. Only exports geometry visible in the scene graph (no post-processing effects or shaders). Mobile is supported for viewing but file download behavior on iOS Safari may vary. Performance cost is negligible for simple meshes; large or highly subdivided geometries will produce large STL files and may stall the main thread during parse.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose geometry and material when the component unmounts; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of measuring the container element; not revoking the object URL after download causing memory leaks; assuming STL supports vertex colors or materials (it does not); calling exporter.parse on the entire scene instead of a specific mesh when only partial export is intended.
accessibilityNotes: The 3D viewport is purely decorative/interactive and should have aria-hidden='true' or a visually hidden description. Export buttons must be real focusable HTML elements (not GUI widgets) with descriptive aria-labels like 'Download STL file'. Provide a static thumbnail or model preview image as a fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion or no WebGL support.

technique: 3D model viewer with USDZ AR export for iOS
description: Displays an interactive 3D product model with orbit controls in a neutral lit environment, and generates a downloadable USDZ file so iOS/iPadOS users can view the product in augmented reality via Apple's AR Quick Look. Ideal for e-commerce product pages, automotive configurators, or any site selling physical goods that benefits from AR try-before-you-buy experiences.
usageNote: Wrap in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js. Move renderer initialization and animation loop into the effect, and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the loop. Replace 'models/gltf/CarbonFrameBike.glb' with a URL to your own hosted GLB asset (CDN, public folder, or API route). The hidden anchor element with id='link' should be rendered in JSX with ref forwarding so exportUSDZ() can trigger it. On iOS the GUI is suppressed — ensure the anchor link is visibly accessible instead.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 for KTX2 texture decompression; USDZ export is CPU/memory intensive and may stall on large meshes or mobile devices. DRACO decompression requires the DRACO decoder WASM to be hosted alongside the app (copy from three/examples/jsm/libs/draco/). The AR Quick Look feature only works on Safari on iOS 12+ and macOS with Safari — Android users get no AR benefit from USDZ.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call dracoLoader.dispose() and renderer.dispose() on unmount causing GPU memory leaks. Not hosting the DRACO and KTX2 decoder assets correctly causing silent load failures. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element dimensions, breaking embedded use. Not revoking the object URL created for the blob, causing memory leaks on repeated exports.
accessibilityNotes: The 3D canvas is not keyboard navigable by default — add aria-label to the canvas and provide a static product image fallback for screen readers. For reduced-motion users, check prefers-reduced-motion and skip playing the AnimationMixer clip. The export link should have descriptive text like 'View in AR' and be reachable via keyboard focus, not just triggered programmatically.

technique: animated ray-intersection debug visualizer with helper overlay
description: A horizontal ray sweeps through a row of bouncing, rotating capsule objects, with a visible raycaster helper line and hit markers showing real-time intersection results. Suits developer tools, interactive 3D configurators, or educational sites explaining spatial picking and collision detection.
usageNote: Port to React/Next.js by wrapping all Three.js setup in a useEffect with a canvas ref and returning a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose(). Install @gsimone/three-raycaster-helper via npm rather than using the CDN import. For react-three-fiber, use useFrame for the animation loop and expose the raycaster via drei's useThree hook. No local assets to replace.
constraints: Requires WebGPU renderer support — falls back gracefully only on browsers with WebGPU enabled (Chrome 113+, not Safari or Firefox stable as of 2024). Performance cost is very low due to minimal geometry. Mobile support is limited by WebGPU availability rather than GPU power.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to remove the resize event listener and dispose geometry/material on component unmount. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of measuring the container element, which breaks embedded or partial-page use. Not calling raycasterHelper.update() after updating hits, causing the helper to show stale intersection state.
accessibilityNotes: Pure canvas content with no semantic HTML; add an aria-label to the canvas element describing the visualization. Provide a reduced-motion fallback by pausing the sine-wave animation when prefers-reduced-motion is set. No keyboard or screen reader interaction is possible with the canvas itself.

technique: UV map wireframe debugger for 3D geometry types
description: Renders flat 2D UV unwrap diagrams for multiple 3D geometry primitives (plane, sphere, box, torus, etc.) as canvas elements in a scrollable document. Best suited for internal developer tools, 3D asset pipelines, texture mapping documentation pages, or educational sites explaining how textures are applied to 3D surfaces.
usageNote: In React or Next.js, call UVsDebug inside a useEffect with a ref to a container div, appending the returned canvas elements programmatically. No three.js WebGL renderer or canvas ref is needed since UVsDebug outputs standalone 2D canvases. No local assets to replace. Install three and import UVsDebug from 'three/addons/utils/UVsDebug.js' via an import map or bundler alias.
constraints: This pattern has negligible GPU cost — it uses only 2D canvas, no WebGL renderer. Mobile supported. Not suited for end-user-facing product pages; intended for developer tooling, documentation, or educational dashboards. Does not animate or render a 3D scene.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose geometries after calling UVsDebug (each geometry allocates buffers). Do not wrap this in an animation loop — it is a static diagnostic tool. Avoid calling it repeatedly on geometry updates without cleaning up previously appended canvases, which causes DOM and memory leaks.
accessibilityNotes: No motion involved, so reduced-motion preferences are inherently respected. Each UV diagram should be wrapped in a figure element with a descriptive alt text or aria-label indicating the geometry type for screen readers. Consider adding a text description of UV layout patterns for visually impaired developers.

technique: real-time physics-based destructible object fracturing with Ammo.js
description: 3D structures (towers, a bridge) shatter into convex debris fragments when struck by a projectile fired by the user, with realistic rigid-body physics, shadows, and orbit camera. Suits interactive product landing pages, game portals, demo showcases, or any site section wanting a dramatic 'break through' or reveal metaphor.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate logic inside a useEffect hook with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; mount the renderer onto the ref element rather than document.getElementById. Load Ammo.js via a CDN script tag or dynamic import before the effect runs. The grid texture at 'textures/grid.png' must be replaced with a hosted URL (public folder, CDN, or a plain color MeshPhongMaterial) — swap the textureLoader.load call or remove it entirely. react-three-fiber is not recommended here because Ammo.js integration relies on imperative mutation patterns that conflict with R3F's declarative model.
constraints: High GPU and CPU cost — Ammo.js wasm runs on the main thread; not suitable for mobile or low-end devices. Requires WebGL with shadow map support. Physics world must be stepped every frame, making 60fps mandatory for stable simulation. Minimum 8 MB Ammo.js wasm binary must be loaded before the scene initialises. Not suitable for background decorative use; best reserved for hero or full-screen interactive sections.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call Ammo().then() before creating any physics objects will throw silent errors. Characters are purely decorative so no screen reader content is required beyond a descriptive aria-label on the canvas.

technique: layered additive skeletal animation blending with crossfade controls

Ideal for interactive character showcases, game-like hero sections, virtual avatar builders, or fitness/sports app previews where a character needs to express multiple states at once.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js, and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and mixer removal. Use react-three-fiber with useAnimations from @react-three/drei for a more idiomatic approach. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using the container's bounding rect breaks layout in non-fullscreen contexts. Not disposing the renderer and removing the animation loop on component unmount leads to ghost renders. Skipping THREE.AnimationUtils.makeClipAdditive on additive clips will produce incorrect bone transforms. Failing to call controls.update() after changing camera position leaves the orbit target misaligned.

The 3D canvas has no inherent screen reader content — add an aria-label or visually hidden description of the character and its purpose. technique: inverse kinematics (IK) skinned character with interactive end-effector control

Replace the hardcoded 'models/gltf/kira.glb' path with your own hosted GLTF/GLB asset (e.g. in /public for Next.js, referenced as '/your-model.glb'); the DRACO decoder path must also point to a hosted copy of the Draco WASM binaries (e.g. from a CDN or /public/draco/).
constraints: Requires WebGL with sufficient GPU for cube-camera reflections (6 render passes per frame) and skinned mesh animation; moderate-to-high GPU cost makes it unsuitable for low-end mobile. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container element breaks layout in React. Failing to pause the mirrorSphereCamera update when the sphere is off-screen wastes 6 render passes per frame.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static poster image of the character as a fallback for browsers without WebGL or users with prefers-reduced-motion. The interactive TransformControls are mouse/pointer-only; add keyboard shortcuts or a slider UI to move the IK target for keyboard and assistive-technology users. No meaningful content is conveyed by the animation, so an aria-hidden canvas with a descriptive aria-label on its container is appropriate.

technique: skeletal animation with morph target blending on a 3D character

Return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose(), mixer removal, and cancelAnimationFrame. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element dimensions breaks embedded layouts. Failing to handle the resize event causes camera distortion. technique: massive batched instanced mesh field with LOD, BVH raycasting, and hover highlighting
description: Renders up to 500,000 procedural 3D objects (torus knots) arranged in a vast grid, automatically switching geometry detail based on camera distance and enabling pixel-accurate mouse hover highlighting via BVH-accelerated raycasting. Suits product configurators, data visualization dashboards, generative art portfolios, or any site section needing a dramatic, interactive 3D field of objects at extreme scale.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate block inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref and return a cleanup function that disposes the renderer, geometry, and BVH trees. BVH computation is async and CPU-heavy on first load; show a loading state. Not suitable for low-power or battery-sensitive contexts. Depends on three-mesh-bvh and @three.ez/batched-mesh-extensions as peer dependencies beyond standard three.js.

Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks in SSR and fixed-layout containers — use the canvas parent's clientWidth/clientHeight. Not handling the async init promise means errors are silently swallowed. Skipping raycaster.firstHitOnly = true dramatically degrades pick performance at this instance count.
accessibilityNotes: The canvas is purely decorative at this scale; add aria-hidden='true' to the canvas element. Provide a static hero image fallback for prefers-reduced-motion or when WebGL is unavailable. Hover interactions are mouse-only — add keyboard navigation or a non-canvas UI layer for screen readers. technique: procedural vertex-colored translucent triangle cloud with slow rotation

Provide a static fallback image or a solid background color via CSS for users with prefers-reduced-motion enabled — listen for the media query and either stop rotation or skip the 3D scene altogether. technique: multi-texture triangle particle cloud with per-face integer texture selection
description: Thousands of randomly scattered triangles slowly rotate in a dark foggy void, each face textured with one of several images selected via a GPU integer attribute. Replace the three local texture paths (crate.gif, FloorsCheckerboard, grasslight) with your own hosted images or import them via next/image public folder URLs passed to THREE.TextureLoader.

Rendering 10 000 triangles with a custom ShaderMaterial is moderately GPU-intensive; reduce triangle count on mobile or low-end devices. The flat integer varyings and sampler2D array require a device that fully supports WebGL2, which excludes some older iOS Safari versions (pre-15).

Not setting gpuType: THREE.IntType on the Int16BufferAttribute causes the shader to receive float data instead of integers. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using the canvas container dimensions breaks responsive layouts. Failing to dispose geometry, material, and textures on component unmount causes memory leaks in SPA navigation. Not handling the window resize event breaks aspect ratio after viewport changes.

Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or stopping the animation loop when the media query matches. Provide a static fallback image (e.g. a screenshot of the scene) via a CSS background-image on the container for users with reduced motion enabled or when WebGL is unavailable.

technique: GPU-only procedural triangle field animated via vertex shader with no CPU geometry data

No external assets means instant load, but the shader source must be available at runtime.

Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight breaks in embedded or split-layout contexts — use the container element's dimensions instead. technique: animated color-mapped particle cloud with GPU-native VBO swapping and progressive draw range
description: Renders 300,000 RGB-colored points in a slowly rotating cube formation that gradually reveals itself then resets, with positions morphing between two layouts every 2 seconds. Suits hero backgrounds for data visualization platforms, analytics dashboards, AI/tech product landing pages, or any site wanting a dense, space-like particle universe aesthetic.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate block inside a useEffect with a canvas ref instead of getElementById('container'). Pass the ref's current element to WebGLRenderer's { canvas } option. Return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose(), clears the setInterval, and removes the resize listener. No local asset paths need replacing.

Mobile devices with less than 2 GB RAM or low-end GPUs may drop frames or crash. antiPatterns: Forgetting to clear the setInterval on component unmount causes memory leaks and ghost renders. Not disposing the GLBufferAttribute native WebGL buffers (gl.deleteBuffer) on teardown leaks GPU memory. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions breaks embedded or partial-page usage. Omitting boundingSphere causes frustum culling to incorrectly cull all particles. Normalizing colors incorrectly when adapting the color math will produce a grey or washed-out cloud.

Provide an aria-hidden='true' on the canvas and a visually-hidden description element for screen readers. technique: animated morphing line cloud with vertex colors
description: A dense 3D cloud of 10,000 connected line segments with position-based vertex coloring that slowly rotates and continuously morphs between two random configurations, creating a softly pulsing nebula-like form. Ideal for hero backgrounds on tech, data, or creative agency sites where an abstract, high-density animated visual is needed.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, wrap all THREE construction inside a useEffect with a canvas ref, return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the animation loop. For react-three-fiber, use a <line> primitive with a bufferGeometry that has morphAttributes set and drive morphTargetInfluences via useFrame. No local assets are referenced, so no path replacement is needed. Remove the Stats import in production.
constraints: High GPU cost due to 10,000 line segments plus morph target data; may drop frames on low-end mobile GPUs. Requires WebGL renderer — no fallback to WebGPU or CSS.
