The morph animation requires morphAttributes support, which is standard in WebGL 2 contexts. Not suitable as a foreground UI element due to visual complexity.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() and material.dispose() on unmount causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks in component-scoped canvases — use the container element's dimensions instead. Skipping computeBoundingSphere() can cause the object to be incorrectly culled. Leaving Stats in production adds an unnecessary DOM overlay.
accessibilityNotes: Wrap the canvas in a region with aria-hidden='true' since it is decorative. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or stopping the animation loop and rendering a single static frame. Provide a static fallback image or a solid color background for environments where WebGL is unavailable. No interactive keyboard or focus targets are present.

technique: animated rotating Koch snowflake fractal line art with vertex colors
description: A set of multi-iteration Koch fractal curves rendered as colorful line segments, slowly rotating in 3D space. Suits hero backgrounds, data visualization intros, science or math-themed sites, generative art portfolios, and loading screens.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect that mounts the renderer to a ref'd <div> or <canvas> and returns a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes the event listener. In react-three-fiber, convert the geometry construction into a useMemo hook producing a BufferGeometry with setIndex/setAttribute calls, then use <lineSegments> with <bufferGeometry> and <lineBasicMaterial>. No local asset paths to replace. Remove the Stats import for production.
constraints: WebGL required; not suitable for Canvas2D fallback. Moderate vertex count (fractal depth 4) is fine on mid-range mobile GPUs, but increasing iteration_count to 5+ can spike vertex counts exponentially. Fixed screen-fill layout assumes a full-viewport canvas.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() and material.dispose() on unmount causing GPU memory leaks; not cancelling the animation loop (store the ID from setAnimationLoop or requestAnimationFrame and cancel on cleanup); hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions for embedded use; omitting the resize listener when embedding in a resizable panel.
accessibilityNotes: Add a prefers-reduced-motion media query check and pause or eliminate the rotation animation (set rotation.z to a constant) when reduced motion is preferred. Provide an aria-label on the canvas element describing it as a decorative fractal animation. Supply a static PNG fallback for screen readers or no-WebGL environments via a <noscript> or feature-detection branch.

technique: rotating color-mapped particle cloud (500k points, vertex colors, fog depth)
description: Half a million colored points fill a dark cubic volume, their hues determined by spatial position, slowly rotating against a near-black foggy background. Ideal for hero backgrounds on tech, data, science, or creative agency sites that need a deep, immersive 'universe of data' aesthetic.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, wrap the entire init/animate logic in a useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer with `renderer.domElement` appended to the ref, and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the animation loop. In react-three-fiber, replace with a <Points> component and a useFrame hook for rotation. No local assets to replace—all geometry is procedurally generated.
constraints: 500,000 points is GPU-heavy; expect 30–60 fps on mid-range desktops but significant frame drops on mobile or integrated graphics. Requires WebGL renderer. Reduce particle count to 50,000–100,000 for mobile targets. Not suitable for low-end devices or battery-sensitive contexts without a quality tier system.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and geometry.dispose() on unmount causes memory leaks in SPAs. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container div's dimensions breaks embedded layouts. Omitting the resize listener causes stretched rendering after viewport changes. Using a very large point size on high-DPI screens can tank performance unexpectedly.
accessibilityNotes: Respect prefers-reduced-motion by stopping or drastically slowing rotation (set rotation speed to near zero). Provide a static dark gradient or screenshot fallback for users who cannot run WebGL. The canvas has no meaningful semantic content, so aria-hidden='true' should be applied. No interactive elements require keyboard or screen-reader handling.

technique: rotating volumetric particle cloud with per-particle positional color
description: Half a million colored points fill a large 3D cube volume, rotating slowly through fog to create a dense, galaxy-like or nebula effect. Ideal for hero backgrounds, data visualization intros, science/tech landing pages, or immersive splash screens.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, initialize inside a useEffect with a canvas ref and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the animation loop. Replace the container getElementById lookup with the ref's current value. In react-three-fiber, use a <points> primitive with bufferGeometry and pointsMaterial inside a useFrame rotation hook. No local assets to replace.
constraints: 500,000 points is GPU-heavy; expect 30–60 fps on mid-range desktops and significant battery drain on mobile. Requires WebGL renderer. Reduce particle count to 50,000–100,000 for mobile or low-power targets. Not suitable for WebGL-unavailable environments.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and geometry.dispose() on unmount causes memory leaks in SPAs. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks in component-scoped canvases — use the container's offsetWidth/offsetHeight instead. Skipping the resize listener causes stretching on window resize. Using PointsMaterial size without sizeAttenuation:true may look flat on some viewports.
accessibilityNotes: Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or skipping the rotation animation and showing a static gradient or still frame instead. The canvas is purely decorative and should have aria-hidden='true'. Ensure any overlaid text maintains sufficient contrast against the dark background. No interactive elements require keyboard focus.

technique: animated random triangle field with custom raw GLSL shaders and per-vertex color
description: A field of 200 randomly positioned, semi-transparent, colorful triangles slowly rotating in 3D space, driven by a time uniform passed to custom vertex and fragment shaders. Suits dark-themed hero sections, creative agency landing pages, generative art portfolios, or abstract data-visualization backgrounds.
usageNote: Wrap initialization in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; pass the ref's current element instead of document.getElementById('container'). Move the vertexShader and fragmentShader strings out of <script id> tags and into JS template literals or separate .glsl files imported as strings. Clean up with renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame on unmount. For react-three-fiber, use useFrame for the animation loop and <rawShaderMaterial> with uniforms passed as a ref to avoid re-renders.
constraints: Requires WebGL support; works on all modern desktop and mobile browsers. Performance cost is low — only 200 triangles — making it safe on mid-range mobile. The RawShaderMaterial requires manually writing all GLSL boilerplate (no three.js built-in uniforms like projectionMatrix are auto-injected, they must be declared explicitly in the shader). Not suitable for WebGPU renderer without rewriting shaders.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to declare built-in uniforms (projectionMatrix, modelViewMatrix) manually in RawShaderMaterial shaders — unlike ShaderMaterial, they are not injected automatically. Not disposing geometry and material on component unmount causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container element's dimensions breaks layout in embedded or partial-page canvases. Forgetting to remove the resize event listener on cleanup.
accessibilityNotes: Add a prefers-reduced-motion media query check to pause or skip the rotation animation (set object.rotation.y to a constant and freeze the time uniform). Provide a static dark-gradient CSS fallback as a background behind the canvas for users with WebGL disabled. The canvas has no meaningful content for screen readers, so add aria-hidden='true' to the canvas element and ensure page content is not dependent on the visual.

technique: GPU-selective line segment culling on a 3D sphere with per-vertex visibility buffer
description: Thousands of colored line segments radiate from the center of a slowly rotating sphere, with individual lines toggled visible or invisible in a single draw call using a custom shader attribute. Suits data visualization hero sections, network topology dashboards, scientific visualization portals, or interactive 3D globe headers where elements need to appear or disappear efficiently without re-uploading geometry.
usageNote: Wrap the renderer setup and animation loop in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; attach the renderer to the ref element instead of document.body. Move the inline vertex and fragment shader scripts into template literal strings or separate .glsl files imported as raw strings. Replace Stats.js with a React-compatible perf monitor or omit it. Wire hideLines/showAllLines to React state or button onClick handlers. No local assets to replace.
constraints: Requires WebGL with custom ShaderMaterial support; works on all modern desktop and mobile WebGL-capable browsers. Performance scales with numLat × numLng (default 20,000 lines): moderate GPU cost for geometry upload but very low per-frame draw cost due to single draw call. On low-end mobile, reduce numLat/numLng. Not suitable for WebGPU-only pipelines without porting the shader.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() and renderer.dispose() on component unmount causing memory leaks; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions; neglecting to set geometry.attributes.visible.needsUpdate = true after mutating the array; embedding shaders as DOM script tags (which do not exist in React) instead of JS strings; not removing the resize event listener on cleanup.
accessibilityNotes: The spinning globe is purely decorative; provide a prefers-reduced-motion media query that stops the rotation (set mesh.rotation to a static value and skip the animation loop update). Add an aria-hidden='true' attribute to the canvas. Ensure any overlaid UI controls (hide/show buttons) are keyboard-focusable and labeled. Offer a static fallback image for users with WebGL disabled.

technique: massive randomized triangle cloud with vertex colors and fog depth
description: Half a million randomly placed, individually colored flat-shaded triangles fill a deep 3D cube that slowly rotates, fading into dark fog at the edges. Suits dark-themed hero sections, creative agency homepages, data visualization backdrops, or immersive loading screens where abstract depth and scale are desired.
usageNote: Port into React/Next.js by wrapping the entire init/animate block inside a useEffect with a canvas ref (replace document.getElementById with the ref), returning a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame. In react-three-fiber, move geometry construction into a useMemo hook and attach the mesh to the scene graph declaratively. No local asset paths need replacing — all geometry is procedurally generated.
constraints: Extremely GPU and memory intensive: 500,000 triangles with Float32, Int16, and Uint8 buffer attributes require a discrete or high-end mobile GPU. Not suitable for low-end Android devices or older iPhones. Requires WebGL1 or WebGL2 renderer. Page load will stall during geometry generation on the main thread unless moved to a Web Worker.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() and renderer.dispose() on unmount causes severe memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks fixed-size containers — use the container's clientWidth/clientHeight instead. Not removing the resize event listener on cleanup causes stale references. Generating 500k triangles synchronously on every re-render in React (e.g. outside useMemo) will freeze the UI.
accessibilityNotes: Wrap the canvas in an aria-hidden container since it is purely decorative. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or disabling the rotation animation (set mesh.rotation to fixed values and skip the animation loop). Provide a static dark-gradient fallback image via CSS for users with motion sensitivity or when WebGL is unavailable.

technique: split-screen dual-camera viewport with perspective/orthographic toggle
description: A split-screen 3D viewer that simultaneously renders the same scene from two camera types (perspective and orthographic) side by side, with visible camera frustum helpers showing the field of view. Suits interactive product configurators, architectural visualization tools, technical 3D editors, or educational platforms that need to show the same content from multiple projections at once.
usageNote: Port into React using a useEffect hook with a canvas ref (or react-three-fiber's <Canvas>). Move init() logic into useEffect, attach the renderer to a ref'd div, and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes event listeners. The split-screen is achieved via setScissor/setViewport — preserve this pattern exactly. Remove Stats if not needed in production. No local assets to replace.
constraints: Rendering the scene twice per frame (once per viewport) roughly doubles GPU draw calls — avoid on low-end mobile GPUs or scenes with high polygon counts. Requires WebGL renderer with scissor test support, which is universally available in modern browsers. Not suitable for full-screen single-view layouts without significant restructuring.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call updateProjectionMatrix() after modifying camera properties like fov or far. Not updating both cameras' aspect ratios on window resize causes distortion. Failing to set setScissorTest(true) causes both viewports to bleed into each other. Hardcoding SCREEN_WIDTH/SCREEN_HEIGHT instead of reading from the container element breaks embedded use cases.
accessibilityNotes: The animation loop runs continuously — provide a prefers-reduced-motion media query check to pause or slow the rotation. Add an aria-label to the canvas element describing the 3D scene. The keyboard toggle (O/P keys) for switching cameras should be documented visibly and also exposed as accessible UI buttons for screen reader users.

technique: multi-viewport split-screen array camera grid
description: A single 3D scene rendered simultaneously from a grid of 6×6 camera viewpoints, each occupying a tile of the screen, creating a surveillance-monitor or kaleidoscopic mosaic effect. Suits creative agency hero sections, product showcases, data visualization dashboards, or artistic portfolio headers that need a striking, non-standard layout.
usageNote: Wrap the init logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref (renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ canvas: canvasRef.current })). Return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes the resize listener. In react-three-fiber this pattern is harder to achieve natively; raw Three.js inside useEffect is the recommended approach. No local assets are used, so no path replacement is needed.
constraints: Renders the full scene N×N times per frame (36 sub-cameras at AMOUNT=6), making the GPU cost multiplicative — reduce AMOUNT to 2–4 for mobile or low-end devices. Requires WebGL (not WebGPU). Shadow maps add additional cost; disable them on mobile. Not suitable as a background effect on content-heavy pages due to frame-rate impact.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to update each subcamera's viewport and aspect ratio on window resize causes misaligned tiles. Not disposing the renderer and removing the animation loop on component unmount causes memory leaks in SPAs. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of a container element breaks embedded or partial-page layouts. Leaving AMOUNT at 6 on mobile will tank performance.
accessibilityNotes: The continuous rotation animation should be paused when the prefers-reduced-motion media query is active — check window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') before starting the animation loop or set mesh.rotation deltas to zero. Provide a static poster image fallback for users with JavaScript disabled. The canvas has no semantic content, so add aria-hidden='true' and ensure any overlaid text is in the DOM.

technique: split-screen logarithmic depth buffer comparison with infinite-scale 3D text labels
description: A side-by-side split viewport showing 3D labeled markers spanning microscopic to cosmic scales, demonstrating how a logarithmic depth buffer eliminates z-fighting artifacts across extreme distance ranges. Ideal for technical product sites, scientific visualization tools, or interactive explainers where objects at vastly different scales must coexist in one 3D scene without visual glitching.
usageNote: Wrap in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; instantiate both WebGLRenderer instances inside the effect and attach them to container divs via ref. Replace the FontLoader path 'fonts/helvetiker_regular.typeface.json' by hosting the typeface JSON in your /public folder and referencing it as '/fonts/helvetiker_regular.typeface.json', or fetch it from a CDN. In react-three-fiber, pass logarithmicDepthBuffer prop to <Canvas>. Clean up both renderers and remove event listeners in the useEffect return function.
constraints: Logarithmic depth buffer requires WebGL 1 extension EXT_frag_depth or WebGL 2; supported on all modern desktop browsers but may degrade on low-end mobile GPUs. The dual-renderer split-screen pattern doubles GPU draw calls, making it unsuitable for performance-constrained environments. Not appropriate when you need a single clean viewport without the comparison UX.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and geometry.dispose() for both renderers on unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding SCREEN_WIDTH/SCREEN_HEIGHT to window dimensions breaks in fixed-size containers — use the parent element's clientWidth/clientHeight instead. Failing to update both cameras and renderers on resize leaves one panel distorted. Not accounting for devicePixelRatio causes blurry output on retina screens.
accessibilityNotes: The continuous zoom animation should respect prefers-reduced-motion; pause or disable auto-zoom when this media query matches. Provide a static screenshot fallback for users without WebGL. All informational content is embedded only in 3D text geometry, so screen readers cannot access it — mirror scale labels in an off-screen accessible HTML list. No keyboard interaction is implemented by default; add keyboard controls or ARIA live regions if the scale data is meaningful to the user.

technique: animated clip-plane particle cloud with GPU culling
description: A dense cloud of randomly positioned, colorful triangles that are dynamically clipped by an animated plane, creating a sweeping reveal/conceal effect as geometry appears and disappears over time. Suits sci-fi product landing pages, data visualization intros, or technical portfolio hero sections that need a restrained but dynamic 3D particle effect.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref or use react-three-fiber with a custom ShaderMaterial. Move the vertexShader and fragmentShader content from inline script tags into template-literal strings or separate .glsl files imported via a bundler plugin. Attach renderer to the ref'd canvas element instead of document.body. Clean up with renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame in the useEffect return. No local asset paths to replace.
constraints: Requires the WEBGL_clip_cull_distance WebGL extension (WebGL 2), which is broadly supported in modern desktop browsers but may be absent on some older mobile GPUs. Falls back gracefully via an in-code extension check. Performance cost is low (200 triangles, simple shader). Not suitable as a primary hero on low-end devices without a static fallback.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to check for the WEBGL_clip_cull_distance extension before enabling it will throw a silent GL error. Omitting material.extensions.clipCullDistance = true disables the clip distance output in the vertex shader. Not calling renderer.setSize on window resize breaks aspect ratio. Leaving the animation loop running after component unmount causes memory leaks in React; always cancel the loop and dispose the renderer.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a prefers-reduced-motion media query check; if motion is reduced, pause the animation loop and render a single static frame. Add an aria-hidden='true' attribute to the canvas so screen readers skip it. Supply a brief aria-label or visually hidden description of the section's purpose nearby.

technique: real-time 3D mesh clipping with local and global clipping planes
description: A 3D object is sliced in real time by invisible mathematical planes, revealing its internal cross-section with clean, anti-aliased edges and correct shadow clipping. Suits product configurators, architectural visualizers, medical/scientific data viewers, or any site section that needs to reveal the interior of a 3D model interactively.
usageNote: Wrap the init and animate logic inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref, passing the ref's current element to the WebGLRenderer constructor instead of appending to document.body. Remove Stats and GUI in production or replace with React state/controls. For react-three-fiber, use the `clippingPlanes` prop on materials and set `gl.localClippingEnabled = true` in a useThree effect. No local assets to replace.
constraints: Requires WebGL with clipping plane support (universally available in modern browsers). Shadow map rendering adds moderate GPU cost; lower shadow map resolution for mobile. Not suitable for very low-end or WebGL-1-only devices if alphaToCoverage is critical. Works best as a focused hero or product detail component rather than a full-page background on battery-constrained devices.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to set `renderer.localClippingEnabled = true` when using per-material clipping planes — without this, local planes are silently ignored. Not calling `material.needsUpdate = true` after changing clipping-related material properties at runtime. Hardcoding `window.innerWidth/innerHeight` instead of measuring the container element, causing layout issues in embedded components. Failing to dispose geometry and material on component unmount in React.
accessibilityNotes: The animation (rotation and scale pulse) should be paused or replaced with a static posed frame when the user has `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` enabled. Provide an aria-label on the canvas describing the 3D content (e.g. 'Interactive 3D cross-section viewer'). The interactive controls are mouse/touch only; expose key controls or sliders as accessible HTML inputs alongside the canvas for keyboard users.

technique: multi-plane volumetric clipping with animated convex hull and cylindrical global clip region
description: A 3D grid of instanced cubes is dynamically carved by animated tetrahedral and cylindrical clipping planes, revealing only the intersection volume in real time. Suits product configurators, architectural section-cut visualizations, medical imaging viewers, or any site feature that needs to expose internal structure of a 3D object.
usageNote: Wrap the entire setup in a React useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer targeting the ref element, tear it all down in the cleanup function. Alternatively use react-three-fiber with a custom <ClippingScene> component and useFrame for the animation loop. No local assets are referenced, so no path replacements are needed. Extract the GUI controls into React state and drive them via props for idiomatic integration.
constraints: Requires WebGL with clipping planes support (nearly universal on desktop; mobile WebGL 1 may have issues with clipShadows on some devices). Rendering 125 instanced shadow-casting meshes with multiple clip planes per frame is moderate GPU cost—budget accordingly on low-end mobile. Not suited for WebGPU renderer without porting the clipping plane logic.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose(), geometry.dispose(), and material.dispose() on unmount will leak GPU memory. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks in embedded or resizable containers—use a ResizeObserver on the container element instead. Omitting renderer.localClippingEnabled = true will silently disable all per-material clipping planes. Not updating clippingPlanes array references (mutating in place is required here, not reassigning).
accessibilityNotes: Add a prefers-reduced-motion media query check before starting the animation loop; if reduced motion is preferred, render a single static frame and pause. Provide a descriptive aria-label on the canvas element such as 'Interactive 3D cross-section visualization'. No keyboard navigation is inherent—if OrbitControls are exposed to end users, ensure focus management and document keyboard shortcuts. A static screenshot fallback image should be available for screen readers via a visually-hidden sibling.

technique: multi-plane clipping intersection reveal on nested concentric spheres
description: Three orthogonal clipping planes slice through a stack of colorful concentric spheres, revealing their layered interiors in real time. Suits product configurators, medical/scientific visualization sections, or interactive 'inside look' hero panels where users can explore internal structure.
usageNote: Port into React/Next.js by wrapping all Three.js setup inside a useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer targeting the ref element, set renderer.localClippingEnabled = true (this is essential and easy to forget), and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose(). With react-three-fiber, use the <Canvas> gl prop {{ localClippingEnabled: true }} and place clipping logic in a useFrame hook. No local asset paths to replace. GUI controls can be replaced with React state and onChange handlers wired to the clipPlanes array.
constraints: Requires WebGL with local clipping support (renderer.localClippingEnabled must be true); broadly supported on desktop and modern mobile. Performance is moderate — 15 sphere meshes with DoubleSide rendering and alphaToCoverage adds fillrate cost on low-end mobile GPUs. Not suitable for scenes already pushing triangle budgets. PlaneHelper objects should be removed or hidden in production.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to set renderer.localClippingEnabled = true causes clipping to silently do nothing. Not calling material.needsUpdate = true after changing alphaToCoverage. Using window.innerWidth/innerHeight directly instead of the container element dimensions, which breaks embedded or non-fullscreen layouts. Not disposing geometries and materials on component unmount in React.
accessibilityNotes: The scene is purely decorative/visual; provide a static fallback image for users with prefers-reduced-motion or no WebGL support. Ensure any interactive GUI controls are keyboard-accessible (lil-gui supports keyboard by default) or replace with labelled HTML range inputs. Add an aria-label to the canvas element describing the visualization.

technique: 3D cross-section clipping with stencil buffer cap fill
description: A complex 3D object (torus knot) is sliced open along three adjustable axis-aligned planes, revealing a solid-colored filled interior cap rather than an empty hole. This suits product visualization pages, medical/engineering model viewers, or interactive explainer sections where showing internal structure adds narrative depth.
usageNote: Port to React/Next.js by wrapping all Three.js setup inside a useEffect with a canvas ref, returning a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the animation loop. Alternatively use react-three-fiber with a custom <ClippedModel> component and drei's <Plane> helpers. The renderer must be initialized with { stencil: true } and renderer.localClippingEnabled = true. No local assets are used, so no path replacement is needed.
constraints: Requires WebGL stencil buffer support (renderer must be created with stencil: true); virtually all desktop and modern mobile GPUs support this. Rendering three stencil groups plus shadow maps is moderately expensive — avoid using this for many simultaneous objects or very low-end mobile. Shadow maps add additional GPU cost.
antiPatterns: Forgetting renderer.localClippingEnabled = true will silently disable all clipping. Not clearing the stencil buffer between plane renders (po.onAfterRender calling renderer.clearStencil) causes incorrect cap fill artifacts. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a ResizeObserver on the container div breaks embedding in partial-page layouts. Forgetting to dispose geometry and materials on component unmount causes WebGL context memory leaks.
accessibilityNotes: The rotating animation should be paused via prefers-reduced-motion media query or by exposing a toggle (the params.animate flag already exists for this). Provide a static fallback screenshot for screen readers via an aria-label on the canvas and a visually hidden description of what the model shows. Clipping controls should be keyboard-accessible if exposed as sliders.

technique: animated displacement sphere with per-vertex noise and color-cycling shader
description: A rotating sphere whose surface seethes and pulses via per-vertex displacement driven by sine waves and random noise, with a continuously hue-shifting color and a tiling texture overlay. Suits dramatic hero sections, creative agency landing pages, music/entertainment apps, or any site that needs a living, organic 3D centerpiece.
usageNote: Wrap the init/animate logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref (assign renderer.domElement to the ref instead of appending to a container div). Return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes the resize listener. Replace the vertex/fragment shaders from script tags with template literal strings stored in JS variables. The water.jpg texture must be replaced with a URL-imported asset (e.g., import texUrl from './assets/water.jpg' in a bundler, or a CDN URL); three/addons Stats can be omitted in production. With react-three-fiber, use useFrame for the animation loop and shaderMaterial as a JSX primitive.
constraints: Requires WebGL 1 or higher; works on most modern mobile browsers but the 128×64 sphere with per-frame Float32Array writes is moderately GPU/CPU intensive. On low-end mobile devices, reduce segments/rings (e.g., 64×32) to maintain 60 fps. Not suitable for server-side rendering without a headless GL context.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() and shaderMaterial.dispose() on unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of the container's bounding rect breaks layout inside constrained divs. Mutating displacement every frame without setting needsUpdate=true will silently freeze the effect. Leaving Stats.js visible in production adds unwanted UI overlay.
accessibilityNotes: Respect prefers-reduced-motion by halting the animation loop and showing a static screenshot or a still frame of the sphere. The canvas carries no semantic content so add aria-hidden='true' and place meaningful text content outside it. Provide a visible static fallback (e.g., a blurred screenshot background) for users with WebGL disabled or unsupported browsers.

technique: animated wireframe text with per-vertex color displacement and additive blending
description: 3D bold text rendered as a shimmering, color-cycling wireframe with per-vertex noise displacement that makes the letters appear to vibrate and breathe. Ideal for hero sections, splash screens, loading screens, or brand identity moments on creative agency, portfolio, or tech product sites.
usageNote: Wrap the renderer setup and animation loop in a React useEffect with a canvas ref, returning a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame. For react-three-fiber, use a custom shader material with shaderMaterial from @react-three/drei and a useFrame hook for the per-frame displacement update. Replace the local font path ('fonts/helvetiker_bold.typeface.json') by hosting the typeface JSON in your public/ directory or fetching it from a CDN such as unpkg (e.g. https://unpkg.com/three/examples/fonts/helvetiker_bold.typeface.json). The vertex and fragment shaders must be extracted from inline script tags into JS string literals or .glsl files imported via a bundler plugin.
constraints: Requires WebGL with shader support (ShaderMaterial); not suitable for WebGL-unavailable environments. Per-frame updates to a Float32BufferAttribute across potentially thousands of vertices can be CPU-intensive—consider capping text complexity (curveSegments, bevelSegments) on mobile. The effect relies on additive blending and transparency, so it performs best on dark backgrounds. Mobile GPU performance may degrade with very large or complex geometry.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call attributes.displacement.needsUpdate = true each frame will freeze the vibration effect. Not disposing geometry and material on component unmount causes GPU memory leaks in SPAs. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of the container element's dimensions breaks layout in non-fullscreen contexts. Omitting camera aspect ratio update on resize produces distorted text. Neglecting to handle the async font load (scene added before font resolves) causes a blank canvas.
accessibilityNotes: This is a purely decorative animated element; provide a static text alternative via an aria-label or visually hidden <h1> so screen readers convey the text content. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or skipping the animation loop (check window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')) and optionally showing a static snapshot of the text instead. Do not rely on this animation to convey critical information.

technique: animated pulsing particle cloud with per-particle size oscillation and custom shader coloring
description: A dense cloud of 100,000 glowing spark particles slowly rotating in 3D space, with individual particles pulsing in size over time and colored in a warm-to-cool gradient split by position. Ideal for hero backgrounds on tech, creative agency, data visualization, or immersive marketing sites.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, wrap the entire init/animate logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref, pass the ref element to the WebGLRenderer constructor instead of appending to a container div, and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame. Inline the vertex and fragment shader strings as JS template literals rather than reading from script tags via document.getElementById. Replace the local spark texture path with a CDN-hosted sprite, a base64-encoded data URI, or a static asset served from your /public folder.
constraints: Rendering 100,000 points with a custom ShaderMaterial and per-frame attribute updates is GPU-intensive; reduce the particle count to 20,000–40,000 for mid-range mobile devices. Requires WebGL (not WebGL2 exclusive, but WebGL must be available). The additive blending and transparent flag make overdraw expensive on low-end GPUs. Not suitable for pages requiring critical above-the-fold performance budgets without lazy-loading or a reduced-particle fallback.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call attributes.size.needsUpdate = true each frame will break the animation. Hardcoding WIDTH/HEIGHT at module load time instead of reading window dimensions inside the resize handler causes layout bugs on orientation change. Not disposing the BufferGeometry and ShaderMaterial on component unmount causes GPU memory leaks in SPAs. Leaving the Stats panel in production builds exposes internal frame-rate UI to end users.
accessibilityNotes: Check prefers-reduced-motion media query and either stop the animation loop or render a static single frame when it is set. Provide a static fallback image (e.g. a screenshot of the particle field) for environments where WebGL is unavailable. The canvas element should have aria-hidden='true' and role='presentation' since it conveys no semantic content; place meaningful page headings and text outside the canvas so screen readers ignore the visual effect entirely.

technique: custom-attribute billboard particle cloud with depth-sorted transparency and per-vertex animated sizes
description: A slowly rotating 3D point cloud shaped as a sphere and inner cube, where each particle is a textured disc billboard with individually animated sizes and HSL-gradient coloring. Suits hero backgrounds for tech products, data visualization platforms, science or space-themed sites, or any brand wanting an abstract, living 3D presence.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate block in a React useEffect with a canvas ref, assign the renderer to the ref's current element, and return a cleanup that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the animation loop. Replace 'textures/sprites/disc.png' with an imported asset (e.g. import discUrl from './disc.png' in Vite/Next.js with next/image asset handling, or store it in /public and reference '/disc.png'). The vertex and fragment shaders must be inlined as template-literal strings rather than read from <script> tags in the DOM. In react-three-fiber, use <points> with a custom shaderMaterial and useFrame for the animation loop.
constraints: Requires WebGL with shader support; not compatible with WebGPU renderer without porting shaders. The per-frame depth sort (sortPoints) is O(n log n) CPU work every frame — keep particle count under ~5 000 for smooth 60 fps on mid-range mobile. On low-end or thermal-throttled mobile GPUs transparent point sprites can be costly; consider disabling depth sorting or reducing segments/rings. Needs a disc texture asset to be bundled or hosted.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() and material.dispose() on unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding WIDTH/HEIGHT at module load time instead of reading from the container element breaks SSR and dynamic layouts. Omitting 'needsUpdate = true' on the size attribute stops animation. Leaving shader code in HTML <script> tags rather than inlining as strings will break in component-based frameworks. Forgetting to remove the resize event listener on cleanup will fire on stale renderer instances.
accessibilityNotes:
Add a prefers-reduced-motion media query check; if true, freeze sphere.rotation and skip the size animation loop, rendering a single static frame. Provide an aria-hidden='true' on the canvas and a visually hidden descriptive

for screen readers. Consider a static fallback image for users with no WebGL support detected via a try/catch on WebGLRenderer construction.

technique: custom-attribute particle cloud with billboard sprites and alpha-tested texture
description: Tens of thousands of glowing ball-sprite particles form a slowly rotating cube wireframe outline with a dense inner particle cloud, using per-particle color gradients and variable sizes. Ideal for hero backgrounds on tech, data, or creative agency sites that need an immersive, high-density 3D ambient effect.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref: create renderer targeting the ref element, return a cleanup that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the animation loop. For react-three-fiber, use <Points> with a custom ShaderMaterial and Float32BufferAttribute setup inside a useFrame hook. The ball.png sprite must be replaced with a self-hosted asset (e.g. /public/textures/ball.png in Next.js) or a base64-encoded data URI; the vertex and fragment shaders must be moved from inline <script type='x-shader'> tags into JS template literals or imported GLSL files.
constraints: High GPU cost: ~100k+ points with a custom shader per frame. Not suitable for mid-range or low-end mobile GPUs. Requires WebGL 1 or higher. Should be gated behind a performance check (navigator.hardwareConcurrency, deviceMemory) or disabled on mobile breakpoints. Degrades gracefully if WebGL unavailable but needs a fallback branch.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose geometry, material, and texture on component unmount causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/HEIGHT breaks SSR in Next.js — use the container element's dimensions instead. Omitting the resize event listener cleanup causes stale closures. Inlining shader code in HTML script tags breaks in JSX; shaders must be JS strings or imported modules.
accessibilityNotes: Respect prefers-reduced-motion by stopping rotation or replacing with a static screenshot fallback. The canvas has no semantic content, so add aria-hidden='true' and role='presentation'. Ensure any foreground text above the canvas meets contrast requirements independently of the animation. No keyboard interaction required since this is a purely decorative background.

technique: interactive decal projection onto 3D mesh surface via raycasting
description: Users click on a 3D model to splatter textured decals (stickers, stamps, paint splashes, bullet holes, graffiti) that conform to the surface geometry. Ideal for product customization tools, avatar editors, game item painters, or interactive storytelling experiences where users apply markings to a 3D object.
usageNote: Wrap initialization in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; attach the renderer to the ref instead of document.getElementById. Use react-three-fiber's useLoader for GLTFLoader and useTexture for decal textures. Replace all local asset paths (textures/decal/*, models/gltf/LeePerrySmith/*) with your own CDN-hosted or /public-folder assets. DecalGeometry must be imported from three/addons and will need to be re-exported or shimmed if using r3f. The decal array should be stored in a React ref to avoid stale closure issues during disposal.
constraints: Requires WebGL with polygon offset support (broadly available). Each decal adds a new draw call and geometry allocation, so hundreds of decals will degrade performance, especially on mobile GPUs. The source mesh must have sufficient polygon density for decals to conform accurately to surface normals. Not suitable for flat/2D UI contexts. Mobile touch events work but pointer event handling may need adaptation.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() and material.dispose() on removed decals causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks in embedded or multi-panel layouts — use container element dimensions instead. Not updating the renderer pixel ratio on resize leads to blurry output on high-DPI screens. Reusing the same DecalGeometry instance instead of creating a new one per click will produce incorrect results.
accessibilityNotes: The interaction is entirely pointer/mouse driven with no keyboard or screen reader equivalent. Provide a static preview image of the decorated model as a fallback for users who cannot interact. Add aria-hidden to the canvas and expose a text description of the customization state. For reduced-motion preferences, consider disabling rotation animation but the core click-to-place mechanic itself is not motion-heavy.

technique: depth texture readback with post-processing pass
description: Renders a scene into an offscreen render target, then reads back the depth buffer as a texture to drive a full-screen post-processing shader — enabling depth-based effects like fog, depth-of-field halos, or X-ray outlines. Suits interactive product viewers, sci-fi dashboards, or any site section that needs cinematic depth-aware visual FX.
usageNote: Port into React/Next.js using a useEffect with a canvas ref: instantiate WebGLRenderer against the ref, set up the render loop with requestAnimationFrame inside useEffect, and clean up via the returned destructor. In react-three-fiber use a useFrame hook inside a custom EffectComposer-style component, or use drei's RenderTexture. Replace the inline script-tag shaders (#post-vert, #post-frag) with JS template-literal strings passed directly to ShaderMaterial. No local assets to replace.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 for DepthTexture support (FloatType depth especially); not supported on some older mobile GPUs. MSAA samples >0 further limits compatibility. Medium–high GPU cost due to double render pass. Not suitable for low-end mobile or battery-sensitive contexts. WebGPU renderer requires separate adaptation.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call target.dispose() when the component unmounts or when render target params change (causes GPU memory leaks). Not updating target.setSize() on window resize (creates blurry or mismatched depth). Hardcoding window.innerWidth/Height instead of the canvas container size. Placing shader code in DOM script tags instead of JS strings when bundling. Failing to update camera near/far uniforms if the camera is modified after init.
accessibilityNotes: This is a purely decorative rendering effect. Wrap it in a prefers-reduced-motion media query and skip or simplify the animation loop (e.g. render a single static frame) when reduced motion is preferred. Provide an aria-hidden canvas and a meaningful text or image fallback in a noscript or visually-hidden element. No interactive keyboard targets are present, so no focus management is needed.

technique: anaglyph stereo 3D effect with animated reflective sphere field and mouse parallax
description: A field of hundreds of reflective spheres orbiting in 3D space rendered with red-cyan anaglyph stereo separation, creating a classic 3D-glasses effect. Suits immersive landing pages, retro-futuristic brand experiences, science or technology promotional sites, or any hero section meant to evoke depth and spectacle.
usageNote: Wrap initialization in a useEffect hook with a canvas ref; append renderer.domElement to the ref instead of document.body. Replace the cube texture paths (textures/cube/pisa/*.png) with your own hosted HDR or cube map images — use CubeTextureLoader with absolute URLs or import them via your bundler. AnaglyphEffect wraps the renderer, so pass the renderer instance to it after creation. Clean up by calling renderer.dispose() and effect removal in the useEffect return function.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer; the anaglyph effect doubles the render passes (once per eye), roughly doubling GPU cost. Not suitable for low-end mobile devices or pages where performance budget is tight. Requires users to have red-cyan 3D glasses for the stereo depth effect to work, otherwise it appears as a colour-shifted scene. Not meaningful without those glasses for typical web visitors.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call effect.setSize on resize instead of renderer.setSize — the AnaglyphEffect owns the output size. Not disposing the renderer and geometry on component unmount causing memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of measuring the container element, which breaks embedded or partial-viewport layouts. Leaving the animation loop running after component unmount by not cancelling the animation frame.
accessibilityNotes: The red-cyan colour shift makes text or UI overlaid on this scene nearly unreadable; avoid placing content over it. Users with colour vision deficiencies (particularly red-green colour blindness) will see little to no stereo effect. Provide a reduced-motion fallback that disables the animation loop and shows a static screenshot or simpler background. The scene has no semantic content, so ensure the canvas has aria-hidden='true' and that any meaningful page content is in the DOM separately.

technique: real-time ASCII art post-processing effect on animated 3D scene
description: A 3D scene rendered entirely as animated ASCII characters — a bouncing, rotating sphere cast in text art on a black background. Suits retro-themed landing pages, creative agency hero sections, developer portfolios, or nostalgic branding experiences that want a lo-fi, hacker-aesthetic visual.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, wrap setup in a useEffect with an empty dependency array; attach the AsciiEffect's domElement (a div, not a canvas) to a container ref via containerRef.current.appendChild(effect.domElement). Store renderer, effect, and controls in refs to survive re-renders. Clean up with renderer.dispose() and effect.domElement.remove() in the useEffect return. No local assets to replace. react-three-fiber is not recommended here since AsciiEffect operates on the raw renderer outside R3F's render pipeline.
constraints: ASCII post-processing is CPU/DOM intensive because it writes large amounts of styled text nodes every frame; avoid on low-end mobile or battery-sensitive contexts. Requires WebGL renderer as the underlying render source. Not suitable for pixel-perfect UI overlays. Works best at moderate resolutions — very large viewports dramatically increase DOM node count.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to append effect.domElement instead of renderer.domElement causes a blank screen. Attaching TrackballControls to renderer.domElement instead of effect.domElement breaks pointer interaction. Not calling effect.setSize on resize causes misaligned ASCII output. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks embedded or partial-viewport usage — use the container element's dimensions instead.
accessibilityNotes: The ASCII output is a div of text characters with no semantic meaning; add aria-hidden='true' to effect.domElement and provide a visually-hidden descriptive alternative. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or disabling the animation loop and showing a static ASCII frame instead. The text characters are not screen-reader meaningful. Ensure sufficient color contrast between character color and background (white-on-black passes WCAG AA).

technique: parallax barrier autostereoscopic 3D effect with animated sphere field
description: Renders a field of hundreds of reflective spheres orbiting through a panoramic environment, split into left/right eye views via a parallax barrier effect that creates glasses-free 3D depth on compatible lenticular displays. Best suited for kiosk installations, digital signage, product showcase displays, or experimental immersive landing pages targeting autostereoscopic hardware.
usageNote: In React or Next.js, wrap all setup in a useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer targeting the ref element, instantiate ParallaxBarrierEffect wrapping it, store the animation loop ID for cleanup, and call effect.dispose() on unmount. Replace the local cube texture paths (textures/cube/pisa/) with your own CDN-hosted cube map images (six faces: px, nx, py, ny, pz, nz) passed to CubeTextureLoader. In react-three-fiber, this effect is harder to integrate natively and vanilla three.js with useEffect is strongly preferred.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer; ParallaxBarrierEffect is only visually meaningful on physical parallax barrier / lenticular displays — on standard monitors it produces a split double-image artifact. Rendering two eye views per frame roughly doubles GPU cost. Not suitable for mobile-first or general-audience web pages. Desktop only with specific hardware for true effect.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose the renderer and effect on component unmount causing memory leaks; hardcoding window.innerWidth/Height instead of using container element dimensions; not updating camera.aspect and effect.setSize together on resize; expecting the 3D effect to be visible on non-lenticular monitors without explanation to users.
accessibilityNotes: Continuous camera animation based on mouse movement can cause vestibular discomfort; respect prefers-reduced-motion by disabling mouse-tracking movement and freezing sphere orbits. Provide a static fallback image for users who cannot view 3D content. No keyboard interactivity is present; add aria-hidden to the canvas and surface key content through normal DOM elements.

technique: side-by-side stereo 3D split-screen with animated refractive sphere field
description: The screen is split into two mirrored viewports showing a field of glassy, refracting spheres orbiting through a 360° panoramic skybox environment, producing a stereoscopic 3D effect compatible with VR cardboard viewers or anaglyph glasses. Ideal for immersive landing pages, VR product previews, science/space-themed hero sections, or entertainment sites targeting headset or cardboard viewer users.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, initialize inside a useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer targeting the ref element, instantiate StereoEffect wrapping that renderer, and run the animation loop with renderer.setAnimationLoop or a requestAnimationFrame ref cleaned up on unmount. Replace the local cube texture path (textures/cube/Park3Med/) with publicly hosted HDR or cube-map images (e.g. via CDN or placed in /public in Next.js) and pass the full URL to CubeTextureLoader.setPath(). In react-three-fiber, StereoEffect must be applied outside R3F's render pipeline as a post-processing wrapper around the vanilla renderer.
constraints: Requires WebGL; the split-screen stereo effect halves horizontal resolution, so it looks best on high-DPI wide displays. Performance cost is moderate-to-high due to the scene being rendered twice per frame plus 500 animated meshes with environment mapping. Not suitable for low-end mobile GPUs. No AR/VR API dependency — works with passive cardboard viewers only.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call effect.setSize() on resize (not renderer.setSize) breaks the split layout. Calling renderer.setSize instead of effect.setSize causes misaligned stereo. Not disposing CubeTexture and geometry on unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/Height breaks in SSR (Next.js) — guard with typeof window !== 'undefined'. Neglecting to update camera.aspect on resize causes distorted perspective.
accessibilityNotes: The constant orbital animation and split-screen flicker can trigger motion sickness or vestibular disorders — provide a reduced-motion fallback that pauses animation and shows a single static viewport (remove StereoEffect, freeze the animation loop). Add an aria-hidden='true' on the canvas and provide a meaningful text or image alternative for screen readers. No keyboard interaction is present; if mouse parallax is kept, ensure an equivalent touch/gyroscope path is available for mobile VR use.

technique: framebuffer texture capture with dual-scene HUD overlay
description: A rainbow-animated Gosper space-filling curve rotates in 3D while a live framebuffer snapshot of the scene center is captured each frame and displayed as a picture-in-picture thumbnail in the corner. Suits creative agency homepages, data visualization dashboards, or interactive art portfolio sections that need a dynamic self-referential preview or minimap effect.
usageNote: Wrap all init and animate logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref; pass the ref's current element to WebGLRenderer instead of appending to document.body. Tear down with renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame in the cleanup return. In react-three-fiber this pattern is harder to replicate natively because r3f owns the render loop; use useThree to access gl and manually call copyFramebufferToTexture inside a useFrame callback, maintaining a separate orthographic scene via a second <Canvas> or a manual scene ref. No local assets are needed.
constraints: Requires WebGL1 or WebGL2 renderer with framebuffer read-back support; copyFramebufferToTexture is not available in WebGPU renderer. The DynamicDrawUsage color buffer and per-frame full color update are CPU-intensive and scale poorly with vertex count. Mobile support is functional but the high dpr textureSize (128 * devicePixelRatio) may be large on 3× screens. Not suitable for environments that block readback (e.g., certain privacy-hardened browsers).
antiPatterns: Forgetting to set renderer.autoClear = false causes the orthographic overlay to erase the 3D scene before readback. Not updating both camera projection matrices on resize breaks the HUD alignment. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container element breaks layout in embedded components. Forgetting to call colorAttribute.needsUpdate = true stalls color animation. Failing to dispose the FramebufferTexture and geometry on unmount leaks GPU memory.
accessibilityNotes: The continuous rainbow color animation and rotating curve may trigger photosensitive reactions; provide a prefers-reduced-motion media query that pauses the animation loop or replaces it with a static screenshot. The canvas has no semantic role; add aria-hidden='true' and provide a text description or static fallback image for screen readers. The color-only encoding of the curve data is not distinguishable for users with color vision deficiency; consider adding a shape or contrast-based fallback.

technique: PBR material matrix grid — roughness/metalness parameter sweep with uniform environment lighting
description: An 11×11 grid of spheres arranged across a neutral grey background, each sphere varying in roughness (X axis) and metalness (Y axis) using physically-based materials — creating a visual material selector or swatch chart. Ideal for product configurators, material library showcases, or design-system documentation pages.
usageNote: Wrap renderer creation and the Promise chain inside a useEffect hook with a canvas ref as the mount target; replace document.body.appendChild with ref.current.appendChild. In react-three-fiber, map the grid with <mesh> components using MeshPhysicalMaterial props driven by state. The scene generates its own flat-colour PMREM environment at runtime so no external HDR asset is needed — replace the grey Color with any brand colour.
constraints: Rendering 121 MeshPhysicalMaterial spheres is GPU-intensive; target mid-range desktop hardware. Mobile performance will degrade significantly — consider reducing grid size (e.g. 6×6) or switching to MeshStandardMaterial. Requires WebGL2-capable renderer. Not suitable for low-end or legacy devices.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call pmremGenerator.dispose() after generating the radiance map causes GPU memory leaks. Not removing the resize event listener on component unmount causes stale closures. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of measuring the container div breaks embedded layouts. Neglecting renderer.dispose() and geometry.dispose() on unmount leaks resources in React strict mode.
accessibilityNotes: The scene is purely decorative/informational; add an aria-label on the canvas describing it as a material properties chart. Provide a static screenshot fallback via a <noscript> image or a CSS background for users with reduced-motion preferences or when WebGL is unavailable. The GUI toggle for tint visibility should also be exposed as a labelled checkbox in the DOM for screen reader access.

technique: rotating 3D geometry showcase grid with orbiting camera
description: A top-down grid of diverse 3D shapes (spheres, cubes, toruses, Klein bottles, Möbius strips, and more) all spinning in unison while the camera orbits around them in a slow circle. Suits a creative agency hero section, a 3D tool or library landing page, or an interactive 'capabilities' showcase that communicates depth and technical sophistication.
usageNote: Port into React/Next.js by moving all init logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref: assign renderer.domElement to the ref, call renderer.setAnimationLoop inside the effect, and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame. With react-three-fiber, map each THREE.Mesh to a <mesh> component and use useFrame for the rotation and camera orbit. Replace the local UV grid texture ('textures/uv_grid_opengl.jpg') with a public URL, a Next.js public folder path ('/textures/uv_grid_opengl.jpg'), or a procedural MeshNormalMaterial/MeshStandardMaterial to avoid the asset dependency entirely.
constraints: Rendering ~16 distinct meshes simultaneously is moderate GPU cost; acceptable on mid-range desktop and modern mobile but the Phong material plus anisotropic filtering may struggle on low-end Android devices. Requires WebGL (not WebGL2-only). ParametricGeometry add-on must be explicitly imported. Not suitable for contexts where bundle size is tightly constrained without tree-shaking the unused geometries.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() and material.dispose() on unmount causes GPU memory leaks in single-page apps. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container element's clientWidth/clientHeight breaks embedded or partial-page layouts. Not removing the resize event listener on cleanup leads to stale closures. Leaving Stats.js panel visible in production. Applying the same shared material mutably across all meshes without cloning can cause unexpected side effects if any mesh later needs individual material properties.
accessibilityNotes: The continuous camera orbit and per-mesh rotation are persistent motion; wrap the animation loop in a prefers-reduced-motion media query check and pause or stop rotation/orbit for users who opt out. Provide a static poster image or CSS fallback background for screen readers and environments where WebGL is unavailable. The canvas has no semantic content, so add aria-hidden='true' and ensure any surrounding text conveys the page's message independently.

technique: vertex-colored polyhedra trio with mouse parallax and fake soft shadow
description: Three low-poly icosahedra with per-vertex gradient coloring (rainbow HSL, monochromatic, and warm orange) sit above soft radial shadow discs and rotate in response to mouse movement, giving a tactile, geometric feel. Ideal for creative agency hero sections, design portfolio backdrops, or data-visualization product landing pages that want vivid, interactive 3D geometry without photorealistic assets.
usageNote: Wrap init/animate in a useEffect with a canvas ref and append renderer.domElement to that ref instead of getElementById('container'). Return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes event listeners. In react-three-fiber, map each mesh to a <mesh> with a bufferGeometry whose color attribute is set programmatically; use useFrame for the camera parallax logic. No external asset paths need replacing—all geometry and textures are generated procedurally at runtime.
constraints: Requires WebGL 1 or higher; works on virtually all modern desktop and mobile GPUs. Three simultaneous icosahedra with wireframe overlays are lightweight (moderate vertex count). Mobile performance is good but the mouse-parallax effect should be adapted to touch events (touchmove) for mobile UX. Not suitable for contexts requiring WebGPU-only renderers without adaptation.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose all three cloned geometries and their wireframe meshes on unmount causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks SSR in Next.js—use the container element's dimensions instead. Omitting the resize handler causes the aspect ratio to desync. Sharing the same material instance across all three meshes would break independent coloring—each geometry needs its own color attribute.
accessibilityNotes: Add a prefers-reduced-motion media query check; if active, stop the animation loop and render a single static frame. Provide a visually equivalent static PNG fallback as a <noscript> or CSS background for screen readers and JS-disabled environments. The canvas has no inherent semantic content, so add aria-hidden='true' and place meaningful text content outside the canvas in the DOM.

technique: 3D mesh with data-driven vertex color mapping using a lookup table (LUT) and color legend sprite
description: A 3D mesh whose surface is colored by a scalar data attribute (e.g. pressure, temperature, stress) using a gradient color map (rainbow, cool-to-warm, blackbody, grayscale), with a color legend bar overlaid in screen space. Suits scientific dashboards, engineering analysis tools, medical visualization apps, or any data-rich product that needs to communicate spatial variation of a quantity across a 3D surface.
usageNote: Wrap initialization in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; assign renderer.domElement to the ref instead of appending to a container div. Replace the BufferGeometryLoader call pointing to 'models/json/pressure.json' with your own geometry source (fetch from an API, import a local asset via Next.js public folder, or use a generated procedural geometry). The LUT and vertex coloring logic is self-contained and portable. Use react-three-fiber if you want declarative scene management, but the Lut addon works fine in vanilla mode inside a useEffect.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer with vertex color support (universally available in modern browsers). Moderate GPU cost scales with mesh vertex count. The dual-scene (3D + orthographic UI overlay) pattern with renderer.autoClear = false requires careful render order management. Not suitable for very low-end mobile GPUs with extremely high-polygon meshes. The color legend sprite requires a CanvasTexture, which is supported everywhere.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() and material.dispose() on unmount, causing GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions. Forgetting to set colors.needsUpdate = true after modifying vertex colors. Neglecting to update the orthographic camera's frustum if the canvas aspect ratio changes. Assuming the external JSON model path exists — it must be replaced with a valid asset.
accessibilityNotes: The visualization conveys data purely through color, which is inaccessible to color-blind users; provide an alternative data table or allow color map selection including accessible palettes. Add an aria-label to the canvas element describing the dataset. For reduced-motion preferences, the OrbitControls interaction is user-initiated so it is acceptable, but auto-rotation (if added) should be disabled via a prefers-reduced-motion media query check. Provide a static image fallback (e.g. a screenshot of the default view) for screen readers or environments where WebGL is unavailable.

technique: convex hull mesh with orbiting point cloud
description: A semi-transparent 3D convex hull wraps a set of glowing point vertices, slowly auto-rotating while the user can orbit around it. Suits data visualization dashboards, molecular/scientific product pages, or abstract hero sections for tech or SaaS brands.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, initialize the renderer inside a useEffect with a canvas ref and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the animation loop. For react-three-fiber, replace with <ConvexGeometry> via drei or a custom geometry hook. Replace 'textures/sprites/disc.png' with a publicly hosted disc sprite (e.g. from your /public folder) or generate a circular sprite procedurally on a canvas element to eliminate the external asset dependency.
constraints: Requires WebGL support; ConvexGeometry uses a convex hull algorithm (O(n log n)) so it suits small-to-medium vertex counts (<5000 points). Generally performant on mid-range mobile but OrbitControls touch handling may need tuning. Not suited for very low-end devices without simplifying vertex counts.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and geometry.dispose() on unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of measuring the container element breaks layout inside fixed panels or sidebars. Not removing the resize event listener on cleanup causes stale references. Skipping the deleteAttribute('normal'/'uv') step before mergeVertices will produce duplicate vertices and a malformed convex hull.
accessibilityNotes: Wrap the canvas in a div with role='img' and an aria-label describing the shape. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or eliminating the auto-rotation (set group.rotation.y to a fixed value). Provide a static screenshot fallback via a <noscript> or CSS background for users without WebGL. The interactive orbit is mouse/touch only; keyboard navigation is not natively supported by OrbitControls.

technique: real-time constructive solid geometry (CSG) boolean operations on 3D meshes
description: Two animated 3D shapes continuously intersect, subtract from, or add to each other in real time, producing a morphing composite solid with dynamic shadows. Well suited for a product configurator, creative tools landing page, or interactive explainer showing how shapes combine.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate block in a React useEffect with a canvas ref, or use react-three-fiber with a custom hook; install 'three-bvh-csg' via npm and import { SUBTRACTION, INTERSECTION, ADDITION, Brush, Evaluator } from it. Remove Stats and lil-gui in production; expose operation mode via React state instead. Use renderer.setSize with the ref's clientWidth/clientHeight rather than window dimensions.
constraints: CSG re-evaluation runs every frame which is CPU-intensive; not suitable for low-end mobile or battery-constrained devices. Requires WebGL with shadow map support. Performance degrades with high-poly input geometries — keep polygon counts moderate. Not suitable as a background element on content-heavy pages.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose the previous result geometry before re-evaluation each frame causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks layout in component-based apps. Not calling controls.dispose() and renderer.dispose() on component unmount leaks WebGL contexts. Leaving Stats.js and lil-gui in production adds unnecessary overhead.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static image fallback (e.g. a pre-rendered PNG of the composite shape) when prefers-reduced-motion is set, since the geometry morphs continuously. The canvas has no semantic content, so add aria-hidden='true' and ensure surrounding UI conveys the same information. No keyboard interaction is required for the decorative version; if used as a configurator, expose controls as accessible form inputs.

technique: textured rotating 3D cube with continuous spin animation
description: A single texture-mapped box rotates continuously on two axes, filling the viewport. Suits hero sections, loading screens, product showcase teasers, or brand identity pages that want a tactile 3D object as a focal point.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, move all init logic into a useEffect with a canvas ref, assign renderer.domElement to the ref instead of appending to document.body, and store the animation frame ID for cleanup. Replace the local 'textures/crate.gif' path with a URL in your /public folder (e.g. '/textures/crate.gif') or a CDN URL passed as a prop. With react-three-fiber, replace the imperative setup with a <mesh> containing <boxGeometry> and <meshBasicMaterial map={useTexture(...)}> inside a useFrame rotation update.
constraints: Very low GPU cost — a single draw call with one texture. Runs well on all mobile devices and low-end hardware. Requires WebGL (not WebGL2 specifically). Not suited for pages that need multiple complex objects without extending the scene; the full-viewport approach means it should live in a dedicated canvas layer if combined with HTML content.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and geometry.dispose() / material.dispose() on unmount causes memory leaks in SPA routing. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of measuring the parent container breaks layout in embedded contexts. Omitting the resize listener causes stretching on orientation change. Loading the texture inside animate() instead of once in init creates redundant network requests.
accessibilityNotes: Wrap the canvas in an element with role='img' and an aria-label describing the visual. Honor prefers-reduced-motion by checking the media query on init and setting rotation deltas to zero if matched, rendering a static frame instead. Provide a <noscript> fallback image for users without JavaScript.

technique: 3D shape extrusion along spline paths with bevel geometry
description: Displays solid 3D objects formed by extruding 2D cross-section shapes (triangle, star) along curved spline paths, plus a flat beveled extrusion, all lit with warm point lighting against a dark background. Suits hero sections for architecture, product design, manufacturing, or engineering-focused websites that want to convey structural sophistication.
usageNote: Wrap the init and animate logic inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref, or use react-three-fiber with a useFrame hook. Assign renderer.domElement to the ref'd container div and clean up with renderer.dispose() on unmount. TrackballControls must be imported from 'three/addons/controls/TrackballControls.js' and attached to the canvas element. No local assets are used, so no path replacements are needed.
constraints: Requires WebGL support; not suitable for very low-end mobile GPUs due to high step counts (100–200 segments per extruded path). ExtrudeGeometry with 200 steps can generate thousands of triangles, making it moderately expensive. Desktop-first experience recommended; test on mid-range mobile before shipping.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() and material.dispose() on component unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks layouts inside fixed-size containers — replace with container.clientWidth/clientHeight. Neglecting controls.dispose() on cleanup will leave stale event listeners. Not calling controls.handleResize() after window resize breaks TrackballControls tracking.
accessibilityNotes: This is a purely decorative 3D canvas; add aria-hidden='true' to the canvas element. Provide a static poster image or CSS gradient fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion enabled by pausing the animation loop. Ensure no critical content or interactive controls exist only inside the canvas.

technique: 3D spline tube extrusion with animated camera fly-through
description: Renders smooth 3D tube meshes extruded along mathematical spline curves (knots, helices, heart curves, etc.) with an optional first-person camera that flies along the tube path. Suits immersive hero sections, product visualization tunnels, data pipeline illustrations, or abstract 3D brand experiences.
usageNote: Port into React/Next.js using a useEffect hook with a canvas ref: initialize the renderer targeting the ref, set up the scene, animate with requestAnimationFrame stored in a ref, and clean up on unmount by calling renderer.dispose() and cancelling the animation frame. For react-three-fiber, use useFrame for the animation loop and drei's OrbitControls. No local assets are needed — all geometry is procedurally generated, so no asset path replacement is required. The GUI controls (lil-gui) should be replaced with React state and UI components.
constraints: Moderate GPU cost due to continuous tube geometry generation and optional camera helper rendering; geometry must be re-created on parameter change which is expensive — debounce user inputs. Works on mobile WebGL but high radiusSegments and extrusionSegments values may cause frame drops on low-end devices. Requires WebGL renderer; no WebGPU-specific features used so it is broadly compatible.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call mesh.geometry.dispose() and scene.remove(mesh) before rebuilding the tube on parameter change causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions breaks layout in embedded or responsive contexts. Not removing the animation frame loop and renderer on React component unmount causes duplicate renderers. Leaving the lil-gui panel attached to document.body instead of a scoped container pollutes the DOM.
accessibilityNotes: Respect prefers-reduced-motion by disabling the camera fly-through animation and defaulting to static OrbitControls view. Provide a static PNG fallback or a CSS-only alternative for users who have JavaScript or WebGL disabled. The canvas element should have a descriptive aria-label such as 'Interactive 3D spline tube visualization'. Ensure GUI controls are keyboard-navigable or replaced with accessible HTML form elements.

technique: procedural voxel terrain with first-person navigation
description: A navigable 3D block-based landscape generated with Perlin noise, rendered as a merged voxel mesh with tiled textures and first-person camera controls. Suits gaming portals, virtual world landing pages, interactive portfolios, or any site wanting an immersive exploreable environment as a hero or background scene.
usageNote: Wrap initialization in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; pass the ref's current element as the renderer container instead of document.getElementById. Replace 'textures/minecraft/atlas.png' with a hosted URL (e.g. via /public in Next.js or a CDN path) and supply your own tileable block texture atlas. Use react-three-fiber's Canvas and useThree if you prefer a declarative approach, but the imperative style works fine in a useEffect with cleanup returning renderer.dispose() and controls.dispose().
constraints: High GPU and CPU cost at init due to geometry merging of a 128×128 voxel world; not suitable for mobile or low-end devices without reducing worldWidth/worldDepth significantly. Requires WebGL renderer. First-person controls rely on pointer events and are desktop-centric; touch support needs additional work.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to merge geometries into a single draw call (huge performance hit if each voxel face is a separate mesh). Not disposing merged geometry and texture on component unmount causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of the container's bounding rect breaks layouts where the canvas is not full-screen. Not calling controls.update(delta) in the animation loop causes the camera to stop responding.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static screenshot or illustrated fallback image for users with prefers-reduced-motion or those unable to interact with 3D. Add an aria-hidden='true' attribute to the canvas and ensure any overlaid UI text has proper ARIA roles. Keyboard navigation is partially supported by FirstPersonControls (WASD/arrow keys) but should be documented for users. Screen readers receive no meaningful information from the 3D scene itself.

technique: NURBS curves, surfaces, and volumes with interactive rotation
description: Renders smooth mathematically-defined freeform 3D curves and sculpted surfaces that rotate in response to pointer drag, demonstrating organic, smoothly-flowing 3D shapes. Suits product configurators, CAD-adjacent design tools, automotive/industrial design showcases, or any site that needs to display precision free-form 3D geometry in a browser.
usageNote: Wrap all init/animation logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; attach the renderer to the ref element instead of document.body. Replace the local UV grid texture path ('textures/uv_grid_opengl.jpg') with a texture hosted in your /public directory or a CDN URL passed as a prop. For react-three-fiber, use useLoader(TextureLoader, url) and map NURBSSurface through a custom geometry hook via useEffect on BufferGeometry.
