NURBSCurve, NURBSSurface, and NURBSVolume are three.js addons and can be imported directly from 'three/addons/curves/...' assuming an import map or bundler alias is set up.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer; does not work with WebGPU or CSS renderers. ParametricGeometry tessellation resolution (currently 20×20) can be increased for quality at a moderate GPU cost, but stay below 100×100 on mobile. NURBS volume rendering samples surface slices so complexity scales with control point count. Not suitable for very low-end or legacy mobile devices without reducing tessellation.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() and material.dispose() on component unmount causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight breaks in container-embedded canvases — use the parent element's dimensions instead. Not removing pointer event listeners on cleanup causes stale closures. Recomputing NURBS control points every render frame is expensive; compute once and cache.
accessibilityNotes: No keyboard or screen reader interaction is provided. Add an aria-label to the canvas describing the 3D content. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by disabling the auto-rotation and pointer drag animation, or replacing the scene with a static rendered image. Provide an alt text or descriptive caption in adjacent HTML for screen reader users.

technique: 2D custom shape geometry with flat, extruded, wireframe, and point-cloud variations plus interactive rotation
description: Renders a collection of custom vector shapes (like geographic outlines or arbitrary polygons) displayed simultaneously as flat filled meshes, textured surfaces, extruded 3D solids, line outlines, and point clouds — all rotating with mouse drag. Suits product configurators, data-driven infographics, branded shape libraries, or interactive map/logo reveal sections.
usageNote: Wrap the init/animate logic in a useEffect with a canvas ref and pass the ref to the WebGLRenderer instead of appending to document.body. Use react-three-fiber's useFrame for the animation loop. Replace the local texture path ('textures/uv_grid_opengl.jpg') with an asset imported via your bundler (e.g. import uvGrid from './assets/uv_grid_opengl.jpg') or a public URL. Define your custom shape point arrays as constants outside the component for stability.
constraints: Rendering many shape variants (flat, extruded, lines, points) multiplies draw calls significantly — profile on mobile before shipping more than ~10 shapes. Requires WebGL (not WebGPU). ExtrudeGeometry can be CPU-heavy for complex paths with many bevel segments; simplify bevel settings for low-end devices.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() and material.dispose() on unmount causes memory leaks, especially with many shape variants. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions breaks embedded layouts. Not updating windowHalfX on resize causes incorrect pointer-based rotation. Sharing a single texture instance across materials without cloning can cause unexpected UV or colorSpace issues.
accessibilityNotes: The interactive rotation is purely decorative; provide a static SVG or image fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion. All shape content is non-textual, so add an aria-label on the canvas describing the shapes shown. No keyboard interaction is implemented — if shapes convey data, expose that data in accessible HTML alongside the canvas.

technique: interactive 3D spline path editor with drag handles
description: A 3D interactive curve editor where users can drag control points to reshape a smooth Catmull-Rom spline path in real time. Suits creative tools, route/path configuration UIs, animation timeline builders, or any app that needs users to visually define a curved trajectory or shape in 3D space.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref: instantiate renderer, scene, camera, and controls inside the effect, return a cleanup function that disposes renderer and removes event listeners. With react-three-fiber, use @react-three/drei's TransformControls and OrbitControls components and manage spline state with useRef/useState. No local assets are used, so no asset path replacement is needed. Export the spline point positions as JSON for backend persistence.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer with shadow map support; moderately GPU-intensive due to real-time spline recalculation and shadow rendering. On mobile, TransformControls drag interactions are awkward with touch and may need custom touch handling. Not suitable for very low-end devices. Minimum three.js r140+ recommended for stable CatmullRomCurve3 API.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose BufferGeometry and LineBasicMaterial clones when control points are removed causing memory leaks; not removing pointer event listeners on component unmount; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions; failing to disable OrbitControls while TransformControls is active causing conflicting drag behavior.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a reduced-motion fallback that disables orbit animation and shows a static top-down screenshot of the spline. Expose control point coordinates as editable number inputs for keyboard-only users. The canvas has no inherent screen reader meaning, so add an aria-label describing the editor purpose and provide a text-based coordinate output panel.

technique: interactive 3D parametric object viewer with multiple shading modes and orbit controls
description: A richly shaded 3D object rendered with selectable materials including wireframe, flat, smooth, glossy, textured, and environment-mapped reflective finishes, orbit-controllable by mouse drag. Ideal for product configurator sections, 3D asset showcases, or interactive portfolio pieces where users explore a model from any angle.
usageNote: Wrap the Three.js setup in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; assign renderer.domElement to the ref instead of appending to document.body. Replace TeapotGeometry with your own product geometry (GLTFLoader etc.). Swap the local texture paths (textures/uv_grid_opengl.jpg and textures/cube/pisa/) with CDN-hosted or public-folder assets, or generate a procedural environment map with PMREMGenerator to remove the cubemap dependency entirely.
constraints: Requires WebGL1/2; tessellation at high levels (30–50) is moderately GPU-intensive and may be slow on low-end mobile GPUs. Reflective mode loads a six-image cubemap which adds network cost. OrbitControls adds touch support but pinch-zoom should be tested on iOS Safari. Not suitable for render pipelines requiring WebGPU.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call teapot.geometry.dispose() before recreating geometry on parameter change (causes GPU memory leak). Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container div's clientWidth/clientHeight, which breaks layout in embedded panels. Not removing the resize event listener on component unmount in React. Leaving the GUI (lil-gui) visible in production without conditionally hiding it.
accessibilityNotes: The 3D canvas has no semantic meaning to screen readers; add an aria-label and role='img' to the canvas element describing the object. Provide a static fallback image via a <noscript> tag or a CSS background. For reduced-motion preferences (prefers-reduced-motion), disable auto-rotation or any animation loop and keep the scene static until user interaction. Orbit controls are mouse/touch-driven; add keyboard arrow-key handlers for users who cannot use a pointer.

technique: procedural heightmap terrain with first-person navigation and exponential fog
description: A vast, walkable 3D landscape generated from Perlin noise with warm sandy terrain colors and distance fog that fades the horizon—ideal for hero sections of travel, gaming, outdoor, or world-building websites that want an immersive flythrough environment.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate block inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref, returning a cleanup that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the animation loop. Replace renderer.setSize and camera.aspect updates with a ResizeObserver on the container ref rather than window. In Next.js, import this component dynamically with ssr:false since it requires browser APIs. No local asset paths are used—terrain and texture are fully procedural via ImprovedNoise and Canvas 2D, so no asset replacement is needed.
constraints: Requires WebGL 1 or higher; the 256x256 plane with full texture generation is moderately GPU-intensive and may drop frames on low-end mobile GPUs. FirstPersonControls require mouse/keyboard input which is not touch-friendly by default—add touch event handling or swap for OrbitControls on mobile. Not suitable for inline content sections; best as a full-screen or large-format background canvas.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call controls.dispose() and renderer.dispose() on component unmount, causing memory leaks and multiple animation loops. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of measuring the container element, breaking layout in non-full-screen contexts. Not removing the window resize listener on cleanup. Overriding window.Math.random inside the module scope is dangerous in a shared app—isolate the seeded random into a local closure instead.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static screenshot or CSS gradient fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion enabled by skipping the animation loop and rendering a single frame. The canvas has no semantic content, so add aria-hidden='true' and ensure any overlaid text has sufficient contrast against the warm fog color. Keyboard navigation of the first-person controls works via WASD/arrow keys but should be documented or replaced with passive camera animation for non-interactive hero use.

technique: procedural heightmap terrain with baked lighting and raycasting surface pointer
description: A vast, orbitally explorable 3D landscape generated from Perlin noise with sun-baked color shading, rendering as rolling hills in earthy brown-green tones. Ideal for outdoor/adventure brand hero sections, game landing pages, geographic visualization intros, or any site needing an immersive world-exploration aesthetic.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate block inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref, assigning the renderer's domElement to a container div via ref.current.appendChild. Tear down with renderer.dispose() and controls.dispose() in the cleanup return. In Next.js, use dynamic import with ssr:false since it accesses window and document. No local assets are needed — the heightmap and texture are fully procedurally generated at runtime using ImprovedNoise and Canvas 2D APIs.
constraints: Generates a 256x256 vertex plane (~65k vertices) and a 1024x1024 canvas texture — moderate GPU cost. OrbitControls limits maxPolarAngle to prevent going below terrain. Not suitable for low-end mobile GPUs or battery-sensitive contexts. Requires WebGL (not WebGPU). Works best at fullscreen or large viewport sizes. Terrain is randomly seeded each load so appearance varies.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose(), geometry.dispose(), and texture.dispose() on unmount causes memory leaks in SPA routing. Not removing the pointermove event listener on cleanup will cause errors after component unmount. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions breaks embedded layouts. Re-running generateHeight on every render is wasteful — generate once on mount only.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static screenshot fallback or CSS background image for users with prefers-reduced-motion, since the orbitally animated 3D terrain may cause vestibular discomfort. The scene has no interactive controls beyond mouse/pointer — add keyboard orbit support via OrbitControls keys config for accessibility. Add an aria-hidden='true' attribute to the canvas and a visually-hidden descriptive text for screen readers.

technique: 3D extruded text geometry with bevel, lighting, and drag-to-rotate interaction
description: Renders user-editable text as fully three-dimensional extruded letterforms with beveled edges, dynamic colored lighting, and a reflective ground plane — all draggable with mouse/touch. Ideal for hero sections, brand statements, product launch pages, or interactive typographic art installations on creative or portfolio sites.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js, passing the ref's current element as the renderer's domElement target instead of appending to document.body. Replace FontLoader URLs (e.g. 'fonts/optimer_bold.typeface.json') with versioned public-folder paths or imports from a CDN like unpkg (e.g. 'https://unpkg.com/three@<version>/examples/fonts/optimer_bold.typeface.json'). In react-three-fiber, use @react-three/drei's <Text3D> component which wraps TextGeometry and handles font loading declaratively.
constraints: TextGeometry is CPU-intensive at creation time; avoid regenerating geometry on every keystroke without debouncing. Requires WebGL renderer — no WebGPU or CSS3D fallback. On low-end mobile devices, reduce curveSegments and disable bevel to stay within budget. Not suitable for large paragraphs or dynamic body copy; best for short strings (under ~20 characters).
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call textGeo.dispose() and remove old mesh from scene before creating new geometry on text changes causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container element's dimensions breaks embedded use. Not debouncing font loads on rapid font-switching triggers race conditions. Leaving the animation loop running after component unmount in React wastes GPU resources — always cancel with renderer.setAnimationLoop(null) in the useEffect cleanup.
accessibilityNotes: The 3D canvas has no semantic text content; add an aria-label or visually-hidden <span> mirroring the displayed text for screen readers. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by disabling the auto-rotation and pointer-drag rotation, showing the text statically centered. The keyboard text-input feature is a nice progressive enhancement but requires the canvas container to be focusable (tabIndex=0) with a visible focus ring and instructions for sighted keyboard users.

technique: 3D outlined text with semi-transparent fill using font geometry
description: Renders multi-line 3D text as crisp vector outlines with a semi-transparent filled mesh behind them, creating a clean blueprint or design-sketch aesthetic. Suits hero sections, loading screens, brand identity displays, or interactive 'about' pages where typographic styling needs a dimensional, artistic quality.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js, attaching the renderer to the ref instead of document.body. Replace the local font path ('fonts/helvetiker_regular.typeface.json') by hosting the typeface JSON in your /public folder or importing it via a CDN URL (e.g. from the three.js GitHub raw assets). In react-three-fiber, use @react-three/drei's <Text3D> component with a font prop pointing to the hosted JSON, which handles FontLoader internally.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer; not suitable for canvas or SVG fallback. Font JSON file must be served from an accessible URL — the local asset path will not exist in a user project. CPU cost for ShapeGeometry is low after initial load; GPU cost is minimal. Works well on mobile but OrbitControls touch handling should be tested for scroll conflicts. Only one font style is supported per loaded JSON.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to host the typeface JSON file and referencing the original local path which will 404. Not disposing ShapeGeometry and line BufferGeometry instances when the component unmounts, causing memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container element's dimensions, breaking layout in embedded or partial-page use. Forgetting to call controls.dispose() and removing the resize event listener on cleanup.
accessibilityNotes: The 3D text is not readable by screen readers — always include an accessible HTML text alternative (e.g. an aria-label on the canvas or a visually-hidden element). Respect prefers-reduced-motion by skipping OrbitControls auto-rotation if added. Provide a static image fallback for users with WebGL disabled. Ensure sufficient color contrast if the text color is used for informational content.

technique: 3D stroke text rendering with multi-directional script support (LTR, RTL, vertical)
description: Renders multilingual 3D text with outlined stroke styling and a semi-transparent fill, supporting left-to-right, right-to-left, and top-to-bottom writing directions simultaneously. Suits internationalized landing pages, typographic hero sections, multilingual brand showcases, or creative portfolio headers where script diversity is a design feature.
usageNote: Wrap init logic in a useEffect hook with a canvas ref; assign renderer.domElement to the ref and pass the ref's current to OrbitControls. Replace the local font JSON path with a URL to a hosted typeface.json file (e.g. from a CDN, a /public folder in Next.js, or a dynamic import). In react-three-fiber, use useLoader(FontLoader, url) and build the geometry inside a useMemo. Clean up renderer and controls in the useEffect return function.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer; not suitable for CSS or SVG fallback contexts. ShapeGeometry and SVGLoader stroke generation are CPU-heavy for very long strings. Mobile performance is acceptable for short text blocks but degrades with many glyphs. The font JSON must be a three.js typeface.json format, not a raw OTF/TTF; only fonts pre-converted to this format work.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose ShapeGeometry and stroke geometry objects when the component unmounts, causing GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container ref for responsive sizing. Not handling the async font load before attempting to render, which causes a blank scene. Reusing the same shapes array after mutating it by pushing holeShapes into it, which can corrupt re-renders if the function is called repeatedly.
accessibilityNotes:
All text content is rendered purely as 3D geometry and is invisible to screen readers; provide a visually hidden HTML equivalent (aria-label or a hidden

) for every text string displayed. For reduced-motion users, disable OrbitControls auto-rotate if added, and consider replacing the interactive 3D view with a static image fallback via a prefers-reduced-motion media query.

technique: GPU-accelerated boid flocking simulation with instanced bird geometry
description: Thousands of stylized birds flock together in real time, banking and turning as a living murmuration that responds to mouse movement. Ideal for immersive hero sections, nature or travel brand landing pages, creative agency portfolios, or any site wanting an organic, life-filled ambient background.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer targeting the ref element instead of appending to document.body, store the animation frame ID and call renderer.setAnimationLoop(null) plus renderer.dispose() in the cleanup. In Next.js mark the component 'use client' and guard with typeof window !== 'undefined'. The GPU shader strings are currently read from inline <script> tags via document.getElementById; migrate these to imported GLSL string constants (template literals or .glsl files with a Webpack/Vite raw loader) so they work in a module bundler. No local asset paths need replacing.
constraints: Requires WebGL with floating-point render target support (OES_texture_float or WebGL2); will silently fail on devices without this extension. GPU computation is heavy: budget 4–8ms per frame on mid-range mobile GPUs, and reduce the WIDTH constant (e.g. from 32 to 16) for mobile to keep BIRDS count manageable. Not suitable as a secondary background element on content-dense pages due to its full-viewport GPU cost.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose the GPUComputationRenderer render targets and the BirdGeometry on component unmount causes GPU memory leaks in SPAs. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the canvas container dimensions breaks layout in constrained contexts. Leaving the lil-gui Stats overlay visible in production. Not clamping the simulation bounds when resizing leads to birds escaping the visible area permanently.
accessibilityNotes: Respect prefers-reduced-motion by skipping the animation loop entirely and rendering a single static frame of the flock, or replacing with a high-quality still image. The canvas carries no semantic information so add aria-hidden='true' and role='presentation'. Provide a descriptive aria-label on the parent section element. Ensure any overlaid text meets contrast requirements against the white foggy background.

technique: GPU-accelerated boids flocking simulation with skinned mesh instancing
description: Thousands of animated birds (or flamingos) flock together in 3D space, following emergent separation, alignment, and cohesion rules computed entirely on the GPU via ping-pong render targets. Ideal for hero sections of nature, travel, wildlife, or creative agency sites that want a living, organic background with a sense of wonder.
usageNote: Wrap the entire setup in a React useEffect with a canvas ref, returning a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the animation frame. Replace the GLB asset paths (models/gltf/Parrot.glb, models/gltf/Flamingo.glb) with paths inside your /public directory (Next.js) or hosted CDN URLs. GPUComputationRenderer must be imported from the three/addons path; ensure your bundler or import map resolves three/addons correctly. With react-three-fiber, prefer useThree/useFrame hooks but note GPUComputationRenderer tightly couples to the raw WebGLRenderer, so accessing gl.getContext or gl directly is necessary.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 or a capable WebGL1 context with OES_texture_float support for GPUComputationRenderer; will fail on low-end mobile GPUs and older Safari versions without fallback. Simulating 4096 birds is moderate–high GPU cost; reduce WIDTH constant (e.g. 32 → 1024 birds) for mobile. Not suitable for server-side rendering without dynamic import guards. Desktop and high-end mobile only for full resolution.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose the GPUComputationRenderer render targets and the BirdGeometry on component unmount, causing GPU memory leaks on route changes. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the canvas container dimensions breaks responsive layouts. Not guarding against missing WebGL2 extensions before calling GPUComputationRenderer will throw silent errors. Using the same static selectModel seed across hot-reloads in dev without cleanup causes duplicate meshes.
accessibilityNotes: Wrap the canvas in an aria-hidden='true' container so screen readers skip it entirely. Provide a prefers-reduced-motion media query check; if reduced motion is preferred, skip the animation loop or replace with a static hero image of birds. Ensure any overlaid text has sufficient contrast regardless of the animated background color.

technique: GPU-accelerated gravitational N-body particle simulation (protoplanetary disk)
description: Thousands of glowing particles orbit and clump under simulated gravity, forming a swirling disk that mimics planetary formation. Ideal for science, space, or technology brand hero sections, data visualization intros, or immersive loading screens that convey scale and complexity.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate block inside a React useEffect with a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes the DOM element. Pass a canvas ref instead of appending to document.body. In Next.js, guard with typeof window !== 'undefined' and use dynamic import with ssr:false. The GPUComputationRenderer requires inline shader scripts (currently read via document.getElementById); replace these with raw GLSL strings stored as JS template literals or imported .glsl files so they work in a module bundler without DOM script tags.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 or WebGL1 with floating-point texture extensions (OES_texture_float); will silently fail or error on devices lacking these. High GPU compute cost — 4096 particles updated per frame via ping-pong render targets. Not suitable for mid-range mobile GPUs or battery-sensitive contexts. Desktop-first pattern; test carefully on integrated graphics.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call gpuCompute.dispose() and renderer.dispose() on component unmount causing GPU memory leaks. Leaving shader source in HTML script tags breaks SSR and module bundlers — must extract to JS strings. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions breaks layout in embedded or split-pane UIs. Not removing the resize event listener on unmount. Assuming the simulation can be paused by stopping the animation loop without resetting render targets.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static high-resolution screenshot or CSS gradient fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion enabled. The canvas is purely decorative; add aria-hidden='true' and role='presentation' to the canvas element. Ensure any overlaid text maintains sufficient contrast against the dark particle background. LightProbeGenerator.fromCubeTexture works the same way once the texture loads. Dispose the loader and renderer on component unmount.
constraints: Requires WebGL with cube texture support (broadly available). The CubeTextureLoader fetches six images so network latency matters; use compressed textures or a small cube map resolution for mobile. LightProbe baking from a cube texture is a one-time CPU cost and is acceptable on most devices. Not suitable for very low-end or WebGL1-only contexts if high-res cube maps are used.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose the CubeTexture and mesh geometry/material on unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of the container element's dimensions breaks layout in embedded or multi-panel apps. Skipping renderer.setPixelRatio causes blurriness on high-DPI screens. Not updating camera.aspect and calling updateProjectionMatrix on resize distorts the sphere. Leaving the LightProbeHelper visible in production adds visual clutter.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static fallback image of the reflective sphere for users with prefers-reduced-motion or when WebGL is unavailable. The canvas has no inherent keyboard focus or screen reader meaning; add aria-hidden='true' and supply an adjacent text description of the visual for screen readers. OrbitControls mouse interaction is decorative; disable or gate it behind a user gesture if the sphere is purely presentational.

technique: environment-mapped light probe extracted from cube camera for image-based lighting
description: A 360-degree panoramic environment captured into a cube render target and converted into a spherical harmonic light probe, which then illuminates scene objects with realistic ambient lighting derived from the surroundings. Ideal for product showcases, luxury brand landing pages, or 3D configurators where physically plausible environmental lighting is needed without expensive real-time ray tracing.
usageNote: In React or Next.js, wrap all initialization inside a useEffect with a canvas ref and return a cleanup function that disposes the renderer. In react-three-fiber, use the useEnvironment or useCubeCamera hooks as alternatives, or place the imperative LightProbeGenerator call inside a useEffect after the canvas is mounted. Replace the local 'textures/cube/pisa/*.png' cube face images with your own hosted equirectangular or cube-face HDR/PNG environment assets; RGBELoader can also be used to load a single .hdr file converted to a cube render target.
constraints: Requires WebGL with cube render target support (no WebGPU path here). Generating the cube render target at 256px is moderate GPU cost at init time but minimal at runtime since the probe is baked. Not suitable for dynamic lighting environments that change at runtime. Works on most modern mobile GPUs but cube render target generation may spike frame time on low-end devices.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose the WebGLCubeRenderTarget and cubeCamera when the component unmounts, causing GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the canvas container dimensions, which breaks embedded layouts. Not awaiting the async LightProbeGenerator call before rendering, resulting in a black or unlit scene. Leaving the LightProbeHelper visible in production builds — it is a debug aid only.
accessibilityNotes: This is a purely decorative 3D background; wrap the canvas in an aria-hidden container and provide a static fallback image (e.g., a screenshot of the environment) via a <noscript> tag or CSS background for users with reduced motion preferences or no WebGL support. Keyboard and screen reader users should never be routed into the 3D canvas for content.

technique: light probe volume GI baking in a Cornell box scene
description: A physically-based interior room with colored accent walls receives volumetric indirect lighting baked from a 3D grid of light probes, producing realistic color bleeding and global illumination on objects. Suits product configurator rooms, architectural visualization sections, virtual showrooms, or any premium interior 3D experience.
usageNote: Wrap renderer creation and the async bake() call inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js. The LightProbeGridWebGL bake() is async so await it inside an async IIFE within useEffect. Use react-three-fiber cautiously as LightProbeGridWebGL is a custom three.js addon that extends Object3D directly — it is easier to keep this as vanilla three.js mounted to a ref'd canvas. Clean up with renderer.dispose() and controls.dispose() in the useEffect return. No local asset paths need replacing.
constraints: Requires WebGL1 renderer (not WebGPU). The bake step is CPU/GPU intensive and blocks rendering briefly; higher resolutions (>8) can cause noticeable frame drops on mid-range GPUs. Not suitable for mobile low-end devices or scenes requiring real-time dynamic GI. Shadow maps and tone mapping are required for correct output. Static bake means probe grid must be rebaked if scene geometry or lights change at runtime.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call probes.dispose() before recreating at new resolution causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a ResizeObserver breaks layout in embedded canvases. Placing probe grid without centering it on the scene volume causes incorrect irradiance sampling. Skipping renderer.shadowMap.enabled causes flat unlit appearance.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static screenshot fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion enabled, as the OrbitControls interaction is non-essential. Add an aria-label to the canvas element describing the 3D scene. Keyboard orbit control is not natively supported; add Tab-focusable UI controls if the 3D view conveys content rather than being purely decorative.

technique: light probe volume grid for multi-room indirect lighting simulation
description: A two-room architectural interior separated by a wall with a doorway, where each room is lit by distinct colored light (red and blue) and a grid of light probes captures per-room indirect illumination, making objects like metallic spheres and torus knots reflect correct ambient color bleed from their surroundings. Suits product showcase pages, virtual showroom walkthroughs, architectural visualization previews, or 3D museum/gallery environments embedded in a website.
usageNote: Wrap initialization in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js, return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes the event listener. Use react-three-fiber alternatively and place LightProbeGridWebGL setup inside a useEffect or a custom R3F component. No local assets are referenced so no path replacement is needed, but ensure three/addons imports resolve correctly via an import map or bundler alias (e.g., Vite's resolve.alias for 'three/addons').
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer with support for render targets; LightProbeGridWebGL captures scene radiance into probes which is GPU-intensive at init time. Not recommended for low-end mobile GPUs or scenarios requiring more than ~30 probes per room. Best suited for desktop or high-end tablet experiences. The multi-room probe separation means scene geometry changes require probe rebaking.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call probeGrid.dispose() on unmount causing GPU memory leaks; not handling window resize with camera.aspect and renderer.setSize updates; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container element's dimensions; reusing the same probe grid across rooms with different dominant lighting colors, washing out the color-separation effect; placing probe grids without accounting for wall occlusion boundaries.
accessibilityNotes: This is a purely decorative or exploratory 3D scene with no interactive UI beyond orbit controls; provide a static screenshot fallback via a <noscript> or prefers-reduced-motion media query that disables animation and shows a still render. Add an aria-label to the canvas element describing the scene (e.g., 'Interactive 3D architectural interior visualization'). Orbit controls are mouse/touch driven — add keyboard navigation instructions or disable the canvas for screen-reader users with aria-hidden='true' and provide equivalent text content.

technique: volumetric light probe grid with global illumination baking in a real-time 3D architectural scene
description: A fully lit 3D interior/exterior architectural environment using a grid of light probes to simulate indirect global illumination, complete with a physically-based sky and sun. Ideal for real estate visualization, architectural walkthroughs, virtual venue tours, heritage site exploration, or any product that benefits from photorealistic indoor/outdoor rendering.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate logic inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref (renderer.domElement appended to the ref, not document.body). Return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose(), controls.dispose(), and cancelAnimationFrame. For react-three-fiber, this pattern is too imperative and WebGL-specific to map cleanly — stick with vanilla three.js + useEffect. Replace the KhronosGroup GitHub URLs with your own hosted GLTF assets (CDN or /public folder in Next.js). The LightProbeGridWebGL addon must be imported directly from node_modules or bundled — verify your bundler resolves three/addons correctly.
constraints: Very high GPU cost due to multi-pass light probe baking across a 3D grid; not suitable for mobile or low-end devices. Requires WebGL (not WebGPU). The baking loop runs over multiple frames and will cause visible stuttering on first load. Probe grid resolution must be tuned carefully to balance quality vs performance. Not appropriate for simple landing pages or content-heavy sites where 3D is decorative.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose the LightProbeGrid and its render targets on component unmount causes major memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element dimensions breaks layout in non-fullscreen contexts. Not removing the animation loop before unmount causes double-rendering. Failing to strip embedded lights from the loaded GLTF model results in double lighting. Leaving the GUI (lil-gui) mounted after React unmount leaves orphan DOM nodes.
accessibilityNotes: This is a fully immersive 3D scene with first-person keyboard/mouse controls — provide a visible skip link or fallback static screenshot for users who prefer reduced motion or use assistive technology. First-person controls (WASD + mouse) are not keyboard-accessible in a standard sense; add ARIA role='application' and describe the scene in an aria-label. Offer a 2D floor plan or image gallery as a reduced-motion alternative.

technique: outdoor sky dome with hemisphere + directional lighting and animated 3D model
description: A naturalistic outdoor scene featuring a gradient sky dome, warm ground plane, and soft dual-light setup (sky-to-ground hemisphere light plus a sun-like directional light with shadows), suitable for hero backgrounds on nature, travel, wildlife, or brand storytelling sites where an airy, daylight atmosphere is needed.
usageNote: Wrap initialization in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; attach the renderer to the ref instead of getElementById. Dispose the renderer and remove the animation loop on cleanup. Replace 'models/gltf/Flamingo.glb' with any publicly hosted GLTF/GLB URL or a file served from /public in Next.js. The vertex/fragment shader scripts embedded in HTML <script> tags must be converted to JS template literal strings or imported as glsl files. Consider react-three-fiber for a more idiomatic React integration.
constraints: Requires WebGL with shadow map support; moderately GPU-intensive due to 2048x2048 shadow map and custom sky shader. Performs well on mid-range desktop GPUs; on mobile, reduce shadow map size to 512 or 1024 and consider disabling shadows entirely. Not suitable for contexts requiring extremely lightweight pages.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose the renderer, geometry, and materials on component unmount causing memory leaks; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container element's dimensions; omitting the resize event listener cleanup; not converting inline HTML shader scripts to JS strings when moving to a module-based framework; neglecting to set renderer.setPixelRatio for sharp rendering on HiDPI screens.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static poster image fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion enabled; pause or skip the animation loop when the media query matches. The canvas has no inherent semantic meaning so add aria-hidden='true' and ensure any overlaid text content is in real DOM elements. Screen readers will ignore the canvas entirely, so do not convey meaningful information solely through the 3D scene.

technique: physically-based interior lighting with real-world lumen/lux values and dynamic shadows
description: A photorealistic interior scene with a hanging point light bulb casting warm shadows on a hardwood floor and textured objects, with adjustable ambient sky irradiance simulating everything from moonless night to direct sunlight. Suits product showcase pages, architectural visualization sections, interactive room configurators, or luxury brand hero scenes where lighting realism communicates quality.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref and a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose(). Replace local texture paths (hardwood, brick, earth) with your own CDN-hosted or public-folder textures — the pattern expects diffuse, bump, and roughness maps. With react-three-fiber, use <pointLight> with the 'power' prop (in lumens) and <hemisphereLight> intensity scaled to lux values, and set renderer.physicallyCorrectLights=true (or useLegacyLights=false in r155+). Expose bulbPower and hemiIrradiance as React state to drive a UI slider or preset selector.
constraints: Requires WebGL with shadow map support; shadow rendering is moderately expensive — avoid more than 2-3 shadow-casting lights simultaneously on mobile. PointLight shadow maps are cube maps (6 renders per frame) so limit to one physical bulb on low-end devices. Not suitable for purely 2D or CSS-based UIs. Physically correct lighting requires tone mapping (THREE.ReinhardToneMapping or ACESFilmicToneMapping) to look correct.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to set renderer.physicallyCorrectLights = true (pre-r155) will make lumen/lux values appear wildly incorrect. Not disposing textures and geometry on component unmount causes memory leaks in SPAs. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of the container's clientWidth/clientHeight breaks layout in non-fullscreen embeds. Omitting renderer.setPixelRatio(window.devicePixelRatio) causes blurry output on HiDPI screens. Using MeshBasicMaterial instead of MeshStandardMaterial breaks the PBR lighting entirely.
accessibilityNotes: This scene is purely decorative/presentational; provide a meaningful aria-label on the canvas element and a static fallback image for users with prefers-reduced-motion or no WebGL support. The interactive orbit controls should be keyboard-accessible or disabled with a note. Avoid using the lighting state to convey critical information without a text equivalent.

technique: animated colored rect area lights casting soft planar illumination on 3D geometry
description: Three large colored rectangular light panels (red, green, blue) slowly rotate and cast soft, realistic area lighting onto a reflective torus knot and a dark checkerboard floor, producing smooth color-blended shadows. Suits a high-end product showcase, creative agency hero, or interactive brand experience where dramatic atmospheric lighting is the focal point.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer targeting the ref element instead of appending to document.body, store the animation frame ID for cleanup, and call renderer.dispose() on unmount. In react-three-fiber use <rectAreaLight> primitives and call RectAreaLightUniformsLib.init() once outside the component (e.g. in a module-level side effect). No local assets are needed—the checker texture is generated procedurally via CanvasTexture.
constraints: RectAreaLight requires MeshStandardMaterial or MeshPhysicalMaterial and does NOT work with MeshLambertMaterial or MeshPhongMaterial. It is GPU-intensive due to LTC (linearly transformed cosines) lookups; avoid using more than 4–6 rect area lights simultaneously. Performance degrades on low-end mobile GPUs; test on target devices. Requires WebGL2 for best results but works in WebGL1 with the UniformsLib init.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call RectAreaLightUniformsLib.init() before adding any RectAreaLight will produce black/unlit surfaces. Skipping renderer.dispose() and geometry/material disposal on component unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of the container element's dimensions breaks layout in embedded contexts. Not updating camera.aspect on resize produces distorted rendering.
accessibilityNotes: The scene is purely decorative; add aria-hidden='true' to the canvas element. Provide a static fallback image for users with prefers-reduced-motion or when WebGL is unavailable. Pause or freeze light rotation animations when the prefers-reduced-motion media query is active by checking it before starting the animation loop. No interactive keyboard targets exist so no focus management is needed.

technique: spotlight with texture projection, penumbra, and real-time shadow casting
description: A cone of light with a soft, textured beam illuminates a 3D subject against a grey floor, producing dramatic projected shadows and light patterns. Ideal for product showcases, hero sections, luxury brand landing pages, or interactive stage/exhibit presentations.
usageNote: Wrap the init and animate logic inside a useEffect hook with a canvas ref in React/Next.js, attaching the renderer to the ref instead of document.body. Use react-three-fiber alternatively by mapping SpotLight props to JSX. Replace the PLY model with your own asset hosted on a CDN or public folder — any THREE.Mesh works as the lit subject. Host textures (disturb.jpg, colors.png, uv_grid_opengl.jpg) in your public directory and update the TextureLoader path accordingly. Remove the lil-gui panel for production and drive spotlight parameters from your app state instead.
constraints: Requires WebGL with shadow map support; shadow map rendering is moderately GPU-intensive. PCF shadows and spotlight texture projection may underperform on low-end mobile GPUs. Not suitable for scenes needing many simultaneous shadow-casting spotlights. Works best on desktop and mid-to-high-end mobile. Tone mapping (NeutralToneMapping) requires a capable GPU and may affect color accuracy on older devices.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and remove the canvas on component unmount causing memory leaks. Not handling window resize (camera aspect and renderer size must update together). Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of measuring the container element. Leaving the SpotLightHelper and CameraHelper visible in production. Forgetting to set renderer.shadowMap.enabled = true before adding shadow-casting lights. Not calling geometry.computeVertexNormals() on loaded models, resulting in flat shading.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static fallback image (e.g. a pre-rendered screenshot) for users with prefers-reduced-motion or when WebGL is unavailable. The 3D canvas has no inherent keyboard or screen reader content; add an aria-label on the canvas element and a visually-hidden description of the scene. The GUI controls are mouse-only; if exposed to users, replace with accessible HTML inputs. Ensure surrounding page content is not obscured by the full-screen canvas.

technique: animated multi-color spotlights with shadow casting and smooth position tweening
description: Three colored spotlights (orange, green, purple) slowly drift and shift their cone angles over a flat surface and a small object, casting dynamic shadows and blending colored light pools. Suits hero sections for entertainment, gaming, nightlife, or product showcase sites that want a dramatic stage-lighting atmosphere.
usageNote: Wrap the setup in a React useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer targeting the ref element instead of appending to document.body, store the animation frame id returned by setAnimationLoop for cleanup, and call renderer.dispose() plus controls.dispose() on unmount. The TWEEN update loop (setTimeout calling updateTweens) should also be cleared on unmount using a ref-stored timeout id. No local asset paths need replacement. For react-three-fiber, map spotlights to <spotLight> JSX and use useFrame for TWEEN.update() calls.
constraints: Requires WebGL with shadow map support (PCFShadowMap); three simultaneous shadow-casting spotlights are moderately expensive — avoid on low-end mobile GPUs or reduce shadow map resolution. Desktop and mid-range mobile are fine. Not suitable for contexts requiring very high frame rates alongside other heavy GPU workloads.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to cancel the setTimeout chain on component unmount causes memory leaks and continued GPU work after navigation. Not calling renderer.setSize on resize breaks aspect ratio. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of the container element dimensions breaks embedded use. Failing to dispose geometry, materials, and the renderer on unmount accumulates GPU memory.
accessibilityNotes: Add a prefers-reduced-motion media query check: if reduced motion is preferred, stop the TWEEN animations and keep lights static. Provide a static image fallback for users with no WebGL support using a <noscript> or a canvas-unsupported check. The canvas itself should have aria-hidden='true' and role='presentation' since it is purely decorative; ensure any overlaid text has sufficient contrast against the dynamic colored lighting.

technique: dynamic sun-sky system with cascaded shadow maps and time-of-day lighting
description: A physically-based outdoor scene with a procedural sky, sun positioned by azimuth and elevation, warm-to-cool color grading at dusk/dawn, atmospheric fog, and high-quality cascaded shadow maps across a large terrain. Ideal for real estate visualization, outdoor product showcases, architectural walkthroughs, game landing pages, or any site needing a photorealistic open-world environment.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer targeting the ref element, set up the animation loop, and return a cleanup that calls renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame. In Next.js mark the component 'use client' and guard with typeof window checks. The SunLight, Sky, and FirstPersonControls addons are npm-installed with three; import them directly. No local assets are referenced so no path replacement is needed. Replace FirstPersonControls with OrbitControls or pointer-lock controls to suit your UX.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 for PMREM generation and shadow map quality; shadow cascade resolution of 2048 is GPU-heavy and may drop below 30fps on mid-range mobile GPUs. The scene is designed for large viewport rendering; avoid using it in small card components. Not suitable for WebGPU renderer without porting SunLight and Sky shaders.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose the PMREM renderTarget on every sun update causes a GPU memory leak. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a ResizeObserver breaks layout in constrained containers. Not pausing the animation loop when the canvas is off-screen wastes GPU. Skipping renderer.shadowMap.enabled = true removes all shadows silently.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static hero image fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion set; pause or skip the FirstPersonControls animation loop in that case. The 3D scene is purely decorative, so wrap the canvas in an aria-hidden container and supply visible alt text or a caption. Keyboard navigation is not meaningful here; ensure interactive UI controls (GUI sliders) have proper label elements.

technique: vertex-colored 3D Hilbert curve line art with mouse parallax
description: Six glowing, rainbow-gradient 3D space-filling curves (Hilbert curves) arranged in a 2×3 grid rotate gently and respond to mouse movement, creating a mesmerizing mathematical line art display. Ideal for tech brand hero sections, data visualization landing pages, creative agency backgrounds, or developer tool marketing sites that want to communicate complexity and precision visually.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate block inside a React useEffect with a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes the DOM canvas. Pass a ref to a container div and append renderer.domElement to it instead of document.body. In Next.js, guard with typeof window !== 'undefined' and use dynamic import with ssr:false. No local assets to replace. For react-three-fiber, reproduce the BufferGeometry vertex color setup inside useEffect hooks on a <lineSegments> or <line> primitive with a <bufferGeometry> and <lineBasicMaterial vertexColors>.

Renders 6 separate Line objects each with hundreds of vertices — low-to-moderate GPU cost, fine on mid-range mobile. Does not use post-processing so no HDR or bloom without adding EffectComposer. Not suitable as an inline component due to full-viewport takeover; best as a canvas background layer with CSS pointer-events managed carefully.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose all 6 BufferGeometry instances and the shared LineBasicMaterial on unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using the container element dimensions breaks layout in non-full-page contexts. Forgetting to remove the pointermove event listener on cleanup causes stale closures. Not calling renderer.setPixelRatio(window.devicePixelRatio) produces blurry output on retina displays.
accessibilityNotes: Add a prefers-reduced-motion media query check: if reduced motion is preferred, stop the animation loop (cancel setAnimationLoop) and render a single static frame, or replace with a CSS-animated SVG fallback. The canvas element should have aria-hidden='true' and role='presentation' since it is purely decorative. No keyboard interaction is required as mouse parallax is enhancement-only.

technique: animated dashed line wireframes with spline and box geometry
description: A dark scene featuring a continuously rotating 3D Hilbert-curve spline rendered in white dashed lines alongside a dashed wireframe cube in amber — both slowly spinning in place. Suits tech product landing pages, developer tool dashboards, data visualization hero sections, or any context needing a precise, architectural aesthetic.
usageNote: In React or Next.js, mount inside a useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer targeting the ref element instead of appending to document.body, store the animation loop ID and cancel it on cleanup, and call renderer.dispose() on unmount. With react-three-fiber, use <line> and <lineSegments> primitives with lineDashedMaterial and call computeLineDistances() via a useEffect on the mesh ref. No local assets are needed — all geometry is procedurally generated.
constraints: LineDashedMaterial requires computeLineDistances() to be called after any geometry transform or it will render as solid lines. Performance is light — suitable for mobile and mid-range hardware. Requires WebGL renderer; no WebGPU path is used. The Hilbert3D utility from GeometryUtils must be imported from the three/addons path and may need to be shimmed in bundler configs that do not alias three/addons.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call computeLineDistances() after adding or transforming line objects is the most common mistake. Also: hardcoding WIDTH/HEIGHT instead of reading from the container element causes layout issues in embedded components; not removing the resize event listener on unmount causes memory leaks; not disposing geometry and material on cleanup leads to GPU memory leaks in SPAs.
accessibilityNotes: Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or stopping the rotation animation loop — detect via window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') and skip requestAnimationFrame updates. Provide a static fallback image of the scene for users with JavaScript disabled or no WebGL support. The canvas has no semantic meaning so add aria-hidden='true' and ensure surrounding content conveys context to screen readers.

technique: thick configurable 3D line rendering with vertex colors along a Hilbert curve spline
description: A luminous, rainbow-colored 3D space-filling curve rendered with controllable line thickness and optional dashing, orbiting in 3D with a picture-in-picture inset viewport. Ideal for data visualization hero sections, network topology displays, scientific or generative art backgrounds, and portfolio intros that need elegant animated line art.
usageNote: Wrap the init and animate logic inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref (renderer.domElement appended to the ref's container), or use react-three-fiber with a custom LineSegments2/Line2 abstraction. Clean up by calling renderer.dispose(), controls.dispose(), and removing the animation loop in the useEffect return. The inset viewport uses scissor/viewport tricks that work fine in both React and vanilla setups as long as the renderer size stays in sync with the container. No local asset paths are used so no substitution is needed.

Moderately GPU-intensive on mobile due to per-pixel line width computation; consider reducing linewidth and divisions on low-end devices. The dual-viewport (scissor) technique adds a second render pass per frame.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call matLine.resolution.set(width, height) on resize—thick lines will scale incorrectly. Not disposing LineGeometry and LineMaterial on unmount causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of the canvas container size breaks embedded use. Forgetting renderer.setScissorTest(false) after the inset pass corrupts subsequent renders.
accessibilityNotes: The animation is continuous rotation/orbit; wrap renderer.setAnimationLoop in a check for window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') and pause or replace with a static render. Provide an aria-hidden='true' on the canvas and a visually-hidden text description of the decorative graphic for screen readers. No interactive keyboard controls are exposed by default beyond OrbitControls mouse interaction.

technique: thick configurable 3D line rendering with raycaster hover detection

usageNote: Wrap the renderer, scene, camera, and animation loop inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref, returning a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame. For react-three-fiber, replace LineMaterial, Line2, and LineSegments2 with @react-three/drei's Line component which wraps these addons. Mobile support is functional but linewidth in world units may render inconsistently across mobile GPU drivers. The raycaster hover detection adds CPU cost per frame.

Not disposing LineGeometry and LineMaterial on component unmount causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/Height instead of reading from the container ref breaks embedded canvas sizing. Omitting computeLineDistances() breaks dashed line rendering if dashes are later added.

The spiral visualization carries no semantic content, so an aria-hidden wrapper and a descriptive aria-label on the canvas are recommended. Hover intersection markers are purely visual with no keyboard equivalent; avoid conveying critical data through them alone.

technique: thick wireframe mesh with pixel-width line control and picture-in-picture inset viewport
description: A 3D geometric mesh (icosahedron) rendered as a stylized wireframe with controllable thick lines and optional dashing, plus a small inset preview window showing the same scene from a secondary camera. Suits developer tools, data visualization dashboards, product configurators, or tech-aesthetic hero sections that want a structural, blueprint-like aesthetic.
usageNote: Wrap the renderer initialization in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js, attaching the renderer to the ref element instead of document.body. Use a cleanup return to call renderer.dispose() and remove the animation loop. The GUI and Stats panels are debug tools and should be removed for production. Replace the IcosahedronGeometry with any THREE geometry (e.g. loaded GLTF mesh) to wireframe arbitrary product shapes. The inset viewport uses scissor/viewport split on one renderer, which works fine in a single canvas.

The pixel-width line feature relies on a screen-resolution uniform and may render inconsistently on some mobile GPU drivers. The inset viewport renders the scene twice per frame, doubling draw calls.

Provide a static fallback image via a noscript tag or CSS background for users without WebGL support.
