usageNote: Wrap initialization in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; assign renderer.domElement to the ref instead of appending to document.body. Clean up with renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame in the useEffect return. Replace the HDR texture path ('textures/equirectangular/quarry_01_1k.hdr') with a hosted CDN URL or import via Next.js public folder (/public/textures/...). In react-three-fiber, use <CubeCamera> from @react-three/drei which wraps this pattern declaratively.
constraints: High GPU cost: cubeCamera.update() re-renders the scene six times per frame for the cube render target—avoid on low-end mobile or limit update frequency (e.g., every other frame). Requires WebGL2 for HalfFloatType render targets in some environments. HDR loading is asynchronous; show a fallback until the environment is ready. Not suitable for scenes needing many such reflective objects simultaneously.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call cubeCamera.update(renderer, scene) each frame breaks reflections. Not disposing cubeRenderTarget and material on unmount leaks GPU memory. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks in embedded or partial-page canvas contexts—use the container element's dimensions instead. Leaving the GUI (lil-gui) in production builds exposes internal material parameters to end users.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static high-quality render as a fallback image for users with prefers-reduced-motion or when WebGL is unavailable. The auto-rotating camera should be paused or slowed when reduced motion is detected (check window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')). The canvas has no semantic content so add aria-hidden='true' and provide adjacent descriptive text for screen readers.

technique: reflective sphere with custom cubemap mipmaps for environment mapping quality comparison
description: Two highly reflective spheres sit side by side, each mirror-mapping a surrounding environment using different mipmap strategies (manually authored vs GPU-generated), producing smooth, glossy reflections. Ideal for product configurators, material showcases, luxury e-commerce hero sections, or any site needing high-quality environmental reflections on 3D objects.
usageNote: Wrap the init logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js, or use react-three-fiber with a <mesh> and MeshBasicMaterial envMap prop. Replace the local 'textures/cube/angus/' path with your own CDN-hosted cubemap face images (6 faces per mip level, up to 9 levels); alternatively use a single equirectangular HDR loaded via RGBELoader and converted with PMREMGenerator, which is simpler and avoids the multi-file mipmap loading pattern. Clean up with renderer.dispose() on component unmount.
constraints: Requires WebGL with cube texture support (universally available on modern browsers). Loading 9 mip levels × 6 faces = 54 image requests is expensive on slow connections; batch or lazy-load where possible. High polygon sphere (128×128 segments) adds GPU vertex cost; reduce for mobile. Not suitable for WebGPU renderer without texture format adjustments.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call cubeTexture.dispose() and autoCubeTexture.dispose() on unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of the container element dimensions breaks embedded canvas layouts. Skipping needsUpdate=true after modifying texture properties results in stale rendering. Using generateMipmaps=true with manually supplied mipmaps will discard the manual ones.
accessibilityNotes: The scene is purely decorative/visual with no interactive UI beyond orbit controls. Add an aria-hidden='true' attribute to the canvas element. Provide a static fallback image for users with prefers-reduced-motion or no WebGL support. OrbitControls are not keyboard-navigable by default; for accessibility add keyboard event handlers or disable controls for decorative use cases.

technique: glass-refraction 3D sculpture with cubemap environment and mouse parallax
description: Three glass-like sculptural figures rendered with cube-map refraction bending the surrounding panoramic environment through them, set against a photographic skybox, with the camera gently tracking the mouse. Ideal for luxury product showcases, gemstone or crystal material studies, premium brand hero sections, or jewellery / glassware e-commerce landing pages.
usageNote: Wrap the init/animate logic inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer targeting ref.current instead of creating a div, and return a cleanup that calls renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame. Replace the PLY model path with a URL served from your public folder or a CDN (e.g. /models/lucy.ply), and replace the six cubemap texture paths with your own HDR or cube-face images hosted publicly. In react-three-fiber, use <mesh> with a meshPhongMaterial envMap from a CubeTextureLoader loaded in a useLoader hook, and set the texture mapping to THREE.CubeRefractionMapping after load.
constraints: Requires WebGL with cube-texture support (all modern browsers). Rendering three high-poly meshes with environment mapping is GPU-intensive — budget roughly 16–20 ms per frame on mid-range mobile GPUs; reduce polygon count or drop to one mesh on mobile. The PLY binary loader adds ~50 KB bundle weight. Not suitable for low-end or WebGL-unsupported devices.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() and material.dispose() on unmount causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/Height breaks in contained layouts — always derive dimensions from the parent element. Omitting textureCube.mapping = THREE.CubeRefractionMapping results in reflection instead of refraction. Not calling camera.updateProjectionMatrix() after resize breaks the aspect ratio.

Provide a high-quality poster image as a fallback for browsers without WebGL. The canvas carries no semantic content, so add aria-hidden='true' and surface product or brand information in adjacent DOM text for screen readers.

technique: custom cubemap mipmap rendering with color-coded LOD visualization on reflective spheres

The 512px cubemap render target is reasonable for most desktop GPUs but should be reduced to 128–256 on mobile. Not suitable for situations requiring WebGPU or server-side rendering.

Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks in embedded canvases — use the container element's dimensions instead. Use aria-hidden='true' on the canvas and provide a descriptive aria-label on the containing section. technique: physically-based 3D model viewer with displacement, normal, and AO maps plus environment reflections

Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions. Neglecting to call controls.update() each frame when enableDamping is true. Applying displacement map to a low-poly mesh expecting visible surface detail. Not handling the OBJLoader async callback failure case.

technique: 360-degree environment map reflection and refraction on a 3D sphere with skybox background
description: A reflective or refractive 3D sphere rendered against a seamless photographic or cubemap skybox environment, creating a mirror-like or glass-like orb effect. Add an aria-label to the canvas element describing the decorative 3D content for screen readers.

technique: HDR equirectangular image-based lighting with PBR materials

technique: PBR material showcase with prefiltered HDR environment lighting (PMREM cubemap)

technique: grounded HDR skybox with physically-based 3D product viewer

technique: HDR environment mapped physically-based material with PMREM skybox

Provide a static fallback image (a rendered product photo) for browsers without WebGL. technique: matcap-shaded 3D model with normal map and drag-and-drop texture swapping
description: A richly lit 3D model rendered with a matcap (material capture) shader that fakes complex studio lighting without any scene lights, enhanced by a normal map for surface detail. Ideal for product showcases, digital art galleries, avatar previews, or luxury brand hero sections where a sculptural, photographic-quality 3D object is needed with minimal rendering overhead.

Replace the EXR matcap path and GLTF model path with assets served from /public or a CDN (e.g. useLoader(EXRLoader, '/matcaps/mymatcap.exr')); the normal map JPEG should similarly be hosted and referenced via an absolute or relative URL from the public folder.

Provide a static fallback image of the model for users with prefers-reduced-motion or for environments without WebGL. Screen readers cannot interpret the 3D content, so supply an aria-label or visually hidden description of the depicted object.

technique: animated vertex-shader twist deformation on 3D mesh with custom GLSL injection
description: Two mirrored 3D head models continuously twist and undulate using a sinusoidal vertex deformation shader, rendered with normal-mapped surface coloring. Suits creative agency hero sections, interactive product showcases, or experimental art/portfolio sites that need a striking, living 3D centerpiece.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes the canvas. In Next.js use dynamic import with ssr:false. Replace the LeePerrySmith.glb path with any GLTF/GLB hosted on your CDN or in /public — the twist shader works on any mesh geometry. With react-three-fiber, implement onBeforeCompile inside a useMemo-created material and pass it to a <mesh>.
constraints: Requires WebGL with vertex shader support (universal on modern browsers). The custom GLSL injection via onBeforeCompile ties this to Three.js's internal shader chunks — upgrading Three.js versions may break the #include <begin_vertex> replacement. Moderate GPU cost from per-frame scene traversal and shader uniform updates; suitable for desktop and mid-range mobile but avoid using multiple high-poly meshes on low-end devices.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and geometry.dispose() on unmount causing memory leaks; not handling window resize leading to stretched canvas; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container ref for embedded use; reusing the same material instance for both meshes without customProgramCacheKey causing WebGL to share a single program and ignore the different twist amount; forgetting to store the shader reference in material.userData before the uniform is updated in the render loop.
accessibilityNotes: Add a prefers-reduced-motion media query check and pause the animation loop (cancel requestAnimationFrame or skip uniform time updates) when motion is reduced. Provide a static poster image fallback for users with no WebGL support. The canvas should have aria-hidden='true' and role='presentation' since it is purely decorative; do not rely on it to convey content.

technique: normal-mapped 3D head model with cinematic post-processing (bleach bypass, color correction, FXAA)
description: A photorealistic human head rendered with diffuse, specular, and normal maps under dynamic lighting, finished with bleach bypass and color correction post-processing for a filmic look. Suits luxury fashion, game studio portfolios, digital-human showcases, or high-end product/character reveals.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, wrap the entire init block in a useEffect with a canvas ref passed to the WebGLRenderer constructor (new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ canvas: ref.current })). Return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose(), composer dispose, and removes the resize listener. Replace all local asset paths (Map-COL.jpg, Map-SPEC.jpg, Infinite-Level_02_Tangent_SmoothUV.jpg, LeePerrySmith.glb) with paths to your own assets served from /public or a CDN. In react-three-fiber, use useLoader(GLTFLoader, url) and apply the MeshPhongMaterial with normalMap manually; post-processing requires @react-three/postprocessing.
constraints: Requires WebGL with support for HalfFloatType render targets and DepthTexture, which excludes very old mobile browsers. The multi-pass EffectComposer pipeline (5 passes) is moderately GPU-intensive; avoid on low-end mobile or battery-sensitive contexts. Orbit controls restrict pan, keeping focus on the model. GLTF model and three texture maps must be self-hosted or CDN-served due to CORS.

Not setting diffuseMap.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace causes washed-out color. Reusing the same WebGLRenderTarget without disposing it on unmount leaks GPU memory. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container ref breaks embedded or partial-page layouts. Omitting renderer.autoClear = false when using EffectComposer causes flickering.

Provide a static hero image fallback using a CSS background-image for users with prefers-reduced-motion or when WebGL is unavailable. Add an aria-hidden='true' attribute to the canvas and a visually-hidden text alternative describing the 3D content for screen readers. Avoid autoplay of any camera animations without a user gesture.

technique: interactive 3D model viewer with object-space normal map shading
description: A high-fidelity 3D sculpted bust with realistic surface detail rendered via object-space normal mapping, lit by a camera-attached point light that follows user interaction. Ideal for luxury product showcases, museum or cultural heritage displays, portfolio hero sections, or any site needing a premium interactive 3D artifact viewer.

Return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes event listeners. Replace the local GLB path ('models/gltf/Nefertiti/Nefertiti.glb') with a URL-imported asset (e.g. placed in /public and referenced as '/models/yourModel.glb'), or use a CDN-hosted GLB. Use a prefers-reduced-motion media query to disable auto-rotation or any animation loops. Screen readers cannot interpret 3D content — include a text description of the displayed object nearby in the DOM.

technique: clearcoat PBR material showcase with orbiting point light and HDR environment

Ideal for product configurator pages, luxury brand hero sections, or material/finish selectors for automotive, jewelry, or consumer electronics sites.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate block inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref, passing the ref's current element to the WebGLRenderer constructor instead of appending to document.body. Replace all local texture paths (textures/carbon/, textures/water/, etc.) with paths under /public or CDN URLs; replace the pisaHDR cube map with your own HDR set loaded via HDRCubeTextureLoader or switch to RGBELoader + a single .hdr file for simplicity. High fill-rate cost due to four high-poly spheres with multi-layer normal maps and clearcoat; avoid running more than a handful of such materials simultaneously. Not suitable for low-end mobile GPUs without LOD reduction or material simplification.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and texture.dispose() on unmount in React causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using a container div's offsetWidth/offsetHeight breaks embedded or partial-page layouts. Omitting the colorSpace assignment on the diffuse texture produces washed-out colors. Using RepeatWrapping without setting repeat values leaves textures looking flat. Not setting renderer.toneMapping and toneMappingExposure will make the HDR-lit scene appear overblown.
accessibilityNotes: The orbiting point light and rotating group constitute continuous motion; respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing the animation loop or stopping the light orbit when the media query matches. Provide a static fallback image of the material grid for users with reduced motion or when WebGL is unavailable. The canvas has no semantic content, so add aria-hidden='true' and place descriptive text or a visible label nearby for screen readers.

technique: physically-based glass transmission sphere with HDR environment lighting
description: A translucent glass sphere rendered with realistic light transmission, refraction (IOR), and specular highlights against an HDR environment panorama. Ideal for luxury product pages, jewelry or glassware showcases, perfume brand hero sections, or any high-end e-commerce experience that needs photorealistic material rendering.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/render logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js, or use react-three-fiber with a <mesh> and MeshPhysicalMaterial with transmission={1}. Replace the local HDR texture path ('textures/equirectangular/royal_esplanade_2k.hdr.jpg') with a publicly hosted or bundled asset imported via your build system (e.g., import hdrUrl from './assets/env.hdr.jpg' in Vite, or place it in /public in Next.js and reference '/env.hdr.jpg'). Remove the lil-gui panel for production builds and bake parameter values directly into the material.
constraints: WebGL renderer required — WebGPU not targeted here. Transmission rendering is GPU-expensive because it requires an extra render pass; avoid using many transmissive objects simultaneously. Mobile GPUs may struggle with transmissionResolutionScale=1; reduce to 0.5 or lower for mobile. Requires THREE.MeshPhysicalMaterial support (three.js r130+). HDR environment loading adds significant network payload.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose the UltraHDR texture and geometry on component unmount, causing memory leaks in SPAs. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container ref for embedded sections. Leaving the lil-gui debug panel in production. Not setting renderer.transmissionResolutionScale lower on mobile, causing severe frame drops. Neglecting to call renderer.setPixelRatio(window.devicePixelRatio) correctly when embedding in a partial-page canvas.
accessibilityNotes: Add a prefers-reduced-motion media query check; if reduced motion is preferred, stop OrbitControls auto-rotate and freeze the scene or replace with a static hero image. Wrap the canvas in a <figure> with a descriptive aria-label such as 'Rotating glass sphere product visualization'. Ensure any text overlaid on the canvas has sufficient contrast. Provide a static fallback image for environments where WebGL is unavailable.

technique: physically-based glass/crystal 3D object with transmission, attenuation, and alpha transparency on transparent canvas
description: A photorealistic glass or crystal object rendered with light transmission, color attenuation, IOR refraction, and specular highlights against a transparent (alpha) background, allowing page content or CSS backgrounds to show through the canvas. Ideal for luxury product showcases, hero sections, premium brand landing pages, or interactive material configurators where the 3D element must integrate seamlessly with the underlying web page design.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref, or use react-three-fiber with a Canvas that has 'gl={{ alpha: true }}'. The renderer is initialized with 'alpha: true' which is essential to preserve. Replace 'textures/equirectangular/royal_esplanade_2k.hdr.jpg' with a CDN-hosted UltraHDR or standard HDR equirectangular for environment lighting, and replace 'models/gltf/DragonAttenuation.glb' with your own GLTF model that uses MeshPhysicalMaterial with transmission properties. In r3f, use <mesh material={new THREE.MeshPhysicalMaterial({transmission:1,...})} /> and the <Environment> component from @react-three/drei for the HDR.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 for physical transmission to work correctly; transmission rendering is GPU-intensive and may drop below 60fps on mid-range mobile devices. The alpha canvas compositing only works if the renderer domElement is layered over HTML via CSS (position:absolute). Not suitable for scenes requiring many transmissive objects simultaneously. Requires a modern browser with MeshPhysicalMaterial transmission support.
antiPatterns: Forgetting 'alpha: true' on WebGLRenderer breaks page background bleed-through. Not setting 'renderer.domElement.style.position = absolute' causes layout issues when overlaying HTML. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using a container ref breaks in component-based frameworks. Forgetting to call 'material.needsUpdate = true' when toggling transparent flag causes rendering artifacts. Not disposing the HDR texture and geometry on component unmount causes memory leaks.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static PNG fallback of the hero object for users with prefers-reduced-motion or no WebGL support. The interactive orbit controls have no keyboard equivalents by default — add keyboard event listeners or expose discrete rotation buttons for accessibility. Screen readers will not perceive the 3D canvas; add an aria-label or visually-hidden description of the product/object being displayed.

technique: subsurface scattering shader on organic 3D mesh with multi-point lighting
description: A 3D organic model rendered with translucent skin-like shading where light visually penetrates the surface, simulating the look of wax, skin, marble, or biological tissue under multiple colored light sources. Ideal for luxury product showcases, medical or scientific visualizations, jewelry or cosmetics product pages, or high-end hero sections where materials need to feel physically tactile and premium.
usageNote: Port into React/Next.js using a useEffect hook with a canvas ref to mount the renderer, and clean up with renderer.dispose() on unmount. Alternatively use react-three-fiber with a custom ShaderMaterial and the SubsurfaceScatteringShader uniforms. Replace the local FBX model path (models/fbx/stanford-bunny.fbx) and texture paths (white.jpg, bunny_thickness.jpg) with your own hosted assets or Next.js public folder paths. The thickness map (a grayscale texture encoding mesh depth) is critical and must be pre-baked for your specific model in a tool like Blender.
constraints: Requires WebGL with shader support; not suitable for WebGL1-only environments. The ShaderMaterial with lights:true is moderately GPU-intensive and may perform poorly on low-end mobile GPUs. FBX loading adds initial load time. Best suited for hero or spotlight sections rather than repeated instances. Thickness map must be custom-generated per model, limiting rapid asset swapping.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to bake a thickness map for your own model (using a generic one gives wrong scattering). Not calling renderer.dispose() and geometry/material.dispose() on React unmount causing memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions. Omitting lights:true on the ShaderMaterial causing the shader to receive no lighting data. Neglecting to set colorSpace on loaded textures leading to washed-out colors.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static high-quality rendered image fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion enabled or when WebGL is unavailable. The 3D canvas is purely decorative so aria-hidden='true' should be set on the container. No interactive keyboard controls are required for a display-only showcase, but if OrbitControls are exposed to users add keyboard focus and ARIA labels for the canvas.

technique: split-screen anisotropic vs non-anisotropic texture quality comparison on a receding ground plane
description: A side-by-side split-screen view of a textured ground plane extending to the horizon, comparing high-quality anisotropic texture filtering against standard filtering. Suits documentation sites, graphics settings tutorials, quality comparison tools, or any 3D product configurator that needs to showcase rendering fidelity options.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, place the renderer initialization inside a useEffect with a canvas ref, returning a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose(). With react-three-fiber, use two <Canvas> elements side by side or a single canvas with scissor rendering via useFrame and gl.setScissor. Replace 'textures/crate.gif' with a URL from your public directory or a CDN-hosted texture (e.g. '/textures/floor.jpg').
constraints: Requires WebGL with anisotropic filtering extension (EXT_texture_filter_anisotropic) for the quality difference to be visible; nearly all desktop GPUs support it but some mobile GPUs or WebGL1 fallbacks may report maxAnisotropy of 0. Scissor-based split-screen is efficient but the dual-scene architecture doubles draw calls. Performance cost is low on desktop, moderate on low-end mobile due to large plane geometry and high repeat count.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.setScissorTest(false) after rendering causes subsequent DOM overlays to be clipped. Hardcoding SCREEN_WIDTH/SCREEN_HEIGHT instead of listening to window resize events breaks layout on orientation change or panel resize. Not disposing both textures (texture1, texture2) and their materials on unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Using renderer.autoClear=false without an explicit renderer.clear() call each frame causes frame ghosting.
accessibilityNotes: The scene responds to mouse movement for camera panning; provide a static fallback image for users with prefers-reduced-motion or on devices without pointer input. The split-screen comparison carries no semantic meaning to screen readers—add aria-label or visually hidden text explaining the left vs right difference. Keyboard navigation is not implemented and should be added (e.g. arrow keys for camera pan) if the comparison is a core UI feature.

technique: live canvas drawing projected as texture onto a rotating 3D object
description: A spinning 3D cube whose surface displays whatever the user draws on a 2D canvas in real time, creating an interactive graffiti-on-object effect. Suits creative portfolio sites, product customization tools, educational coding demos, or interactive art sections where users can paint directly onto a 3D object.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, wrap all Three.js setup in a useEffect with a cleanup return that disposes renderer, geometry, and material. Attach the renderer to a div via a useRef. The drawing canvas can be a hidden or sibling DOM element referenced with a second useRef. In react-three-fiber, use a useRef on a CanvasTexture and update needsUpdate inside a useFrame hook; bind pointer events directly to the canvas element. No local asset paths need replacing — this example is entirely self-contained.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer; not suitable for SSR without guards. Canvas texture updates trigger GPU re-uploads on every draw stroke, which is low cost for small textures (128×128 here) but scales poorly with high-resolution canvases. Touch input works well on mobile via pointer events. The rotating cube loop runs continuously regardless of user interaction.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to set material.map.needsUpdate = true after every stroke will freeze the texture. Not calling renderer.dispose() and geometry.dispose() on unmount causes memory leaks in SPAs. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/Height instead of measuring a container element breaks embedded layouts. Skipping pointer capture means strokes drop when the cursor leaves the canvas during fast movement.
accessibilityNotes: The 3D canvas is purely decorative/interactive but has no keyboard access or screen reader label; add aria-label and role='img' to the renderer canvas for screen readers. Provide a reduced-motion fallback by pausing mesh rotation when prefers-reduced-motion is set. Offer a static preview image as a noscript or CSS fallback for non-WebGL environments.

technique: split-screen texture filtering comparison with mouse parallax camera
description: A side-by-side split-screen renders the same framed image and checkered floor twice — once with linear (smooth) texture filtering and once with nearest-neighbor (pixelated) filtering — while the camera follows the mouse slowly, creating a parallax gallery effect. Ideal for a product or portfolio site that needs to showcase image quality comparisons, art print shops, or photo galleries with an interactive preview component.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; attach the renderer to the ref instead of appending to document.body. Use renderer.domElement passed to the ref container. Replace the local texture path ('textures/758px-Canestra_di_frutta_(Caravaggio).jpg') with an asset from your /public folder or a CDN URL passed in as a prop. Clean up with renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame in the useEffect return. For react-three-fiber, manage the two scenes manually via useThree and gl.setScissor in a custom render loop.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer with scissor test support (universally available). Runs two full scene renders per frame, roughly doubling draw call cost — acceptable for low-poly scenes like this but avoid adding many high-poly objects. Mobile performance is fine at typical resolutions; high device pixel ratios may cause fill-rate pressure. Not suitable for server-side rendering without a canvas polyfill.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.setScissorTest(false) after the split render causes clipping artifacts elsewhere. Hardcoding SCREEN_WIDTH/SCREEN_HEIGHT without a resize listener breaks layout on window resize — add a ResizeObserver or window resize handler. Not disposing both scenes' geometries and textures on unmount causes memory leaks. Cloning textures without setting needsUpdate = true on the clone leads to a blank second panel.
accessibilityNotes: The canvas has no semantic role or alt text — add aria-label='Interactive texture quality comparison' to the container div. Provide a static side-by-side JPEG fallback image inside a <noscript> tag. For reduced-motion preferences, detect prefers-reduced-motion and freeze the camera position instead of following the mouse, stopping the parallax drift entirely.

technique: interactive HTML-as-texture mapped onto a rotating 3D rounded box
description: A reflective rounded cube slowly rotates with rich HTML content (formatted text, emoji, RTL text, inline images, SVG, and interactive form elements) rendered directly onto its surface as a live texture. Suits product showcase pages, creative agency landing pages, or interactive portfolio sections where blending DOM UI with 3D geometry creates a striking focal point.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate block inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js, or use react-three-fiber with a custom <mesh> and a useFrame hook for animation. The HTMLTexture constructor accepts a DOM element, so create it via document.createElement inside the effect (not JSX) to keep it off the visible DOM. Replace the local image path 'textures/758px-Canestra_di_frutta_(Caravaggio).jpg' with any publicly hosted image URL or import a local asset through your bundler (e.g., Next.js public folder or Vite asset import). The three-html-render polyfill must also be installed via npm.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 or a browser supporting the HTML-in-Canvas API or the three-html-render polyfill; rendering HTML to a texture is GPU- and CPU-intensive, so limit to one or two such objects per scene. Not suitable for performance-critical mobile experiences or low-end devices. Interactive elements inside the texture require the InteractionManager addon for raycasting; pointer events inside the HTML are proxied, not native, so complex widget trees may behave unexpectedly.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call interactions.update() each frame breaks all click/hover events on the mesh. Not disposing the HTMLTexture on component unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight without a resize handler breaks layout on viewport change. Placing the element inside the visible DOM instead of keeping it detached may cause double-rendering artifacts. Skipping the polyfill check in browsers without native HTML-in-Canvas support will silently produce a blank texture.
accessibilityNotes: The 3D rotating animation should respect prefers-reduced-motion; add a check to stop or greatly reduce rotation speed when the user has reduced motion enabled. All meaningful content inside the HTML texture is invisible to screen readers since it is painted to a canvas surface—provide equivalent accessible text in the surrounding DOM. Interactive elements (button, input) inside the texture are not keyboard-navigable via standard Tab flow; add visible fallback controls outside the 3D scene for keyboard and assistive technology users.

technique: split-screen mipmap LOD comparison with framed image display
description: Two side-by-side 3D scenes display the same image mounted as a framed artwork above a receding tiled floor, each using different texture filtering strategies (linear/trilinear vs nearest-neighbor mipmapping) with fog fading into darkness. Suited for image quality comparison tools, museum-style digital gallery sections, or technical product showcases demonstrating rendering fidelity.
usageNote: Wrap the entire setup in a React useEffect with a canvas ref, returning a cleanup function that disposes renderer, textures, and removes the canvas. Replace the local JPG path with a public-folder URL or an imported asset URL (e.g. import imgUrl from './your-image.jpg' in a bundler, or place it in /public and reference '/your-image.jpg' in Next.js). The split-screen is achieved via renderer.setViewport/setScissor calls not shown in the truncated snippet — preserve those when porting. For react-three-fiber, use two <Canvas> instances or a custom renderer with manual scissoring via gl.setScissor.

Moderate GPU cost due to two full scenes rendered per frame. Mobile support is generally fine but manual mipmap arrays may behave differently on some mobile GPUs. Not suitable for WebGPU renderer without adaptation.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call texture.dispose() and renderer.dispose() on unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding SCREEN_WIDTH/SCREEN_HEIGHT instead of observing ResizeObserver will break layout on resize. Cloning a texture with .clone() does not deep-copy mipmaps on all driver versions — verify mipmap data is correctly shared. Omitting needsUpdate = true after modifying texture data will silently show stale content.
accessibilityNotes: The canvas has no accessible label or role; add aria-label describing the content (e.g. 'Interactive 3D gallery displaying artwork with texture filtering comparison'). Provide a static fallback inside a

technique: runtime partial texture patching with random color block injection
description: A flat plane displays a checkerboard texture that receives randomly colored 32×32 pixel patches stamped onto it at random positions every 100ms, creating a live mosaic-patching effect. Suits interactive data visualizations, live heatmaps, pixel-art editors, or real-time status boards where regions of a surface need to update independently without re-uploading the full texture.
usageNote: Wrap in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; assign renderer.domElement to the ref. Replace the local checkerboard texture URL with any hosted image (CDN, /public folder, or imported asset). In react-three-fiber, use useTexture for the diffuse map and a useFrame loop with a ref-stored DataTexture. The copyTextureToTexture call and DataTexture creation belong in a useRef to persist across renders.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer with copyTextureToTexture support (WebGL2 preferred). The diffuseMap must have generateMipmaps:false and LinearFilter to accept partial updates correctly. Performance cost is low per frame since only a small 32×32 buffer is written, but frequent GPU texture copies accumulate; avoid sub-100ms intervals on low-end mobile GPUs.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to set generateMipmaps:false and minFilter:LinearFilter will cause incorrect rendering after partial updates. Not disposing dataTexture and geometry on component unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container element breaks layout in embedded components. Assuming the source texture is ready before the async load resolves will throw null errors.
accessibilityNotes: The random color flashing at 10Hz may trigger photosensitivity issues; honour prefers-reduced-motion by pausing the animation loop or reducing update frequency to once per second. Provide a static fallback image for screen readers via an aria-label on the canvas or a visually-hidden description. No keyboard interaction is present so no focus management is needed.

technique: UV texture transform controls (offset, repeat, rotation, center) on a 3D mesh
description: A 3D box with a fully configurable texture transform — adjustable tiling, offset, and rotation around a pivot — rendered in real time. Suits product configurators, material preview tools, or any site where users need to fine-tune how a texture or pattern maps onto a surface.
usageNote: Wrap the renderer setup and animation loop inside a useEffect with a canvas ref (or use react-three-fiber's useTexture and a mesh with texture.offset/repeat/rotation driven by state). Replace the local 'textures/uv_grid_opengl.jpg' path with any hosted image URL or an import of an asset bundled through Next.js's public folder or an image CDN. The GUI controls can be replaced with React UI sliders bound to state that calls updateUvTransform equivalents.
constraints: Requires WebGL support; the texture transform logic is GPU-cheap and runs well on mobile. The OrbitControls interaction means the canvas must receive pointer events. Not suitable for purely static or CSS-driven surfaces. Texture repeat/anisotropy settings benefit from a proper GPU but degrade gracefully.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose the texture and geometry on component unmount causing memory leaks; not calling texture.needsUpdate or re-triggering render after transform changes; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of measuring the container element; leaving matrixAutoUpdate as default and then also manually setting the matrix, causing conflicts.
accessibilityNotes: The spinning/interactive 3D canvas conveys purely visual information; provide a static screenshot fallback via a noscript tag or a CSS background for users with reduced-motion preferences or no WebGL. Add aria-hidden='true' to the canvas and ensure any surrounding UI controls have proper labels for screen readers.

technique: toon-shaded sphere grid with animated point light and outline effect
description: A 3D grid of spheres rendered with cel/toon shading in varying hues and gradient maps, illuminated by an orbiting point light with a cartoon outline effect applied to the whole scene. Suits stylized product configurators, game UI material pickers, or creative agency landing pages that want a distinctive illustrated aesthetic.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer targeting the ref element instead of appending to document.body, store the animation frame ID for cleanup, and call renderer.dispose() on unmount. For react-three-fiber, use drei's OutlineEffect equivalent or a custom effect pass. Replace the local font path 'fonts/gentilis_regular.typeface.json' with a font file hosted in your /public folder or loaded from a CDN such as the three.js GitHub raw assets URL.
constraints: Rendering hundreds of toon-shaded meshes plus OutlineEffect adds a full-scene extra render pass, making this moderately GPU-intensive; avoid on low-end mobile devices. Requires WebGL with sufficient texture units for gradient maps. OrbitControls requires pointer events so touch support works but may feel sluggish on older phones.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose geometry and materials when the component unmounts causes memory leaks. Not cancelling the animation loop (renderer.setAnimationLoop(null)) on cleanup will keep rendering after the component is gone. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of the container element's dimensions breaks layouts where the canvas is not full-screen. Loading the font synchronously before the scene is ready causes race conditions.
accessibilityNotes: The animated orbiting light creates continuous motion; wrap the animation loop in a check against window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') and pause or slow the particleLight orbit. Provide a static fallback image for screen readers via an aria-label on the canvas element. The 3D scene carries no semantic content so role='img' with a descriptive aria-label is sufficient.

technique: video-texture mosaic of animated 3D cubes with bloom post-processing and mouse parallax
description: A live video feed is mapped across a grid of 200 individually colored, rotating 3D cubes that periodically scatter and return, with bloom glow and mouse-driven camera parallax. Suits hero sections, media brand landing pages, entertainment platforms, or any site wanting a dramatic, kinetic video showcase.
usageNote: Wrap all init/animate logic in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; pass the ref's current element as the renderer target instead of appending to document.body. Replace the document.getElementById('video') lookup with a ref to a <video> element rendered in JSX (with autoPlay muted playsInline). EffectComposer must be initialized after the renderer is mounted. Return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes event listeners.
constraints: Requires WebGL with floating-point render targets for EffectComposer/BloomPass; high GPU cost from 200 meshes plus multi-pass post-processing. Not recommended for low-end mobile or battery-sensitive contexts. The live video texture requires browser autoplay permissions (muted video recommended). Desktop-first experience.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call composer.setSize on resize (causes blurry bloom); not disposing individual BoxGeometry and MeshLambertMaterial instances on unmount causing memory leaks; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions; omitting playsInline and muted attributes on the video element which blocks autoplay on mobile; not handling the video 'canplay' event before creating the VideoTexture.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a prefers-reduced-motion media query that stops the animation loop and renders a single static frame or a plain poster image fallback. The video element should have aria-hidden='true' since it is decorative. Ensure any overlaid text has sufficient contrast against the dynamic background. No keyboard interaction is exposed, so no focus management is needed for the canvas itself.

technique: live webcam feed mapped onto a spherical panoramic array of video-textured planes
description: 128 flat panels tiled across the inside of a sphere each display the user's live webcam feed in real time, creating an immersive kaleidoscopic video environment the user can orbit around. Suits interactive art installations, experimental brand experiences, video call backgrounds, or 'about me' pages that want a striking self-referential visual.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, initialize the scene inside a useEffect with a canvas ref (renderer.domElement appended to a container div ref). Store the video element in a useRef so it persists. Call navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia inside the same useEffect and stop all tracks on cleanup (stream.getTracks().forEach(t => t.stop())). With react-three-fiber, use a <mesh> inside a loop with a videoTexture built from a <video> element managed via a ref in a parent component. No local assets to replace.
constraints: Requires getUserMedia (HTTPS or localhost only; not available in all embedded iframes). Camera permission must be granted by the user. Moderate GPU cost due to 128 mesh instances sharing one VideoTexture — acceptable on mid-range desktop GPUs but may degrade on low-end mobile devices. WebGL renderer required. Not suitable for contexts where camera access is unavailable or privacy is a concern.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to stop media stream tracks on component unmount causing the camera light to stay on. Not disposing the VideoTexture when the component unmounts leading to GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using a container element's dimensions. Forgetting to set video.srcObject = null on cleanup. Not handling the getUserMedia rejection gracefully with user-facing UI feedback.
accessibilityNotes: The live camera feed is a visually intensive full-screen experience with no inherent semantic content — add an aria-label on the canvas describing the experience. Provide a visible 'skip' or 'disable camera' button for users who do not wish to grant camera access or find the motion disorienting. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by not starting the animation loop or offering a static placeholder image instead. Ensure the permission prompt is not the only call to action on the page.

technique: dual-mode wireframe rendering with adjustable line thickness via custom ShaderMaterial
description: Renders a 3D mesh in two side-by-side wireframe styles: a standard thin-line wireframe and a smooth, thickness-controllable wireframe using a custom shader with barycentric coordinates. Suits technical product visualizations, developer tools dashboards, 3D model preview pages, or architectural/engineering portfolio sites that want a clean, schematic aesthetic.
usageNote: Wrap the renderer, scene, camera, and OrbitControls setup in a useEffect with a canvas ref (or use react-three-fiber's <Canvas> with a custom ShaderMaterial). The vertex and fragment shaders must be extracted from inline <script> tags and stored as JS template strings or imported GLSL files. Replace the BufferGeometryLoader asset path with a URL to your own hosted JSON geometry, a GLTF/GLB file loaded via GLTFLoader, or a procedural BufferGeometry (e.g. BoxGeometry, SphereGeometry). Remove lil-gui and wire thickness control to React state or a range input instead.
constraints: Requires WebGL with antialias enabled for alphaToCoverage to work correctly; without antialias the thick-wireframe edges will alias badly. Custom ShaderMaterial with barycentric wireframe requires non-indexed geometry (indices must be expanded). Moderate GPU cost for dense meshes. Mobile support is generally fine but line thickness shader may vary on low-end GPUs.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.deleteAttribute or expand indexed geometry before adding barycentric center attributes, which causes incorrect wireframe rendering. Not disposing geometry and materials on component unmount in React. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of measuring the parent container. Leaving the lil-gui DOM element attached after component unmount. Using indexed geometry directly without converting it to non-indexed first.
accessibilityNotes: Pure decorative 3D visualization with no interactive content beyond orbit rotation; add aria-hidden='true' to the canvas. Provide a static screenshot fallback via a <noscript> tag or CSS background for users without JS or WebGL. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by disabling OrbitControls auto-rotation and skipping any animation loop. No keyboard navigation is inherent; if the model conveys information, supplement with text descriptions.

technique: oriented bounding box (OBB) collision detection with click-to-select raycasting
description: A scene of 100 randomly oriented, rotating 3D boxes that turn red when colliding with each other and can be individually selected by clicking, showing a black wireframe highlight. Suited for interactive product configurators, spatial inventory systems, game-like dashboards, or any UI needing real-time 3D collision awareness and object picking.
usageNote: In React or Next.js, wrap all initialization inside a useEffect with a canvas ref and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes event listeners. With react-three-fiber, use useFrame for the animation loop and useRef for OBB userData. Replace the direct document.addEventListener('click') with an onClick prop on the canvas or R3F's raycaster hooks. No local assets are referenced, so no path substitution is needed.
constraints: Running O(n²) OBB intersection checks on 100 objects is moderate CPU cost per frame; scaling beyond ~200 objects without spatial partitioning (e.g., BVH) will degrade performance noticeably. Requires WebGL renderer. Mobile support is functional but touch events are not wired; the click handler must be extended to handle touchstart for mobile selection.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call object.updateMatrixWorld() before updating OBBs causes stale collision data. Not disposing the shared BoxGeometry and per-object materials on unmount leaks GPU memory. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of the container element's dimensions breaks embedded layouts. Omitting controls.update() in the animation loop breaks damping.
accessibilityNotes: The scene is purely decorative/interactive with no keyboard navigation for selecting objects; add tabIndex and keydown handlers to the canvas for keyboard-driven selection. Provide a static screenshot fallback via a noscript tag or CSS background. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or drastically slowing the rotation delta when the media query matches.

technique: smooth quaternion rotation toward moving target (slerp turret tracking)
description: A cone-shaped object smoothly rotates to face a randomly-repositioned target point on an invisible sphere, demonstrating gradual orientation interpolation versus instant look-at. Suits product configurators, interactive 3D dashboards, or game-like UI elements where an object needs to track a moving cursor or waypoint.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref and a cleanup that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the animation loop. In react-three-fiber, use useFrame with a ref to the mesh and call quaternion.rotateTowards() each frame. Replace the setTimeout target cycle with a state-driven callback or a useInterval hook. No local assets are needed.
constraints: Very low GPU cost — just a few simple geometries and no textures. Runs well on mobile. Requires WebGL (not WebGPU). The lil-gui debug panel should be removed or replaced with your own UI controls in production.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to remove the setTimeout loop on component unmount causes memory leaks and ghost animations. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks in embedded canvas contexts — always derive size from a container ref. Not disposing geometry and material on teardown leaks GPU memory. Leaving the debug GUI in production adds unnecessary bundle weight.
accessibilityNotes: Wrap the canvas in an aria-hidden container since it conveys no textual information. Honor prefers-reduced-motion by skipping the rotateTowards animation and jumping instantly to the target orientation (effectively always using lookAt mode). Provide a static screenshot fallback for screen readers or no-JS environments.

technique: batched mesh rendering with per-instance color, transform, and transparency
description: Hundreds of randomly placed, colored, and rotating 3D shapes (cones, boxes, spheres) rendered efficiently using BatchedMesh for minimal draw calls. Ideal for 3D product showcases, data visualization backdrops, interactive hero sections, or any site needing many distinct animated objects without sacrificing performance.
usageNote: Wrap initialization in a useEffect hook with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; assign renderer.domElement to the ref's current container. Replace the top-level init/animate calls with effect setup and a returned cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the animation frame. react-three-fiber users should use <BatchedMesh> via drei or manage the imperative API inside a useEffect inside a <Canvas>. No local assets to replace.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 for BatchedMesh (THREE.BatchedMesh is WebGL2-only); not supported on very old mobile browsers. High object counts (20 000+) remain GPU-friendly due to batching, but the naive fallback mode creates one draw call per object and will tank performance on mobile. Best suited for decorative or data-heavy 3D scenes where instancing alone is insufficient because objects differ in geometry.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call mesh.dispose() and material.dispose() on cleanup causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks layout in component-based apps — use the container element's clientWidth/clientHeight instead. Not removing the renderer's domElement from the DOM on unmount causes duplicate canvases. Setting frustumCulled = false globally without enabling perObjectFrustumCulled wastes GPU on off-screen instances.
accessibilityNotes: Wrap the canvas in a <div role='img' aria-label='...'> describing the decorative scene. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or zeroing rotation speeds; provide a static screenshot fallback via a CSS background-image for users with reduced-motion preferences or no WebGL support. The scene is purely decorative and carries no interactive keyboard or screen-reader requirements, but ensure tab focus is not trapped inside the canvas element.

technique: real-time planar reflectors with Reflector surfaces (floor and wall mirrors)
description: A 3D room scene with a circular floor mirror and a large vertical wall mirror that both render real-time reflections of the environment and animated objects moving through it. Ideal for luxury product showcases, virtual showrooms, jewelry or cosmetics brand pages, or any hero section where a premium, high-gloss aesthetic is needed.
usageNote: Wrap the init and animate logic inside a useEffect hook with a canvas ref in React/Next.js. Attach the renderer to the ref'd canvas element instead of appending to a container div. Use a cleanup return in useEffect to call renderer.dispose() and remove the event listener. react-three-fiber users can use the <Reflector> component from @react-three/drei which wraps the same addon. No local assets are needed; all geometry is procedural.
constraints: Each Reflector maintains its own render target (a full scene re-render from the mirror's perspective), so two mirrors means two extra render passes per frame — this is expensive. Avoid adding more than two or three mirrors. Performance degrades noticeably on mid-range mobile GPUs; consider disabling or substituting a static cubemap reflection on mobile. Requires WebGL1 or WebGL2 renderer; not compatible with WebGPU renderer without porting.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to update the Reflector's render target size on window resize (must call setSize on both groundMirror and verticalMirror). Hardcoding canvas size instead of reading from the container's bounding rect. Not disposing Reflector render targets on component unmount, causing GPU memory leaks. Setting resolutionScale to 1 on all screen sizes without checking devicePixelRatio, which can cause severe overdraw on Retina displays.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static fallback image for users with prefers-reduced-motion enabled by detecting the media query and skipping the animation loop. The 3D canvas is decorative; add aria-hidden='true' to the canvas element and provide meaningful text or image content alongside it for screen reader users. Ensure any UI controls (like the resolution slider) have proper label associations.

technique: 3D text flowing along an editable closed spline curve
description: A looping 3D text mesh continuously travels along a smooth, closed Catmull-Rom spline whose control points can be dragged interactively to reshape the path in real time. Suits hero sections, loading screens, or branding moments on creative agency, game, or entertainment sites where animated typographic motion is a core design element.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate logic in a useEffect with a canvas ref and pass the ref's current element to the WebGLRenderer constructor instead of appending to document.body. Clean up with renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame in the useEffect return. Replace 'fonts/helvetiker_regular.typeface.json' with a font file served from your public/ folder (e.g. '/fonts/helvetiker_regular.typeface.json') or load it from a CDN such as unpkg; alternatively use react-three-fiber with @react-three/drei's <Text3D> component which bundles its own font loading. The Flow modifier from CurveModifier.js must still be imported as a three.js addon.
constraints: Requires WebGL1 or WebGL2; the CurveModifier uses texture-based GPU skinning so it will not run on very old mobile GPUs. The font JSON must be served over HTTP (no file:// protocol). Performance is moderate; a single flowing mesh is fine on mobile but adding many simultaneous Flow instances will stress lower-end devices. TransformControls require pointer events and are not touch-optimised by default.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call flow.updateCurve() after dragging control handles, causing the mesh to follow a stale curve. Not disposing the TextGeometry and Flow object on component unmount, causing GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions, breaking layout in non-fullscreen contexts. Loading the font synchronously or without an error handler, silently producing an empty scene.

Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or stopping the moveAlongCurve animation (set the increment to 0) and hiding the interactive control handles when the media query matches. Keyboard users cannot interact with TransformControls without additional focus management.

technique: instanced 3D objects flowing along multiple editable spline curves
description: Multiple colored 3D text (or mesh) instances animate continuously around two looping spline paths in 3D space, with draggable control handles that reshape the curves in real time. Suits hero sections, loading screens, product showcases, or interactive brand experiences where looping motion along a custom path conveys energy and craftsmanship.
usageNote: Wrap all init/animate logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; assign renderer.domElement to the ref instead of appending to document.body. Remove the Stats panel for production. The font is loaded from a local path ('fonts/helvetiker_regular.typeface.json') — replace it with a URL to a publicly hosted typeface JSON (e.g. from the three.js CDN or your own /public folder). In react-three-fiber, use the CurveModifier addon directly inside a useFrame loop with InstancedFlow managed via useRef.

TransformControls require pointer events and are not mobile-friendly without additional touch handling. Not suitable for purely static or server-rendered pages without a canvas fallback.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() and material.dispose() on unmount causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using the container element dimensions breaks embedded or partial-page usage. Not updating curve lines after handle drag results in visual mismatch. Loading the font synchronously or ignoring the async callback can cause a blank scene. Failing to remove the animation loop (renderer.setAnimationLoop(null)) on component unmount causes loop accumulation.

The 3D text is not readable by screen readers; provide an ARIA label or visually hidden text conveying the same message. Keyboard control of the transform handles is not implemented by default and would require custom key event bindings.

technique: real-time edge-split shading modifier on 3D mesh with interactive normal/angle controls
description: A detailed 3D model rendered with dynamically adjustable hard/soft edge shading, controlled by a cutoff angle parameter. Suits product configurators, 3D asset preview tools, or technical visualization sections where users need to inspect surface quality and shading fidelity of imported models.
usageNote: Port into React/Next.js using a useEffect hook with a canvas ref: instantiate renderer targeting the ref, clean up in the effect's return. For react-three-fiber, wrap EdgeSplitModifier logic in a useMemo that recomputes geometry when cutOffAngle or tryKeepNormals params change. Replace local OBJ and texture asset paths with URLs served from your /public directory or a CDN; pass them as props or environment variables.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer with standard material support; EdgeSplitModifier recomputes geometry on every parameter change so it is CPU-heavy on dense meshes — avoid running on mobile low-end devices. Not suitable for real-time animation loops that change shading params per frame. Best for static or user-triggered updates.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() before replacing mesh.geometry on param change causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight breaks in component-mounted canvases — use the container element's bounds instead. Omitting BufferGeometryUtils.mergeVertices before applying EdgeSplitModifier produces incorrect splits on indexed geometries with duplicate vertices.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static PNG fallback image of the model for users with prefers-reduced-motion or no WebGL support. The interactive GUI controls have no keyboard focus management by default — replace or augment lil-gui with accessible HTML range/checkbox inputs. Add aria-label to the canvas element describing the 3D model being shown.

technique: real-time polygon simplification (LOD mesh reduction) with side-by-side comparison
description: Two 3D model variants are displayed side by side — the original high-poly mesh and a dynamically simplified low-poly version — with a slider controlling the reduction ratio. usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref and attach the renderer to that ref instead of document.body. Clean up with renderer.dispose() on unmount. Replace the hardcoded LeePerrySmith.glb path with a URL from your own CDN, public folder, or a dynamic import. In Next.js, place assets in /public and reference them as '/models/yourModel.glb'. react-three-fiber can be used but the SimplifyModifier is a vanilla three.js addon so it must be called imperatively inside a useEffect or a custom R3F imperative hook.
constraints: SimplifyModifier.modify() is async and CPU-intensive; running it on every slider change on complex meshes can block the main thread — consider debouncing. WebGL required; no WebGPU path. Mobile support is limited by GPU memory and CPU cost of simplification. Not suitable for scenes needing continuous animation loops since render-on-demand is used here.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call simplified.geometry.dispose() before replacing it (causes GPU memory leaks). Calling simplify() synchronously on every frame or slider tick without debounce. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container element's dimensions, which breaks embedded or partial-page canvas layouts. Not cloning the material before mutating flatShading, which would affect the original mesh.
accessibilityNotes: The 3D canvas has no inherent keyboard or screen reader support; add an aria-label to the canvas element describing the model. Provide a static fallback image for users with prefers-reduced-motion or no WebGL support. The GUI slider should be replaced or supplemented with a native HTML range input for keyboard accessibility.

technique: real-time mesh subdivision smoothing with side-by-side comparison
description: Two 3D models are displayed side by side — the original low-poly geometry and its smoothed, subdivided counterpart — with interactive controls for geometry type, subdivision iterations, and shading. Ideal for product configurators, 3D modeling tool demos, or educational/portfolio sections showing geometry quality levels.
usageNote: Wrap the renderer, scene, camera, and controls setup in a useEffect with a canvas ref for React/Next.js. Use react-three-fiber alternatively for a more idiomatic approach. The 'three-subdivide' package (npm install three-subdivide) must be added as a dependency. The UV grid texture referenced by './textures/uv_grid_opengl.jpg' must be replaced with a hosted asset URL (e.g. via Next.js /public folder or a CDN) or swapped for your own product/material texture.
constraints: Moderately expensive: subdivision at 5 iterations can exceed 25,000 triangles quickly, causing frame drops on low-end mobile GPUs. Requires WebGL renderer with support for buffer geometries. Best suited for desktop or high-end mobile. The maxTriangles guard parameter should be respected. Not suitable for scenes requiring many such objects simultaneously.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() and material.dispose() on the old meshes before replacing geometry on each update causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container ref breaks layout in component-based apps. Omitting the resize event listener cleanup in useEffect return will cause stale handlers. Not setting renderer.setPixelRatio before setSize leads to blurry output on retina displays.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static screenshot fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion enabled, as the OrbitControls allow continuous camera rotation. Add aria-label to the canvas element describing the 3D content. GUI controls are mouse-only and not keyboard or screen-reader accessible by default — consider supplementing with accessible HTML controls for key parameters if this is a user-facing configurator.

technique: tessellated 3D text with per-face color animation and displacement shader
description: 3D text is broken into thousands of individually colored triangular faces that pulse and explode outward with a sinusoidal wave, creating a dramatic shattering or crystallizing text effect. Ideal for hero sections, splash screens, or brand statement pages that want a high-impact, tech-forward aesthetic.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React or Next.js. Move the renderer target to the ref element instead of document.getElementById('container'). Replace the local font path 'fonts/helvetiker_bold.typeface.json' with a CDN-hosted typeface JSON (e.g., from the three.js GitHub raw content or jsDelivr) or bundle it in your /public folder. Inline the vertex and fragment shader strings as template literals in JS rather than reading from script tags. Return a cleanup function from useEffect that calls renderer.dispose() and controls.dispose(). In react-three-fiber, use useRef for the mesh, useFrame for the animation loop, and shaderMaterial as a primitive.
constraints: High GPU cost due to dense tessellated geometry and custom shader; not suitable for low-end mobile devices or battery-sensitive contexts. Requires WebGL (not WebGPU). TessellateModifier increases vertex count significantly so avoid using it on very large or complex geometries. TrackballControls requires pointer events and does not work well on touch-only devices without additional configuration.

Hardcoding WIDTH/HEIGHT from window at module load time instead of reading from the container element, breaking SSR in Next.js. Leaving the font load as a side-effectful top-level call instead of inside useEffect, which crashes in SSR environments. Not removing the resize event listener on cleanup. Forgetting to call controls.dispose() on unmount.

technique: interactive mesh morph targets with slider controls (cube-to-sphere and twist deformation)

Return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose(), controls.dispose(), and removes the resize event listener. Works on mobile but the GUI sliders may be difficult to interact with on small touch screens — consider replacing lil-gui with native HTML range inputs. OrbitControls zoom is disabled, keeping the view stable.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() and material.dispose() on unmount causing GPU memory leaks; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of measuring the container element; not cancelling the animation loop (use renderer.setAnimationLoop(null) on cleanup); neglecting to update morphTargetInfluences array indices if morph targets are reordered.

The GUI sliders have no keyboard labels — replace or augment with labelled <input type='range'> elements for screen reader compatibility. Add an aria-label to the canvas describing the interactive 3D shape for non-visual users.

technique: animated 3D face with blend shape morph targets and orbital camera
description: A photorealistic animated human face rendered in 3D with smooth facial expression morph targets (blend shapes) playing back via animation clip, lit by a neutral room environment. Requires a real GLTF model with embedded morph target animations — the local facecap.glb asset will not exist in user projects.

Provide a static hero image fallback for environments where WebGL is unavailable. The 3D canvas has no semantic meaning to screen readers; add aria-hidden='true' and provide descriptive adjacent text or alt content. technique: animated 3D character with morph-target skeletal animation and orbiting camera
description: A fully animated 3D animal character (horse galloping) rendered with smooth morph-target animation while the camera slowly orbits around it, creating a living hero centerpiece. Suits gaming sites, children's platforms, equestrian brands, interactive storytelling sections, or any product page wanting a lively 3D mascot.

Not suitable for very low-end devices or contexts where a static image is preferred. The example is full-viewport; embed in a bounded container div if used as a section widget rather than a hero.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call mixer.stopAllAction() and renderer.dispose() on component unmount causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight breaks fixed-height embedded containers — use the parent element's dimensions instead. Not cloning the AnimationMixer when the same model is reused multiple times will corrupt animation state. Omitting the resize listener causes a stretched canvas after viewport changes.

Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or stopping the animation loop and showing a static poster image instead. Provide a text or image fallback inside a <noscript> tag for environments without JavaScript or WebGL.

technique: animated morph target sphere with particle overlay
description: A glowing 3D sphere continuously morphs between organic shapes while rotating, with a particle point-cloud overlay following the same deformation. Suits hero sections for tech, science, AI, or creative agency sites that want an eye-catching living orb as a focal centerpiece.

Replace the GLTF model path with a hosted URL (CDN, /public folder, or imported via a loader) and replace the disc texture similarly. In react-three-fiber, use useGLTF from @react-three/drei and drive morph influence via useFrame.

Moderate GPU cost due to dual draw calls (mesh + point cloud with morph targets). Acceptable on mid-range mobile but avoid on low-end devices with many other WebGL contexts open.

Not sharing morphTargetInfluences between the mesh and Points object breaks the particle sync. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element dimensions breaks layout in non-fullscreen contexts. Not calling renderer.setPixelRatio causes blurry output on HiDPI screens.

Ensure surrounding text conveys the same information for screen reader users.

technique: real-time webcam face tracking with 3D avatar morph target blendshape mirroring
description: A 3D face avatar rendered in a mirrored selfie view that animates in real time to match the user's facial expressions captured via webcam, using MediaPipe face landmark detection and ARKit-style blendshapes. Suits interactive avatar creators, virtual try-on experiences, accessibility tools using face gestures, or live video call filters.
usageNote: Wrap initialization in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; assign the renderer to the ref instead of appending to document.body. Replace 'models/gltf/facecap.glb' with a hosted asset (CDN, /public folder in Next.js, or a user-supplied GLTF with ARKit blendshapes). KTX2Loader requires a basis transcoder path—set it to '/basis/' served from public. Load MediaPipe via dynamic import or a script tag since it comes from a CDN URL. Tear down the renderer, webcam stream, and MediaPipe FaceLandmarker in the useEffect cleanup function.

CPU/GPU cost is high due to continuous ML inference and morph target updates; not suitable for low-end mobile devices. Desktop Chrome and Edge are best supported. The camera must remain fixed at the origin or the face overlay drifts from the video feed.

Do not forget to stop the webcam MediaStream tracks on component unmount to avoid the camera staying on. Do not resize the renderer without also updating the video plane geometry and camera aspect to match the new video dimensions. Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and cancelling the animation frame on unmount causes memory leaks.
