Users with vestibular disorders may find a live mirror disorienting—offer a toggle to pause or hide the video feed. Provide an aria-label on the canvas describing the interactive avatar. Ensure any UI controls (blendshape sliders) are keyboard-navigable.

technique: multi-scene scissor rendering into scrollable HTML list items
description: A scrollable grid or list where each card contains its own independently interactive 3D object (product, icon, or data entity) rendered by a single shared WebGL canvas using scissor/viewport slicing. Ideal for product catalogues, component libraries, dashboard panels, or any listing page that needs inline 3D previews without spawning multiple renderers.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, use a single useEffect to initialise the renderer and attach it to a full-page canvas ref (position:fixed, pointer-events:none). Render card placeholder divs normally in JSX; the animation loop reads their getBoundingClientRect() each frame. With react-three-fiber this pattern is harder to replicate natively — prefer the vanilla approach with a canvas ref and imperative THREE.WebGLRenderer. No local assets are used, so no path replacement is needed.
constraints: Suits up to ~50–100 simultaneously visible scenes on mid-range desktop hardware; beyond that, draw-call overhead grows linearly. Mobile GPUs may struggle with 40+ scissor passes per frame. Requires WebGL (not WebGPU). The shared-canvas trick requires the canvas to be positioned fixed/absolute and translated with scrollY each frame, which can conflict with CSS stacking contexts.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose geometries and materials when list items are removed from the DOM, causing GPU memory leaks. Not clamping the scissor rect to off-screen items (the example already does this, but removing that check tanks performance). Letting the canvas shrink to zero size on mount before the renderer is initialised. Hardcoding pixel dimensions instead of reading clientWidth/clientHeight. Forgetting to call renderer.setPixelRatio(window.devicePixelRatio) causing blurry renders on retina screens.
accessibilityNotes: Each 3D card should have a sibling text label (already present as descriptionElement) for screen readers. Add aria-hidden='true' to the canvas element so assistive technology ignores it. Provide a prefers-reduced-motion media query that stops the auto-rotation (Date.now() * 0.001 spin) and leaves objects static. A static image or CSS fallback should be offered when WebGL is unavailable.

technique: multi-viewport 3D particle cloud with per-panel orbit controls
description: Multiple independent 3D point-cloud spheres render side-by-side in separate scrollable HTML panels, each with its own camera, orbit controls, and animated particle displacement. Ideal for product comparison sections, data visualization dashboards, interactive science or portfolio showcases, or any layout that needs several simultaneous 3D views embedded within a scrolling page.
usageNote: Wrap in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; instantiate the WebGLRenderer once against the ref, replicate the scissor/viewport loop keyed to getBoundingClientRect of each .view div. In react-three-fiber this pattern is less natural — prefer the vanilla approach with a single renderer and manual scissor splitting. No local assets are used, so no path replacement is needed. Animate via renderer.setAnimationLoop or requestAnimationFrame inside useEffect, and cancel on cleanup.
constraints: Requires WebGL. Each scene is rendered in sequence every frame with scissor clipping, so CPU and GPU cost scales linearly with the number of visible panels; keep panel count below ~12 for mid-range devices. Per-frame vertex displacement is done on the CPU, which becomes a bottleneck at high point counts. Not suitable for mobile with many simultaneous panels due to fillrate and memory pressure.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and controls.dispose() for each scene on component unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Not cancelling the animation loop on unmount causes stacked loops. Hardcoding canvas or container pixel sizes instead of using clientWidth/clientHeight breaks responsive layouts. Failing to set needsUpdate = true on geometry attributes will freeze particle animation. Not checking off-screen rects before rendering wastes GPU on invisible panels.
accessibilityNotes: Add a prefers-reduced-motion media query check before starting the animation loop and either pause it or reduce update frequency. Provide a static poster image or CSS gradient fallback for users with WebGL disabled. Each .view panel should have an aria-label describing its content. Orbit controls are mouse/touch driven and not keyboard accessible; add keyboard shortcuts for rotation if the 3D view is meaningful to the interaction rather than purely decorative.

technique: G-Buffer MRT deferred rendering with normal and diffuse passes
description: A 3D object is rendered into multiple off-screen buffers simultaneously (diffuse color and surface normals), then composited in a post-processing pass. Suits technically impressive hero sections, product configurators, or game-engine-style previews where advanced shading and post-effects are required.
usageNote: Wrap all init/render logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React or Next.js; pass the ref's current element to the WebGLRenderer constructor instead of appending to document.body. Replace the textures/hardwood2_diffuse.jpg path with a URL from your /public folder or a CDN import. Move the inline GLSL script tags into JS template-literal strings or .glsl files imported via a webpack/vite GLSL loader. Use react-three-fiber's useFrame and useThree for a more idiomatic integration, but note that manual RawShaderMaterial and WebGLRenderTarget management must still be handled imperatively.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 for GLSL3 and multiple render targets (MRT); not supported on WebGL1 contexts or very old mobile GPUs. Multi-sample anti-aliasing (samples parameter) adds significant GPU cost. Desktop-class GPUs recommended; test on mid-range mobile before shipping. MSAA on MRTs may be unsupported on some iOS Safari versions.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderTarget.setSize on window resize causes blurry or misaligned buffers. Not disposing the WebGLRenderTarget on component unmount leaks GPU memory. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions breaks embedded layouts. Using SRGBColorSpace on normal maps (should be LinearSRGBColorSpace). Omitting glslVersion: THREE.GLSL3 causes shader compile errors in WebGL2 mode.
accessibilityNotes: No interactive or animated content by default (orbit controls are user-driven, render-on-demand). Add a prefers-reduced-motion media query check to disable orbit controls auto-rotation if added. Provide a static fallback image for screen readers via an aria-label on the canvas and a visually-hidden description of the displayed content. The canvas is not keyboard-navigable by default; add tabIndex and key handlers if interaction is required.

technique: split-screen before/after comparison slider with scissor rendering
description: A draggable vertical divider splits the viewport into two independently rendered 3D scenes, letting users compare two versions of the same object side by side. Ideal for product configurators, material/finish selectors, before/after visualizations, or design review tools on e-commerce, architecture, or SaaS sites.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, wrap in a useEffect with a canvas ref and attach the renderer to that ref instead of document.querySelector. Store sliderPos in a useRef (not useState) to avoid re-renders on drag. Clean up by calling renderer.dispose() and removing event listeners in the useEffect return. With react-three-fiber this pattern is harder to use directly because r3f abstracts the render loop; prefer vanilla three.js inside a useEffect or use r3f's useThree plus a custom render loop via useFrame with manual scissor calls.
constraints: Requires WebGL scissor test support, which is universally available in modern browsers. Runs two full scene render passes per frame, roughly doubling GPU cost compared to a single scene — acceptable for moderate complexity geometry but avoid on mobile with heavy shaders or many objects. The slider interaction disables OrbitControls during drag, which must be re-enabled on pointerup to avoid locking navigation.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.setScissorTest(true) causes both scenes to render over the full canvas. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks on resize and in non-fullscreen containers — use the container element's dimensions instead. Not removing pointermove/pointerup listeners on cleanup causes memory leaks. Sharing a single geometry instance between scenes is fine but sharing materials without cloning can cause unexpected visual cross-contamination. Forgetting to dispose geometry and materials when the component unmounts leaks GPU memory.
accessibilityNotes: The slider is pointer-driven with no keyboard support; add keydown handlers (ArrowLeft/ArrowRight) to move sliderPos programmatically for keyboard accessibility. Provide an ARIA label on the slider element (e.g. role='slider', aria-label='Compare views', aria-valuenow as a percentage). For reduced-motion preferences, disable OrbitControls auto-rotate if added and keep the scenes static by default. Offer a static side-by-side image fallback for screen readers or environments without WebGL.

technique: split-screen multi-viewport 3D with independent cameras
description: Renders a single 3D scene simultaneously from three different camera angles tiled across the screen (a large left panel and two stacked right panels), each with a distinct background color and perspective. Ideal for product showcases, 3D model inspectors, architectural previews, or CAD-style viewers where showing multiple simultaneous viewpoints adds professional value.
usageNote: Port into React/Next.js using a useEffect hook with a canvas ref: set up the renderer once, store view camera objects in a ref array, and drive the animation loop with requestAnimationFrame inside the effect. Clean up with renderer.dispose() on unmount. The multi-viewport logic uses renderer.setViewport and renderer.setScissor calls per frame, which are renderer-level operations — in react-three-fiber this is harder to replicate natively, so a raw three.js approach with a canvas ref is strongly preferred. No local asset paths to replace.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer with scissor test support (universally available). Rendering the full scene multiple times per frame multiplies draw calls by the number of views (3x here), which is moderate-to-high GPU cost. On low-end mobile devices with many objects in the scene, frame rate may drop significantly. Not suitable for scenes with expensive post-processing unless per-view passes are carefully managed.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.setScissorTest(true) before each viewport pass. Not updating camera aspect ratios on window resize, causing distorted viewports. Hardcoding pixel dimensions instead of using fractional viewport values scaled to the current window size. Failing to dispose geometry and materials on component unmount, causing memory leaks in SPA navigation.
accessibilityNotes: All viewports are purely decorative 3D animation. Provide a static screenshot fallback via a <noscript> tag or a CSS background image for users with JavaScript disabled or prefers-reduced-motion set. Wrap the canvas in an aria-hidden='true' container and supply a visually hidden text description of the content. Keyboard interaction is not present and does not need to be added unless the viewer is interactive.

technique: split-screen MSAA comparison with animated 3D object field
description: A side-by-side split-screen view of rotating wireframe-overlaid spheres, comparing standard rendering against multisampled antialiasing (MSAA) via a WebGL renderbuffer. Suits a product or technology landing page that wants to demonstrate rendering quality differences, or any interactive 3D showcase needing smooth edge quality.
usageNote: In React or Next.js, move all imperative setup into a useEffect with a canvas ref (or use react-three-fiber's Canvas). Create the WebGLRenderer targeting the ref element, set autoClear false, and replicate the two EffectComposer pipelines. Tear down renderer and composers in the useEffect cleanup. No local assets are used, so no path replacement is needed. For react-three-fiber, use the gl prop to access the underlying renderer and construct composers manually.
constraints: Requires WebGL 2 for multisampled renderbuffers (samples: 4 on WebGLRenderTarget); falls back gracefully on WebGL 1 but MSAA won't apply. Moderate GPU cost due to two full-scene render passes per frame. Mobile support is limited on lower-end devices due to dual composition passes and scissor test toggling. Not suitable for pure CSS or canvas2D contexts.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call composer.setSize and renderer.setSize together on resize causes mismatched output buffers. Neglecting renderer.autoClear = false breaks the split-screen scissor technique. Hardcoding container dimensions instead of using offsetWidth/offsetHeight breaks responsive layouts. Failing to dispose the renderTarget and geometry on unmount causes GPU memory leaks.
accessibilityNotes: Wrap the animation loop with a prefers-reduced-motion media query check to pause or skip rotation when the user has reduced motion enabled. Provide a static fallback image for users who cannot run WebGL. The canvas element should have an aria-label describing the visual content for screen readers.

technique: 360-degree interactive panorama skybox with drag-to-look controls
description: A fully immersive 360° panoramic environment rendered inside an inverted cube, allowing the user to click and drag to look around in all directions. Ideal for virtual tours, real estate previews, hotel or venue showcases, travel landing pages, or any product/environment that benefits from spatial immersion.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, wrap all init logic in a useEffect with a canvas ref and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes event listeners. Use react-three-fiber alternatively with a <Box> whose geometry is scaled negatively on Z and six MeshBasicMaterial sides. Replace the local atlas texture path with a CDN URL or an imported asset via next/image public folder; the atlas must be a horizontal strip of 6 equal square tiles (right, left, top, bottom, front, back order matching THREE.js CubeCamera convention).
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer; not suitable as a CSS fallback. Performance is low-to-moderate since it renders a single textured box with no lighting, making it mobile-friendly. The atlas image can be large (4K+), so lazy-load or compress it for mobile. OrbitControls with inverted rotateSpeed gives the correct 'look around from inside' behaviour.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call controls.update() inside the animation loop when damping is enabled will cause the inertia effect to break. Not scaling geometry by -1 on Z will render the cube inside-out and show nothing. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container's bounding rect breaks embedded (non-fullscreen) usage. Failing to dispose the six canvas textures and materials on unmount causes memory leaks in SPAs.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static fallback image or descriptive alt text for users who cannot interact with WebGL. Honour prefers-reduced-motion by disabling OrbitControls damping and auto-rotation if present. Add aria-label to the container element describing the panoramic scene. Keyboard navigation is not natively supported by OrbitControls, so consider adding arrow-key listeners that nudge the camera azimuth/elevation for keyboard accessibility.

technique: 360-degree equirectangular panorama viewer with drag-to-look and scroll-to-zoom
description: A fully immersive spherical panorama rendered inside a 3D sphere, allowing users to click-drag to pan around a 360° environment and scroll to zoom. Ideal for virtual tours, real estate walkthroughs, event venue previews, hotel room showcases, or any experience where you want to place the viewer inside a photographic environment.
usageNote: Wrap the init/animate logic inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref or a container div ref; assign renderer.domElement to that ref instead of document.getElementById. Return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes all event listeners. Replace the local texture path with a public URL, an imported asset (via Next.js /public or a CDN), or a dynamic prop passed into the component. In react-three-fiber, use a <mesh> with scale={[-1,1,1]} and a <meshBasicMaterial> with an equirectangular texture loaded via useTexture.
constraints: Requires WebGL support; works well on desktop and modern mobile browsers but high-resolution panorama textures (>4096px) can exceed mobile GPU memory limits. The inverted sphere trick is simple and performant for a single panorama. Not suitable for multiple simultaneous panoramas on one page without significant texture memory management.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose of the texture and geometry on unmount causing memory leaks; not removing pointermove/pointerup listeners on cleanup; hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions; neglecting to update camera.aspect and call updateProjectionMatrix on resize; loading an oversized source image without compression or mip-mapping.
accessibilityNotes: Add a prefers-reduced-motion media query check to disable the auto-rotation (lon += 0.1) and keep the view static by default. Provide a static fallback or element showing a representative still from the panorama for users with JavaScript disabled or unsupported WebGL. Add keyboard arrow-key handlers for panning so mouse-free users can explore. Include an aria-label on the container describing the environment (e.g., 'Interactive 360° panorama of [location]').

technique: GLTF 3D model viewer with HDR environment lighting and orbit controls
description: Renders a fully lit 3D model (e.g. a dungeon environment) inside a WebGL scene using an Ultra HDR equirectangular image for photorealistic ambient and reflection lighting, with interactive 360-degree orbit navigation. Suits product pages, portfolio showcases, game asset previews, real estate walkthroughs, or any site section needing an explorable 3D object or environment.
usageNote: In React or Next.js, wrap initialization in a useEffect with a ref to a container div; return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes the canvas. Replace local asset paths (textures/equirectangular/, models/gltf/) with paths served from your public folder or a CDN URL, passing them to setPath() or directly to load(). With react-three-fiber, use useGLTF from @react-three/drei and useLoader for the HDR texture, and set scene.environment via the <Environment> component.
constraints: Requires WebGL 2 for best performance; HDR environment loading adds a notable initial network cost (2K .hdr.jpg). GPU-intensive for mobile devices, especially with ACES filmic tone mapping. Not suitable for low-end or embedded devices without a lower-poly model and smaller HDR texture. compileAsync helps avoid frame hitches on first render but requires an async-capable pipeline.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and controls.dispose() on unmount causing memory leaks; not handling window resize which breaks aspect ratio; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of measuring a container element; skipping compileAsync causing visible stutter when model first appears; using the same GLTFLoader instance across multiple concurrent loads without cloning scenes.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static fallback image for users with prefers-reduced-motion or those on devices where WebGL is unavailable. Add an aria-label or visually hidden description of the 3D content for screen readers. Keyboard orbit control is not built in by default; consider adding arrow-key handlers to the OrbitControls or documenting mouse/touch usage. Ensure sufficient contrast on any UI overlaid on the canvas.

technique: HDR cubemap PMREM environment mapping with PBR material matrix
description: A grid of physically-based spheres rendered against a softly blurred HDR panoramic environment, each sphere varying in roughness and metalness to showcase realistic reflections and light response. Ideal for product configurators, material pickers, jewelry or luxury goods showcases, and 3D design tool landing pages.
usageNote: In React or Next.js, wrap the init logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref, or use react-three-fiber with <Environment> and <meshPhysicalMaterial>. Replace the HDRCubeTextureLoader path (./textures/cube/pisaHDR/) with your own HDR cubemap files hosted in /public or served via a CDN; alternatively use RGBELoader with a single .hdr equirectangular file and PMREMGenerator.fromEquirectangular() for simpler asset management.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 or strong WebGL1 support; PMREMGenerator is GPU-intensive at load time but idle at runtime. HDR cubemap loading (6 files) adds network overhead — prefer a single equirectangular HDR in production. Not recommended as a primary mobile hero without texture resolution reduction. Orbit controls require pointer events and do not work with touchstart-disabled contexts.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call pmremGenerator.dispose() after generating the env map causes a GPU memory leak. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container ref breaks layout in component-based apps. Not removing the resize event listener on component unmount causes stale closures. Using the raw cubemap texture directly without PMREM conversion produces incorrect specular lighting.
accessibilityNotes: The 3D canvas has no inherent semantic meaning; add an aria-label describing the scene (e.g. 'Interactive 3D material showcase'). For prefers-reduced-motion, disable OrbitControls auto-rotate and freeze the render loop to a single static frame. Provide a fallback static image of the material grid for screen readers and no-WebGL environments via a <noscript> or feature-detection check.

technique: HDR equirectangular environment map with PBR material roughness/metalness grid
description: A 6×5 grid of spheres rendered with physically-based materials spanning the full roughness-to-metalness spectrum, all reflecting a high-dynamic-range panoramic environment loaded as a blurred background. Ideal for product configurators, materials showcases, jewellery/watch sites, or any premium brand page that needs to demonstrate surface finish options in photorealistic lighting.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref, or use react-three-fiber with a useLoader(UltraHDRLoader, url) call inside a Suspense boundary. The UltraHDRLoader path 'textures/equirectangular/royal_esplanade_2k.hdr.jpg' must be replaced with a URL your project actually serves — store the .hdr.jpg in /public (Next.js) or your CDN and pass the absolute/relative URL. PMREMGenerator must run after the renderer is initialised; in r3f call useThree to access the renderer.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 for full HDR fidelity. PMREMGenerator is GPU-intensive at load time; avoid running it on every frame. UltraHDR (.hdr.jpg) files can be 2–8 MB; serve with HTTP/2 and appropriate caching headers. On low-end mobile the 30-sphere scene may drop below 60 fps — reduce sphere count or resolution. Not suitable for WebGPU renderer without a compat layer.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call pmremGenerator.dispose() after generating the env map causes a GPU memory leak. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks in scrollable or embedded canvas contexts — use the container's clientWidth/clientHeight instead. Not removing the resize event listener on component unmount in React will accumulate listeners. Reloading the HDR on every render-cycle re-render is extremely costly.
accessibilityNotes: The canvas conveys no textual information; add an aria-label on the container describing the material visualiser. Provide a static fallback image (screenshot of the sphere grid) for users with prefers-reduced-motion or when WebGL is unavailable. OrbitControls should be keyboard-accessible — ensure the canvas is focusable (tabIndex=0) and document arrow-key behaviour for screen reader users.

technique: HDR environment-mapped PBR material grid with PMREM directional light comparison
description: A grid of physically-based spheres spanning the full roughness (0–1) and metalness spectrum, lit by an HDR environment map and rendered with filmic tone mapping. Ideal for product configurators, material showcases, or design-system pages that need to demonstrate how surface finishes look under realistic lighting.
usageNote: Wrap the init and createObjects logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js, attaching the renderer to the ref element instead of document.body. Replace the local HDR path ('textures/equirectangular/spot1Lux.hdr') with an HDR file served from your public folder or a CDN URL. Use react-three-fiber alternatively via <Canvas> with a useLoader(EXRLoader/RGBELoader) call. Dispose the PMREMGenerator and renderer in the useEffect cleanup function.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 for full PMREM quality; HDR loading adds a network round-trip so use a compressed .hdr or .exr and serve with appropriate cache headers. High GPU cost due to PMREM pre-filtering; avoid on low-end mobile. The GUI toggle comparing PMREM vs directional light is a debug aid and should be removed in production.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call pmremGenerator.dispose() after generating the radiance map causes a GPU memory leak. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks in embedded or multi-panel layouts—use the container element's dimensions instead. Not updating camera.aspect and projection matrix on resize produces distorted spheres. Leaving the lil-gui debug panel in production exposes implementation details.
accessibilityNotes: The 3D canvas has no inherent keyboard or screen reader support; add an aria-label or aria-describedby on the canvas element describing the material showcase. Provide a static fallback image (e.g. a pre-rendered PNG of the sphere grid) for users with prefers-reduced-motion or when WebGL is unavailable. The orbit controls should be supplemented with keyboard shortcuts or a visible UI for users who cannot use a mouse.

technique: billboard particle field with mouse parallax and hue-cycling color
description: 10,000 softly glowing disc-shaped particles fill a deep 3D space with exponential fog and slowly cycle through hues while following cursor movement with a smooth lag. Ideal for hero backgrounds on creative agencies, music platforms, tech startups, or immersive landing pages that want a cosmic or starfield atmosphere.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate block inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js: pass the ref's current element to the WebGLRenderer constructor instead of appending to document.body, and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame. Replace 'textures/sprites/disc.png' with a bundled asset imported via your bundler (e.g. import discUrl from './disc.png') or a hosted CDN URL; alternatively generate a circular sprite programmatically using a Canvas2D radial gradient to eliminate the external dependency entirely.
constraints: Rendering 10,000 points with a texture and fog is moderate GPU cost — runs well on desktop and mid-range mobile; reduce vertex count to 3,000–5,000 for low-end mobile. Requires WebGL1 or WebGL2. Full-screen canvas is not suitable as an inline component; best used as a fixed background layer. The GUI/Stats imports are dev utilities and should be removed for production.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and geometry.dispose() and material.dispose() on unmount causes GPU memory leaks in React SPAs. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of reading from a container ref breaks embedded usage. Leaving the pointermove listener on document.body instead of the canvas element causes interference with page scrolling. Not setting renderer.setPixelRatio can make particles look blurry on retina displays.
accessibilityNotes: Add a prefers-reduced-motion media query check before starting the animation loop; if motion is reduced, render a single static frame or replace the canvas with a static dark gradient background image. The canvas has no semantic content so add aria-hidden='true' to remove it from the accessibility tree. Ensure any overlaid text meets WCAG contrast ratios against the dark animated background.

technique: human-silhouette particle cloud with bloom, film grain, and depth-of-field postprocessing
description: Thousands of glowing particles form slowly morphing human figure silhouettes scattered across a dark, fog-filled space, with bloom glow, film grain, and a soft focus lens effect applied. Ideal for high-impact hero sections on creative agencies, fashion brands, digital art platforms, or cinematic product launches where a dramatic, otherworldly atmosphere is needed.
usageNote: Wrap the init and animate logic inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref, returning a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the animation loop. Replace male02.obj and female02.obj with your own OBJ assets hosted in /public or on a CDN — any humanoid or abstract OBJ will work. In Next.js mark the component 'use client' and guard with typeof window !== 'undefined'. Alternatively use react-three-fiber with a <Canvas> and port the postprocessing stack via @react-three/postprocessing.
constraints: High GPU cost due to multi-pass postprocessing (BloomPass, FilmPass, FocusShader) plus thousands of dynamic particles; not suitable for low-end mobile or battery-sensitive contexts. Requires WebGL 1 or 2 — no WebGPU. Needs CORS-accessible OBJ files at runtime. Performance degrades significantly below 60 fps on integrated graphics.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call composer.setSize and effectFocus uniform updates on window resize, causing blurry or misaligned focus. Not disposing BufferGeometry and PointsMaterial when the component unmounts, causing memory leaks in SPAs. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of reading from the container element, breaking layout in constrained viewports. Omitting renderer.autoClear = false, which breaks the multi-pass composer pipeline.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static poster image fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion enabled, pausing or skipping the animation loop. Add an aria-hidden='true' attribute to the canvas so screen readers ignore it. Include a visible text alternative or heading in the DOM for SEO and assistive technology. Do not rely on the animation to convey functional information.

technique: sprite-textured particle cloud with mouse parallax and hue-cycling color animation
description: Ten thousand textured sprite particles rendered as layered rotating clouds in a deep black fog, with colors that slowly cycle through hues and camera that follows the cursor for a parallax effect. Ideal for immersive hero backgrounds on entertainment, gaming, seasonal (winter/holiday), or creative portfolio sites.
usageNote: Wrap the init/animate logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; pass the ref's current element to the WebGLRenderer instead of appending to document.body. Clean up with renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame in the useEffect return. Replace the five snowflake PNG paths with your own hosted sprite textures (any soft-edged transparent PNGs work) via public folder paths or imported URLs; react-three-fiber's <Points> and <PointsMaterial> can also replace the imperative setup.
constraints: Renders 10,000 points × 5 materials (50,000 effective draw calls worth of particles) which is moderate-to-high GPU cost; runs well on desktop and mid-range mobile but may drop frames on low-end devices. Requires WebGL renderer. Additive blending with depthTest disabled means overdraw cost scales with particle density; reducing vertex count or material layers is the primary optimization lever.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and geometry.dispose() on unmount causing GPU memory leaks; hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using a container element's dimensions; not removing the pointermove and resize event listeners on cleanup; omitting needsUpdate = true after changing material properties; failing to set renderer.setPixelRatio for sharp rendering on high-DPI screens.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a prefers-reduced-motion media query check: if reduced motion is preferred, skip the animation loop or render a single static frame. Add a visually hidden aria-hidden='true' attribute on the canvas so screen readers ignore it. Include a static fallback image or CSS gradient background behind the canvas for users with WebGL disabled or unavailable.

technique: animated particle wave grid with mouse parallax camera
description: A 50×50 grid of white particles undulates in a sine-wave ocean pattern, with particle size pulsing in sync and the camera drifting to follow the mouse cursor. Ideal for hero backgrounds, data-visualization intros, or immersive landing pages for tech, fintech, or creative agencies.
usageNote: In React or Next.js, wrap all init logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref: pass the ref's current element to the WebGLRenderer instead of creating a div, and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the animation loop. In react-three-fiber, use useFrame for the animation loop and useRef for particle geometry. The inline vertex/fragment shaders are in script tags in the original HTML; extract them as template-literal strings in JS or as .glsl files imported via a Vite/webpack GLSL loader.
constraints: Renders 2 500 points per frame with per-frame buffer writes; GPU cost is low-to-moderate. Runs well on mid-range mobile but the continuous buffer updates (needsUpdate every frame) can drain battery on low-end devices. Requires WebGL (not WebGPU). Full-screen canvas means it should only be used as a background layer, not inline in a document flow.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() and renderer.dispose() on unmount causes memory leaks in SPAs. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/Height breaks in SSR (Next.js); guard with typeof window !== 'undefined'. Not removing the pointermove and resize event listeners on cleanup causes stale closures. Leaving the Stats panel visible in production adds an unwanted FPS overlay.
accessibilityNotes: Wrap the canvas in a div with role='img' and aria-label describing the decorative animation. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by skipping the animation loop (count stays at 0, rendering a static flat grid) or replacing with a still screenshot. The effect is purely decorative so no keyboard interaction is needed, but ensure any foreground content layered on top meets contrast requirements against the dark background.

technique: real-time portal rendering with offscreen render targets and frustum-oblique projection
description: Two rectangular portal windows display live views of opposite sides of a room, creating a seamless dimensional-window illusion where objects appear to pass through one portal and emerge from the other. Suits immersive product showcases, virtual showrooms, sci-fi game UIs, or interactive architectural visualization where showing multiple spaces simultaneously adds dramatic depth.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate block inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref, storing renderer and animation frame ID for cleanup. In react-three-fiber this pattern is harder to express natively because it requires manual WebGLRenderTarget management and CameraUtils frame callbacks; prefer a raw three.js useEffect approach. No local assets are used so no path replacement is needed, but ensure CameraUtils and OrbitControls are installed via the three addons package.
constraints: High GPU cost: each frame renders the scene three times (two portal textures + main view). Not recommended on mobile or low-end GPUs without halving render target resolution to 128×128. Requires WebGL2 for reliable render target support. Portal count should stay at two; adding more multiplies draw calls proportionally. localClippingEnabled must be set on the renderer.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose WebGLRenderTarget instances on unmount causes VRAM leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks in embedded canvas contexts; use container.clientWidth instead. Failing to call cameraControls.update() after target changes breaks the orbit pivot. Skipping renderer.localClippingEnabled = true makes clipping planes silently do nothing.
accessibilityNotes: The animation loop runs continuously; honor prefers-reduced-motion by pausing OrbitControls auto-rotate and freezing the bouncing spheres while keeping a static rendered frame visible. Provide an aria-label on the canvas describing the scene for screen readers. No keyboard interaction is exposed by default; add focusable controls for camera navigation to meet WCAG 2.1 AA for interactive 3D content.

technique: dot-screen and RGB shift postprocessing on animated 3D particle field
description: A rotating cloud of randomly scattered geometric shards rendered with a halftone dot-screen overlay and chromatic aberration (RGB shift), producing a retro-psychedelic or lo-fi analog aesthetic. Ideal for creative agency hero sections, music/album pages, festival or event sites, or any brand experience that wants a gritty, avant-garde visual identity.
usageNote: Wrap everything in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js: create the renderer targeting the ref element instead of appending to document.body, store the AnimationLoop ID and call renderer.setAnimationLoop(null) plus composer.dispose() and renderer.dispose() on cleanup. EffectComposer, RenderPass, ShaderPass, and OutputPass work identically in react-three-fiber via the @react-three/postprocessing package, which is the preferred route. No local assets are used, so no path replacement is needed.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer with support for render-to-texture (framebuffers); most modern mobile browsers support this, but multi-pass postprocessing doubles GPU fill-rate cost, so on low-end mobile devices frame rate may drop. Not suitable for content-heavy pages where the canvas is a small inset — works best as a full-viewport background or hero.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call composer.setSize() alongside renderer.setSize() on window resize causes blurry or misaligned postprocessing output. Neglecting to dispose the EffectComposer, its render targets, and all geometry/materials on unmount causes GPU memory leaks in SPAs. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of reading the container element's dimensions breaks embedded layouts.
accessibilityNotes: Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or stopping the animation loop and showing a static screenshot or a plain CSS background instead. The canvas has no inherent keyboard or screen-reader role; add aria-hidden='true' and ensure all meaningful content lives in the DOM outside the canvas. Provide a visible skip or pause control if the animation occupies a large viewport area.

technique: real-time LUT color grading post-processing on 3D scene
description: A 3D scene rendered with swappable cinematic color-grading filters (LUTs) applied as a full-screen post-processing pass, supporting filmic, black-and-white, night-vision, and other looks at adjustable intensity. Ideal for product configurators, interactive lookbooks, photography portfolio sites, or any experience where visual mood and color tone need to match a brand or artistic direction.
usageNote: Wrap all three.js initialization inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; mount the renderer onto the ref instead of appending to document.body. Replace local asset paths (textures/equirectangular/, models/gltf/, luts/) with paths served from your public/ folder or a CDN. The LUT files (.CUBE, .3dl, .png) must be hosted and publicly accessible. Use react-three-fiber's useThree and useFrame hooks as an alternative, adding the EffectComposer via the @react-three/postprocessing package which wraps these passes natively.
constraints: Requires WebGL 1 or 2 renderer with support for EffectComposer and 3D textures (for .texture3D); most modern desktop and mobile browsers support this but very low-end Android devices may not. The LUT post-processing pass adds a moderate GPU cost per frame; running multiple LUT passes simultaneously is not recommended. HDR environment maps increase memory usage significantly on mobile.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call composer.setSize and camera.updateProjectionMatrix on window resize; not disposing LUT textures when switching between them causing GPU memory leaks; hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of reading from the canvas container; loading all LUT files eagerly on mount instead of lazy-loading on demand; omitting the OutputPass before LUTPass which breaks tone-mapping order.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static hero image fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion or when WebGL is unavailable. The color-grading controls (LUT selection, intensity) should be accessible via keyboard if exposed as UI; avoid relying solely on color to convey meaning since LUTs like B&W remove color information entirely. Screen readers receive no information from the canvas, so include descriptive aria-label on the canvas element.

technique: multi-pass postprocessing pipeline with bloom, film grain, sepia, vignette, bleach bypass, dot screen, and masking

description: Renders a 3D scene as glowing white edges on a black background by applying grayscale conversion followed by a Sobel operator shader, creating a stark wireframe-like outline aesthetic. Suits portfolio hero sections, creative agency intros, tech product showcases, or any UI requiring a stylized blueprint or X-ray visual effect.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, mount the renderer inside a useEffect with a canvas ref: create the WebGLRenderer targeting the ref element, set up EffectComposer with LuminosityShader then SobelOperatorShader passes, and clean up renderer and composer on unmount. In react-three-fiber, use the postprocessing library's Effect pipeline instead. No local assets are needed — all geometry is procedural, so no path replacement is required.
constraints: Requires WebGL with floating-point render targets for EffectComposer; not suitable for very low-end mobile GPUs. The multi-pass pipeline (render → grayscale → Sobel) adds GPU overhead, making it moderate cost. The effect is resolution-dependent and must update uniforms on resize. Works best at native pixel ratio; high DPR screens on mobile may degrade performance.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to update effectSobel resolution uniforms on window resize causes blurry or misaligned edges. Not disposing the EffectComposer, RenderPass, and ShaderPasses on component unmount causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions breaks embedding in partial-page layouts. Skipping devicePixelRatio scaling produces soft edges on Retina displays.
accessibilityNotes: The high-contrast black-and-white edge output can actually benefit some low-vision users, but the animated rotating 3D object should respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or disabling the animation loop. Provide a static screenshot fallback for users who disable JavaScript or WebGL. The canvas has no semantic meaning so add aria-hidden='true' and ensure surrounding page content conveys equivalent information.

technique: SSAA (Super-Sample Anti-Aliasing) post-processing with instanced 3D sphere cluster
description: A slowly rotating cluster of dozens of colorful metallic spheres rendered with configurable multi-sample anti-aliasing for crisp, artifact-free edges at any quality level. Suits high-end product showcases, creative agency hero sections, or any 3D scene where visual quality and smooth edges are a priority.
usageNote: Wrap the init, animate, and resize logic inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref; assign renderer.domElement to the ref instead of appending to document.body. Clean up with renderer.dispose(), composer.dispose(), and cancelAnimationFrame in the useEffect return. In react-three-fiber, use the <EffectComposer> from @react-three/postprocessing if available, or drop to an imperative useEffect for the SSAARenderPass. No local assets to replace.
constraints: SSAA is computationally expensive — at level 5 it renders the scene 32 times per frame, making it unsuitable for mobile or low-end GPUs. Requires WebGL 2 for full post-processing stack. Best suited for hero sections or product viewers where frame rate can be capped or quality scaled down dynamically. Not recommended for scenes with many animated elements at high sample levels.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call composer.setSize() and renderer.setSize() together on window resize will cause blurry or misaligned output. Using sampleLevel 4 or 5 on mobile will cause severe frame drops or GPU timeouts. Not disposing the EffectComposer and its render targets on unmount causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of measuring the container element breaks layout in embedded or scrollable contexts.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a prefers-reduced-motion media query check to disable autoRotate and pause the animation loop for users sensitive to motion. Supply a static poster image or CSS background as a fallback for browsers without WebGL support. The canvas has no semantic content so add aria-hidden='true' and ensure any overlaid text has sufficient contrast and is in the DOM independently.

technique: Screen Space Ambient Occlusion (SSAO) post-processing on 3D scene
description: Renders a 3D scene with realistic contact shadows and depth cues using SSAO post-processing, making surfaces appear grounded and volumetric. Ideal for product configurators, architectural visualizations, or premium brand hero sections where physical realism and depth are important.
usageNote: Wrap the init logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js, passing the ref's current element to the renderer instead of appending to document.body. Use renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ canvas: canvasRef.current }) and manage cleanup with a returned dispose function. EffectComposer, SSAOPass, and OutputPass are addons and must be installed via the three/addons path or copied from the three npm package's examples/jsm directory. No local assets are referenced, so no path replacement is needed.
constraints: SSAO is GPU-intensive and may drop below 30fps on low-end mobile GPUs or integrated graphics; WebGL2 is required for depth buffer access used by SSAOPass. Not recommended for pages with many simultaneous heavy DOM elements. Best suited for fullscreen or large-canvas hero experiences on desktop.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call composer.setSize and camera.updateProjectionMatrix on resize breaks the effect at non-default viewports. Skipping the OutputPass causes incorrect color space output. Not disposing the EffectComposer and its passes on component unmount causes GPU memory leaks in React. Hardcoding window dimensions instead of using the container element's dimensions breaks embedded or non-fullscreen layouts.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static fallback image for users with prefers-reduced-motion enabled; the rotating group animation should be paused or removed for those users. The canvas has no inherent keyboard or screen reader role, so add aria-hidden='true' and ensure any meaningful content is conveyed through visible DOM text outside the canvas.

technique: screen-space reflection (SSR) post-processing with ground reflector plane
description: 3D objects sit on a reflective floor surface that mirrors them in real-time using screen-space reflection, producing a polished, studio-quality product-showcase look. Ideal for premium product configurators, luxury brand hero sections, jewelry/watch displays, or architectural visualization landing pages.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref: create renderer targeting the ref's canvas, set up EffectComposer with SSRPass inside the effect, and return a cleanup that disposes the composer and renderer. In Next.js use dynamic import with ssr:false. Replace the Draco bunny model ('models/draco/bunny.drc') with your own Draco-compressed GLB/DRC asset hosted in /public; point DRACOLoader.setDecoderPath() at a CDN or your own /public/draco/ folder. For react-three-fiber, use the postprocessing r3f package (@react-three/postprocessing) instead of manual EffectComposer wiring.
constraints: High GPU cost: SSR is a full-screen screen-space algorithm run every frame and is unsuitable for mobile or low-end hardware. Requires WebGL 2 with depth texture support. Resolution scale should be reduced (0.5 or lower) for acceptable frame rates. Not suitable for scenes requiring reflections of off-screen geometry. Avoid for sites with a predominantly mobile audience.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call composer.setSize() and ssrPass width/height on window resize causes blurry or misaligned reflections. Hardcoding innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container element size breaks embedded or split-layout usage. Not disposing the DRACOLoader after load leaks WebAssembly memory. Skipping groundReflector.visible management makes the reflector plane occlude geometry. Omitting antialias:false on the renderer (SSR already handles it) wastes GPU budget.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static high-quality rendered image fallback via a CSS background or <noscript> for users with reduced-motion preferences or when WebGL is unavailable. Detect prefers-reduced-motion and disable autoRotate and SSR animation loop, showing a still frame instead. The 3D canvas has no inherent keyboard or screen-reader semantics; add aria-label and role='img' to the container element, and ensure surrounding page content conveys the same information the visual communicates.

technique: temporal anti-aliasing (TAA) and super-sampling anti-aliasing (SSAA) postprocessing with accumulation
description: Two rotating 3D cubes — one wireframe, one textured — rendered with configurable TAA/SSAA postprocessing that smooths jagged edges by accumulating multiple jittered samples over time. Suited for product configurators, 3D viewers, or any web app section where high visual quality of 3D geometry is critical and aliasing must be minimized.
usageNote: Wrap all three.js setup in a useEffect with a canvas ref; assign renderer.domElement to the ref instead of appending to document.body. Move the animation loop cleanup into the useEffect return (renderer.setAnimationLoop(null); renderer.dispose()). Replace 'textures/brick_diffuse.jpg' with an asset in your public folder (e.g. '/textures/brick_diffuse.jpg' in Next.js) or import it via a bundler. The GUI is debug-only; in production, wire TAA parameters to your own UI state.
constraints: TAA accumulation only works well when the scene is static or nearly static — fast motion breaks accumulated samples and requires resetting accumulation each frame. Requires WebGL with float render targets for the EffectComposer; not suitable for very low-end mobile GPUs. Higher sample levels (32 samples) carry significant GPU cost and should be capped on mobile.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call composer.setSize() on resize (causes blurry render). Not resetting taaRenderPass.accumulate=false when objects move, causing ghosting. Leaving the stats/GUI DOM nodes mounted after component unmount. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions. Keeping NearestFilter on textures without understanding it disables natural texture smoothing.
accessibilityNotes: Rotation animation should respect prefers-reduced-motion; wrap the rotation update in a media query check or a ref flag and pause animation for users who opt out. Provide a static screenshot fallback for screen readers or environments without WebGL. The canvas has no inherent keyboard focus; add aria-hidden='true' if it is purely decorative, or role='img' with an aria-label if it conveys meaningful content.

technique: texture-masked scene transition between two 3D environments
description: Two distinct 3D scenes cross-dissolve using stylized alpha-mask textures (perlin noise, radial gradients, cell patterns, etc.), creating cinematic wipe or dissolve transitions between full-screen WebGL environments. Ideal for portfolio section changes, product showcase slides, game menu transitions, or any full-page experience that needs visually rich scene-to-scene navigation.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref, or use react-three-fiber with a custom effect composer. The RenderTransitionPass requires EffectComposer; in R3F use @react-three/postprocessing and a custom pass wrapper. Replace the six 'textures/transition/transitionN.png' local paths with hosted URLs (CDN, public folder, or import as modules); these mask textures are critical to the effect and must be supplied. TWEEN animation can be replaced with react-spring or framer-motion driving the transition uniform value.
constraints: Requires WebGL with framebuffer support for EffectComposer (no WebGL1 fallback). Rendering two full scenes plus compositing is GPU-intensive; avoid on low-end mobile or when battery-saving mode is active. Works best as a full-viewport experience rather than an embedded widget. Transition textures (6 PNG files) must be self-hosted.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call composer.setSize and renderer.setSize on window resize causes blurry or misaligned compositing. Not disposing both scenes' geometries and materials on unmount leaks GPU memory. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks in SSR (Next.js); use a ref and ResizeObserver instead. Skipping the optimization that renders only one scene when transition===0 or 1 wastes GPU on every frame.
accessibilityNotes: Respect prefers-reduced-motion by disabling transitionAnimate and sceneAnimate, and either snapping instantly between scenes or showing a static rendered frame of the destination scene. Provide an aria-hidden wrapper around the canvas and communicate page/section changes via an aria-live region so screen readers announce navigation. Add keyboard controls for manually triggering transitions.

technique: HDR bloom post-processing on animated 3D model with tone mapping
description: A glowing, high-dynamic-range 3D model with a luminous bloom effect and filmic tone mapping, giving bright emissive areas a soft, overexposed halo. Ideal for hero sections of gaming, aerospace, sci-fi product, or technology sites that want a premium, cinematic feel with an interactive 3D centerpiece.
usageNote: In React or Next.js, wrap the entire init logic in a useEffect with a canvas ref; assign the renderer to the ref's current element instead of appending to a container div. Use react-three-fiber's <Canvas> with postprocessing library (@react-three/postprocessing) and its <Bloom> component for a more idiomatic approach. Replace the local 'models/gltf/PrimaryIonDrive.glb' path with a URL to your own GLB hosted in /public or on a CDN. Remove the Stats and GUI panels for production builds.
constraints: High GPU cost due to multi-pass EffectComposer rendering; not recommended for low-end mobile devices or battery-sensitive contexts. Requires WebGL2-capable renderer. Performance degrades at high pixel ratios; consider capping devicePixelRatio at 1.5 on mobile. The bloom effect is a full-screen post-process pass adding measurable frame time.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call composer.setSize() and camera.updateProjectionMatrix() on window resize, causing blurry or stretched bloom. Not disposing the EffectComposer, passes, and model geometry/textures on component unmount in React, causing memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/Height instead of using a container element's dimensions, which breaks embedded layouts. Leaving the GUI and Stats panels visible in production.
accessibilityNotes: Respect prefers-reduced-motion by disabling the AnimationMixer update and pausing bloom animation when the media query matches. Provide a static fallback image for users who cannot render WebGL. The canvas has no inherent keyboard or screen-reader content; add an aria-label and role='img' to the canvas element, and ensure surrounding page content conveys the same information.

technique: selective bloom post-processing with click-to-toggle glow on 3D objects
description: A 3D scene of scattered geometric shapes where individual objects can be toggled to emit a luminous bloom glow effect while others remain normal, composited via a dual render-target pipeline. Ideal for sci-fi product showcases, interactive hero sections, data visualization dashboards, or gaming UIs where certain elements need to appear energized or highlighted.
usageNote: Wrap the entire setup in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; assign renderer.domElement to the ref instead of appending to document.body. The inline vertex/fragment shaders (read via document.getElementById) must be converted to JS template literal strings or imported as GLSL modules since script tags are unavailable in JSX. Use a cleanup function in useEffect to dispose the renderer, composers, and event listeners. No local assets are needed.
constraints: Requires WebGL with floating-point render targets (HalfFloatType) and MSAA support; uses two full-screen render passes so GPU cost is roughly 2x a standard scene. Mid-range mobile GPUs may struggle at high resolutions; consider halving pixel ratio on mobile. Not suitable for WebGPU renderer without porting the ShaderPass material.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose both bloomComposer and finalComposer render targets on unmount causing GPU memory leaks; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the canvas container dimensions; omitting the resize handler update for both composers; leaving the inline script-tag shader approach in a bundled React environment causing silent failures.
accessibilityNotes: The animated 3D scene should be paused or replaced with a static image when the prefers-reduced-motion media query is active. Bloom-only interactions are purely decorative and pointer-driven; provide an equivalent non-visual affordance or description for screen reader users. Ensure any surrounding UI text has sufficient contrast against the glowing background.

technique: dissolve/reveal shader with randomized UV tiling on 3D product model
description: A photorealistic 3D shader-ball model with an animated dissolve/disintegration effect and noise-based randomized UV texture sampling, set against an HDR environment. Ideal for luxury product showcases, material configurators, or interactive 3D hero sections where a product appears or disappears dramatically.
usageNote: Wrap the init/render loop inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js, returning a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose(). Replace all local asset paths (textures/jade.jpg, textures/noise.png, models/gltf/ShaderBall2.glb, textures/equirectangular/lobe.hdr) with paths served from your public/ folder or a CDN. Use react-three-fiber as an alternative to avoid manual DOM management, placing the shader customization in a custom material component with onBeforeCompile.
constraints: Requires WebGL with shadow map and ACES filmic tone mapping support; computationally moderate due to custom fragment shader patching, VSM shadow maps, and HDR environment loading. Not suitable for low-end mobile devices or WebGL1-only contexts. DRACO-compressed GLTF requires the DRACO decoder to be accessible at a resolvable path.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose the renderer, textures, and DRACO loader on component unmount; hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using a ResizeObserver tied to the container element; failing to set texture.colorSpace correctly when swapping textures; not handling the async HDR/GLTF load sequence before attaching uniforms; assuming uniforms are populated synchronously before the model loads.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static high-quality product image fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion or when WebGL is unavailable. The 3D canvas is purely decorative and should have aria-hidden='true' with role='presentation'. Ensure any GUI controls have accessible labels if exposed to end users. No keyboard navigation is needed if the canvas is decorative only.

technique: BVH-accelerated raycasting visualization on complex 3D mesh
description: Hundreds of animated rays fire toward a complex 3D model from all directions, with intersection hit points shown as small spheres and ray lines rendered semi-transparently. Suits product configurators, interactive 3D model viewers, or technical/engineering SaaS dashboards that need to demonstrate real-time spatial queries or collision detection on detailed geometry.
usageNote: Wrap the init and animate calls inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref, returning a cleanup function that disposes the renderer and removes event listeners. For react-three-fiber, use the drei library's BVH helpers and useFrame for the animation loop. Replace the local FBX asset (models/fbx/stanford-bunny.fbx) with any FBX hosted on your CDN or a public URL passed as a prop; alternatively swap FBXLoader for GLTFLoader with a .glb asset. Install the three-mesh-bvh package separately via npm and call computeBoundsTree after geometry load.
constraints: Requires WebGL 1 or higher; three-mesh-bvh must be installed as a peer dependency alongside three.js. Casting 150–3000 rays per frame is GPU-intensive; on mobile or low-end devices reduce ray count dramatically (10–30) or disable the feature entirely. The BVH precomputation step adds a brief stall on model load for very high-poly meshes. Not suitable for purely decorative backgrounds due to CPU/GPU cost.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.disposeBoundsTree() and geometry.dispose() on unmount causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a ResizeObserver on the container element breaks layout in embedded or panel contexts. Not cloning the bvh reference before toggling it off means you cannot re-enable BVH without recomputing. Using InstancedMesh without resetting instanceMatrix usage flags can cause stale GPU buffer warnings.
accessibilityNotes: This is a fully animated 3D canvas with no inherent semantic content; add an aria-label on the canvas element describing the visualization. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing the animation loop or reducing ray count to zero when the media query matches. Provide a static screenshot fallback via a <noscript> or CSS background for users without JavaScript or WebGL. No keyboard or screen reader interaction is exposed by default.

technique: hover-highlight sprite picking with raycaster
description: A 3D scene containing billboard sprites that highlight red when the cursor hovers over them, using raycasting for pointer intersection. Suits interactive data-visualization dashboards, map annotation layers, point-of-interest markers on 3D maps, or product configurators where clickable labels float in 3D space.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, wrap the setup in a useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer targeting the ref element instead of appending to document.body, store controls/scene/raycaster as refs, and return a cleanup function that disposes the renderer and removes event listeners. For react-three-fiber use the useThree hook for camera/raycaster and onPointerOver/onPointerOut props on <sprite> elements which simplifies the intersection logic significantly. No local assets are referenced, so no path replacement is needed.
constraints: WebGL renderer required; sprites are always camera-facing (billboards) which is intentional but limits use cases needing directional indicators. Raycasting against many sprites is O(n) and can degrade on mobile with hundreds of markers. sizeAttenuation:false sprites maintain screen-space size regardless of zoom, which may feel unexpected to users.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to remove pointermove and resize event listeners on component unmount causing memory leaks; not calling renderer.dispose() on cleanup; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of measuring the container element, which breaks embedded or multi-panel layouts; neglecting to call controls.dispose() on teardown; not normalizing pointer coordinates relative to the canvas bounding rect when the canvas does not fill the full viewport.
accessibilityNotes: The interaction is purely pointer-driven with no keyboard or screen-reader support. Add ARIA-labelled HTML overlays positioned via 3D-to-2D projection for screen readers. Provide a static fallback image or a simplified 2D list for users with reduced-motion preferences or when WebGL is unavailable. Hover-only highlighting should be supplemented with click/focus states for keyboard navigation.

technique: raycaster UV coordinate picker with dynamic canvas texture overlay
description: A 3D scene with textured meshes (cube, plane, circle) where mouse clicks ray-cast onto surfaces and display a crosshair marker at the exact UV hit point on the texture itself. Suits product configurators, interactive 3D maps, texture inspection tools, or any UI where users need to click on a 3D surface and get feedback about the precise texture coordinate they touched.
usageNote: Port into React using a useEffect with a canvas ref and a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose(). In react-three-fiber, use useThree for raycaster and onPointerDown on mesh primitives to get UV data from the intersection object. Replace 'textures/uv_grid_opengl.jpg' with your own hosted image URL (CDN, public folder, or imported asset) passed as the CanvasTexture background src; in Next.js place it in /public and reference it as '/your-texture.jpg'.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer; canvas-based texture updates on every click are inexpensive but calling needsUpdate per frame would be costly. Works on mobile with pointer events substituted for mouse events. Not suitable for scenes requiring real-time texture streaming on every frame.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call texture.needsUpdate = true after modifying the canvas; not disposing of textures and geometries on component unmount causing memory leaks; hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using a ResizeObserver tied to the container element; sharing the CanvasTexture._parentTexture array as a prototype property (it is shared across all instances — move it to the constructor).
accessibilityNotes: The 3D crosshair marker has no screen reader equivalent; provide a visible text readout of UV coordinates (e.g., an aria-live region) for accessibility. Add a prefers-reduced-motion check to skip any rotation animation. Supply a static fallback image showing the textured mesh for environments without WebGL support.

technique: render-to-texture with float pixel readback and mouse-position sampling
description: A two-pass rendering pipeline that draws animated 3D torus meshes into a floating-point render target, then displays them full-screen while reading back per-pixel RGBA values at the cursor position. Suits scientific visualization tools, GPU-computed data dashboards, or creative coding portfolios where real-time shader output must be inspected or piped into application logic.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate block in a React useEffect with a canvas ref (renderer.domElement appended to the ref). Move the WebGLRenderTarget and Float32Array readback into the render loop closure. For react-three-fiber, use a useFrame hook and a useFBO utility from @react-three/drei; the readRenderTargetPixels call goes at the end of useFrame. No local asset paths need replacing.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 or WebGL1 with EXT_color_buffer_float for FloatType render targets; falls back to UnsignedByteType on older mobile GPUs. readRenderTargetPixels is a GPU stall and should be throttled (e.g., every N frames) in performance-sensitive contexts. High memory cost proportional to render target resolution.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose the WebGLRenderTarget on component unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/Height breaks in resizable containers — use a ResizeObserver and call renderer.setSize plus rtTexture.setSize. Creating a new Float32Array inside the render loop every frame adds GC pressure; allocate it once outside.
accessibilityNotes: The animated mesh rotation should respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or slowing rotation. The pixel-value readout displayed as innerHTML should use an aria-live region so screen readers announce updates. Provide a static screenshot fallback for contexts where WebGL is unavailable.

technique: animated water refraction plane with distortion dudv map
description: A semi-transparent refractive panel with animated rippling water distortion floats in a Cornell-box-style room while a glowing sphere orbits behind it, bending the view of the scene beyond. Suits premium product showcase pages, interactive art installations, luxury brand hero sections, or any site needing a high-end glass or liquid material effect.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate block inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref, assign renderer.domElement to the ref, and return a cleanup that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the animation loop. In Next.js, use dynamic import with ssr:false to avoid window errors. Replace 'textures/waterdudv.jpg' with a path under /public (e.g. '/textures/waterdudv.jpg') or import it via a bundler. The dudvMap is essential for the ripple effect; host it yourself or substitute any greyscale DU/DV distortion texture.
constraints: Requires WebGL 1 or 2; the Refractor renders an off-screen render target (1024×1024) on every frame, making it moderately expensive — avoid on low-end mobile or battery-sensitive contexts. The WaterRefractionShader depends on a DU/DV texture that must be self-hosted. Not suitable as a background element on content-heavy pages where GPU budget is already constrained.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and refractor.material.dispose() on unmount causing memory leaks; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container element's offsetWidth/offsetHeight; neglecting to set dudvMap.wrapS and wrapT to RepeatWrapping, which breaks the distortion tiling; not updating camera.aspect on resize; loading the texture synchronously without awaiting loadAsync, leading to a blank refractor on first render.
accessibilityNotes: Add a prefers-reduced-motion media query check: if reduced motion is preferred, pause the animation loop and show a static screenshot or CSS-based frosted-glass fallback. The canvas has no inherent screen-reader content, so add aria-hidden='true' and provide surrounding semantic HTML to convey page purpose. Keyboard navigation is not applicable to the 3D viewport itself, but OrbitControls can be disabled entirely when the effect is purely decorative.

technique: volumetric 2D texture array slice viewer with render-target post-processing
description: Animates through cross-sectional slices of a 3D volumetric dataset (e.g. medical scan or geological data), rendered onto a flat plane with adjustable intensity, producing a smooth scanning effect. Best suited for medical imaging platforms, scientific data visualization dashboards, or research/portfolio sites that need to communicate depth and layered structure.
usageNote: Wrap the renderer creation and animation loop inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; assign renderer.domElement to the ref instead of appending to a created div. Replace the zip file asset path with a URL from your own CDN, public folder, or an API route serving the binary. The inline shader scripts (document.getElementById) must be moved to JS template literal strings or imported as GLSL files. Use react-three-fiber's useFrame for the animation loop if preferred, but the WebGLArrayRenderTarget and ShaderMaterial must still be created imperatively.
constraints: Requires WebGL 2.0 (not WebGL 1.0), so older iOS Safari and IE11 are unsupported. Loading and decompressing a large zip asset (~7MB+) is expensive on first load. GPU memory usage is significant due to the 3D texture array; avoid on low-end mobile devices. Performance cost is moderate-to-high: two render passes per frame (offscreen render target + scene render).
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.setRenderTarget(null) after the offscreen pass, causing the main scene to render into the wrong buffer. Not disposing the WebGLArrayRenderTarget and DataArrayTexture on component unmount, causing GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a ResizeObserver on the container element. Leaving shader source in HTML script tags instead of porting them to strings when moving to a module-based framework.
accessibilityNotes: The animation auto-plays with no pause control; add a play/pause button and honor prefers-reduced-motion by stopping the depthStep animation and holding on a single slice. Provide a static screenshot fallback for screen readers via an aria-label on the canvas describing the volumetric content. The GUI intensity slider should be keyboard-accessible, which lil-gui handles by default.

technique: depth buffer precision comparison (normal vs logarithmic vs reversed-Z)
description: Three side-by-side 3D viewports display overlapping geometry at extreme depth ranges to compare depth-fighting artifacts across different depth buffer strategies. Best suited for technical documentation sites, WebGL/WebGPU explainer pages, or developer tool dashboards where rendering quality tradeoffs need to be visualized.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, wrap setup inside a useEffect with a cleanup that calls renderer.dispose(). Create three canvas refs, one per renderer (normal, logarithmic, reversed). Replace the global container.getElementById pattern with refs. Use a single shared scene and geometry ref. Resize handlers should use a ResizeObserver on each canvas container rather than window.innerWidth. No local assets are needed.
constraints: Reversed depth buffer (reversedDepthBuffer: true) is a cutting-edge WebGL extension and may not be supported on all browsers or mobile GPUs — verify EXT_clip_control support. Logarithmic depth buffer is broadly supported but has shader compatibility caveats. Running three simultaneous WebGL renderers is expensive; on low-end or mobile devices this will cause frame drops. Not suitable as a decorative background element — purely functional/diagnostic.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call composer.setSize on window resize for all three composers causes mismatched resolutions. Failing to dispose geometries, materials, and render targets on unmount leaks GPU memory. Hardcoding 0.33 * window.innerWidth instead of computing from container dimensions breaks responsive layouts. Sharing a single renderTarget across three renderers without isolating depth textures can cause read/write conflicts.
accessibilityNotes: This is an inherently visual technical comparison with no semantic content — add descriptive ARIA labels to each canvas container (e.g. aria-label='Normal depth buffer rendering'). Provide a static screenshot fallback for screen readers or users with prefers-reduced-motion. The rotating geometry serves a diagnostic purpose, so a paused fallback image is a valid substitute. No keyboard interaction is needed.

technique: render-to-texture with multi-pass shader composition and dynamic texture mapping onto 3D objects
description: An animated scene is rendered into an offscreen buffer first, then that live texture is applied both as a post-processed full-screen overlay and as the surface material on a grid of 3D spheres that react to mouse movement. Suited for creative agency hero sections, digital art portfolios, or interactive product showcases where a dynamic, layered visual effect is needed.
usageNote: In React or Next.js, wrap the entire init/animate logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref, passing the ref's current element to the WebGLRenderer instead of appending to a container div. Use a cleanup function to call renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame. In react-three-fiber, replicate the multi-scene pattern using useFrame and multiple useRef-held WebGLRenderTarget instances. No local asset paths exist, so no replacement is needed. Inline the GLSL shader strings directly (as template literals or imported .glsl files) rather than reading from script tags via getElementById.
constraints: Requires WebGL with render target support; not supported on very old mobile GPUs or WebGL1 contexts without extensions. Moderate-to-high GPU cost due to multiple render passes per frame. The full-screen render target at device pixel ratio can be expensive on high-DPI mobile displays. Best suited for desktop hero sections or GPU-capable mid-to-high-end devices.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose the WebGLRenderTarget when the component unmounts causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight breaks on resize — add a ResizeObserver or window resize listener that updates both the render target size and camera projections. Reading shader source from DOM script tags will not work in component-based frameworks; always convert to inline strings or module imports. Forgetting renderer.autoClear = false breaks the multi-pass compositing.

The canvas has no inherent semantic meaning — add aria-hidden='true' to the canvas element and ensure any surrounding UI content is accessible via standard HTML. No interactive keyboard targets exist within the canvas.

technique: real-time 3D mesh sculpting with brush tools and GLTF export

technique: fullscreen procedural GLSL shader animation (time-driven fragment shader on a screen quad)

technique: animated ocean surface with procedural sky, clouds, and bloom post-processing

technique: directional shadow mapping with animated 3D scene and real-time shadow casting

usageNote: Wrap the init/animate logic inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref, returning a cleanup that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the animation loop.
