technique: cascaded shadow maps (CSM) for large-scale outdoor directional lighting
description: A large outdoor scene with rows of tall buildings or structures casting high-quality shadows across a wide ground plane, with shadows remaining sharp at both near and far distances via multi-cascade shadow splitting. Suits architectural visualizations, open-world game environments, city builder UIs, or any 3D product/environment showcase requiring realistic sunlight across a large area.
usageNote: Wrap the init logic in a useEffect with a canvas ref for React/Next.js. Instantiate renderer targeting the ref element instead of appending to document.body. CSM must be initialized after the renderer and camera exist; call csm.update() inside the animation loop and csm.setupMaterial() on every material that should receive cascaded shadows. Clean up with renderer.dispose() and csm.dispose() in the useEffect return. For react-three-fiber, CSM must be managed imperatively via useEffect or a custom R3F extension since it wraps the scene and camera directly.
constraints: High GPU cost: CSM renders the scene N times (once per cascade, default 4), multiplying draw calls significantly. Not recommended for mobile or low-end GPUs. Requires WebGL with shadow map support (PCFShadowMap). Best suited for scenes with a dominant directional light (sun/moon) and large view distances. Not appropriate for point-light or spot-light dominated scenes.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call csm.setupMaterial() on every material — shadows will silently not appear. Not calling csm.update() in the animation loop causes shadows to lag behind camera movement. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight breaks responsiveness; use a ResizeObserver and update camera.aspect, renderer.setSize, and csm.updateFrustums(). Disposing scene objects without removing them from CSM's internal light list can cause memory leaks.
accessibilityNotes: No interactive or animated elements that users directly control, but the OrbitControls mouse interaction should be supplemented with keyboard equivalents or removed for passive display use. Provide a static screenshot fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion or on devices where WebGL is unavailable. Shadow rendering does not affect screen reader accessibility since the canvas has no semantic content — add aria-hidden='true' and a descriptive aria-label on a sibling element.

technique: billboard sprite field with orthographic HUD overlay
description: Hundreds of textured billboard sprites float in a rotating spherical cloud in 3D space, with fog depth and pulsing scale/opacity animation, while a second orthographic layer pins decorative UI sprites to screen corners and center. Suits hero backgrounds for creative agencies, game landing pages, space-themed apps, or interactive data visualizations where depth and atmosphere are needed.
usageNote: Wrap init() and animate() inside a useEffect with a canvas ref; assign renderer.domElement to the ref instead of appending to document.body. Return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes the event listener. Replace textures/sprite0.png, textures/sprite1.png, textures/sprite2.png with paths inside your /public folder (e.g. /sprites/sprite0.png) or import them as modules. In react-three-fiber, use <sprite> primitives inside a rotating <group> and a separate <Canvas orthographic> for the HUD layer, or keep the vanilla renderer approach inside useEffect for full control.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer; the dual-scene render pass (perspective + orthographic) adds moderate GPU overhead. On low-end mobile devices, reduce the sprite count (amount) from 200 to 50–80. The autoClear=false pattern and clearDepth() call are essential for HUD compositing and must be preserved. Not suitable for CSS or SVG renderers.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and cancel the animation loop on component unmount causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions breaks embedded use. Neglecting to update both cameras (perspective and orthographic) in onWindowResize breaks layout. Sharing a single SpriteMaterial instance across sprites without cloning causes all sprites to share state unintentionally (already handled in the original via .clone()).
accessibilityNotes: Provide a prefers-reduced-motion media query check before starting the animation loop; if reduced motion is preferred, stop rotation and pulsing or render a single static frame. Add an aria-hidden='true' attribute to the canvas element and supply a visually equivalent static background image as a CSS fallback for screen readers and environments where WebGL is unavailable.

technique: continuous geometry and texture creation with immediate disposal (memory stress loop)
description: Each frame creates a new randomly colored sphere with a procedurally generated canvas texture, renders it once, then immediately disposes all GPU resources. This pattern is invisible to end users as a visual feature but demonstrates correct WebGL resource lifecycle management; it suits any site that dynamically generates and destroys 3D objects (product configurators, data-driven visualizations, infinite scroll 3D feeds).
usageNote: In React or Next.js, place the init and animate logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref, returning a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the animation loop. With react-three-fiber, use useFrame to trigger per-frame geometry creation and the useEffect cleanup hook to call geometry.dispose(), material.dispose(), and texture.dispose(). No external assets are needed; canvas textures are generated procedurally at runtime.
constraints: This pattern is GPU-allocation-heavy per frame and should never be used as-is in production UI; its value is as a reference for correct dispose() call ordering. Mobile GPUs may stall under rapid allocation/deallocation cycles. Requires a WebGL-capable renderer. Suitable only when objects are truly transient (created and destroyed within one or a few frames).
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose(), material.dispose(), and texture.dispose() will leak VRAM, causing progressive slowdown or browser crashes. Do not accumulate meshes in the scene without removing them. Never skip scene.remove(mesh) before dispose. Avoid hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight; use a ResizeObserver or the canvas ref dimensions instead.
accessibilityNotes: Because this renders a blank or invisible scene from the user's perspective, no reduced-motion fallback is strictly required. If adapted into a visible animated background, provide a prefers-reduced-motion media query to pause the animation loop and display a static solid-color background. No meaningful content is conveyed so screen reader labeling of the canvas element (aria-hidden='true') is appropriate.

technique: dynamic shader material cycling with GPU memory management
description: A field of 100 spheres scattered in 3D space, each receiving a unique procedurally colored shader that is replaced every frame and immediately disposed. This pattern is suited for stress-testing or validating GPU memory hygiene in WebGL-heavy creative sites, dashboards, or any app that dynamically swaps materials at runtime.
usageNote: Wrap init() in a useEffect with a canvas ref and assign renderer.domElement to the ref node. Move setInterval to inside useEffect and clear it in the cleanup function via clearInterval. The inline script-tag shaders (vertexShader/fragmentShader) should be extracted into JS template-literal strings or imported as GLSL modules rather than read from DOM script tags. No local asset paths to replace.
constraints: This pattern is intentionally GPU-intensive: it creates and destroys 100 ShaderMaterial + WebGLProgram pairs every frame (~60fps), making it suitable only as a memory-management reference, not a production visual. It requires a WebGL-capable browser and a discrete or mid-range GPU; it will thermal-throttle mobile devices quickly. Not suitable for any page where performance or battery life matter.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call mesh.material.dispose() before reassigning materials will cause GPU memory leaks that crash the browser tab over time. Do not omit geometry.dispose() on unmount. Avoid hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight; use a ResizeObserver tied to the container element instead. Do not run the setInterval loop outside a visibility check (Page Visibility API) or it will churn GPU resources even when the tab is hidden.
accessibilityNotes: There is no meaningful content for screen readers; add an aria-hidden='true' attribute to the canvas element. Provide a prefers-reduced-motion media query check that pauses or stops the interval loop entirely. A static fallback image of a neutral 3D sphere arrangement should be offered for users with vestibular disorders or in no-JS environments.

technique: split-screen before/after slider comparing sRGB vs Display P3 wide-gamut color rendering
description: A draggable vertical divider splits the viewport into two panels showing the same image rendered in sRGB (left) and Display P3 wide-gamut color space (right), enabling direct visual comparison. Ideal for photography portfolios, color-management documentation, monitor calibration tools, or any product site wanting to showcase HDR/wide-gamut image quality.
usageNote: Wrap the entire setup in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js. Move renderer creation and event listeners inside the effect and return a cleanup function that disposes the renderer and removes listeners. Replace the local texture paths (textures/wide_gamut/logo_{colorSpace}.png) with your own hosted image URLs or Next.js public-folder paths — you will need two versions of each image, one saved as sRGB and one encoded in Display P3. The slider DOM element should be rendered via JSX and its ref passed into the effect.
constraints: Requires WebGL 1 or 2 with P3 color space support for the wide-gamut effect to be visible; falls back silently to sRGB on unsupported displays and browsers. The scissor-based dual-render approach doubles per-frame GPU draw calls. Best suited for full-viewport hero or comparison sections; not appropriate for small embedded canvases or carousels. Mobile is supported but touch-action must be managed carefully.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and remove window event listeners on unmount causes memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element dimensions breaks layouts where the canvas is not full-viewport. Not calling texture.needsUpdate = true after a gamut change leaves stale color transforms. Using a single scene instead of two separate scissor-split scenes will make the comparison impossible. Failing to re-run THREE.TextureUtils.contain on resize breaks aspect ratio.
accessibilityNotes: The slider is pointer-driven only; add keyboard event listeners (ArrowLeft/ArrowRight) to move sliderPos for keyboard accessibility. Provide a static side-by-side image fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion or for browsers without WebGL. The comparison has no screen-reader description — add an aria-label to the container explaining the color-space comparison and expose slider position as an aria-valuenow attribute.

technique: animated 2D texture array slice viewer with depth scrolling
description: Displays a single flat plane that cycles through sequential slices of a volumetric data stack, producing a smooth flip-book animation of layered image data. Suits medical imaging portals, scientific data visualization dashboards, or any product page needing a dramatic animated reveal of layered content.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref, or use react-three-fiber with a useFrame hook for the depth animation loop. Replace the local zip asset path with a URL to your own hosted texture archive (S3, CDN, etc.) or swap DataArrayTexture for a sequence of standard textures if a zip pipeline is unavailable. The ShaderMaterial vertex and fragment shaders are currently inlined as DOM script tags — move their GLSL source into template literal strings or separate .glsl files imported as raw strings.
constraints: Requires WebGL 2.0 for DataArrayTexture (2D texture array) support — not supported on older iOS Safari or legacy Android browsers. Loading and unzipping a large binary archive on the main thread can block UI briefly; consider a Web Worker. Moderate GPU memory cost proportional to total texture volume. Not suitable for low-end mobile devices with limited GPU memory.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call texture.dispose() and material.dispose() on unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight breaks in React layouts — use the container element's dimensions instead. Leaving the animation loop running after component unmount will throw errors; cancel via renderer.setAnimationLoop(null). Not handling the async load before mesh exists will cause null-reference errors in the animate loop.
accessibilityNotes: The animation auto-plays with no pause control — add a play/pause toggle and respect prefers-reduced-motion by stopping depthStep increments. Provide a static fallback image (e.g. a representative slice as a PNG) for screen readers and no-WebGL environments using a noscript or canvas-unavailable fallback. Add an aria-label to the canvas element describing the visualization content.

technique: animated KTX2 texture array flipbook on a flat plane
description: A full-viewport flat plane cycles through frames of a compressed texture array, creating a smooth flipbook or video-like animation effect. Ideal for hero sections, loading screens, or cinematic backdrops that need GPU-compressed, high-performance image sequences.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, wrap the init logic in a useEffect with a canvas ref and pass the ref to WebGLRenderer instead of creating a div. KTX2Loader requires a transcoder WASM worker — host the Basis Universal transcoder files (from three/examples/jsm/libs/basis/) on your CDN or public folder and call ktx2Loader.setTranscoderPath('/basis/'). Replace the local .ktx2 asset path with your own hosted compressed texture array; generate KTX2 texture arrays from image sequences using the KTX-Software CLI or Squoosh pipelines. Clean up renderer and loader in the useEffect return function.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 for sampler2DArray support (GLSL3); not compatible with WebGL1 fallback. KTX2/Basis Universal transcoding adds a one-time CPU cost on first load. The WASM transcoder may be blocked in strict CSP environments. Mobile GPUs generally support this well but VRAM limits apply for large texture arrays. Not suitable for environments without WebGL2.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call ktx2Loader.setTranscoderPath() causes silent load failures. Not disposing the texture array and geometry on unmount causes VRAM leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the container element size breaks embedded or partial-page use. Embedding shader source in HTML script tags is fragile in React — inline GLSL strings or import raw shader files instead. Omitting detectSupport() call breaks format negotiation.
accessibilityNotes: The animation is purely decorative; add aria-hidden='true' to the canvas container. For reduced-motion preferences (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce), pause the animation loop by not advancing depthStep or freeze on a single frame. Provide a static poster image as a CSS background fallback for environments where WebGL2 is unavailable or the KTX2 fails to load.

technique: compressed texture array with per-layer GPU updates and instanced mesh display
description: Renders a row of three panels side by side, each displaying a independently-updatable frame from a KTX2 compressed texture array, with a control panel to copy any source frame into any destination slot. Suits media-rich sites needing efficient GPU-side image swapping, such as interactive film galleries, sprite-sheet browsers, or multi-panel product image viewers.
usageNote: Wrap the init function inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; pass the ref's current element as the renderer's domElement parent instead of appending to document.body. Replace the KTX2 local asset path ('textures/spiritedaway.ktx2') with a URL from your own CDN or public folder — in Next.js place it under /public and reference it as '/spiritedaway.ktx2'. The GUI (lil-gui) can be replaced with React state and HTML inputs for srcLayer/destLayer controls.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 for texture array support (CompressedArrayTexture); not compatible with WebGL1 or very old mobile browsers. KTX2 compressed textures require Basis Universal transcoder support via KTX2Loader.setTranscoderPath(). GPU memory scales with texture array size and layer count. Desktop-class GPUs recommended for large texture arrays.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call ktx2Loader.setTranscoderPath() before loadAsync, which will silently fail. Not disposing the textureArray and geometry on component unmount causing GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions. Skipping textureArray.addLayerUpdate() and relying only on needsUpdate, which re-uploads all layers instead of just the changed one, wasting bandwidth.
accessibilityNotes: The 3D canvas has no inherent keyboard or screen reader support; add an aria-label to the canvas element describing the content. Provide static fallback images for users with prefers-reduced-motion or those on browsers lacking WebGL2. The lil-gui controls are keyboard accessible by default but should be replaced with properly labelled HTML form controls for production use.

technique: interactive 3D volumetric rendering with isosurface and maximum intensity projection modes
description: Renders a 3D scalar volume dataset as a semi-transparent cloud or solid isosurface using GPU ray-marching shaders, with orbit rotation and adjustable contrast/colormap controls. Suits medical imaging portals, scientific visualization dashboards, radiology SaaS products, or any site needing to display MRI/CT scan data or 3D density fields interactively in the browser.
usageNote: Wrap the renderer initialization in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; assign renderer.domElement to the ref instead of appending to document.body. Replace the NRRDLoader path 'models/nrrd/stent.nrrd' with a URL to your own NRRD file (served from /public or a CDN). Replace colormap texture paths with your own hosted PNGs. Use react-three-fiber with a custom shader material if you prefer a declarative approach, but the vanilla approach with useEffect cleanup (renderer.dispose(), controls.dispose()) is straightforward and recommended here.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 for Data3DTexture (THREE.Data3DTexture) and R32F float texture support; not supported on older iOS Safari or low-end Android devices. GPU memory cost is proportional to volume dimensions (e.g. 512^3 float32 = 512 MB). Not suitable for mobile or low-power devices. The ray-marching shader is computationally expensive and will drop frame rates on integrated graphics.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call texture.needsUpdate = true after creating the Data3DTexture; not disposing the 3D texture and shader material on component unmount causing GPU memory leaks; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a container element size with ResizeObserver; assuming NRRDLoader works without a correct Content-Type header on the server; leaving the GUI attached after unmount.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static screenshot or pre-rendered image fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion or WebGL2-unsupported browsers. Add an aria-label to the canvas element describing the volume content (e.g. 'Interactive 3D scan visualization'). Keyboard users cannot orbit without additional keyboard control bindings on OrbitControls. Screen readers will receive no meaningful content from the canvas; supplement with a text description of what is being visualized.

technique: volumetric ray-marched 3D noise cloud with procedural sky gradient
description: A softly animated volumetric cloud rendered inside a blue-gradient sky sphere, using ray-marched 3D Perlin noise stored in a Data3DTexture. Ideal for hero backgrounds on weather apps, atmospheric landing pages, travel sites, meditation or wellness platforms, or any product that wants an airy, expansive environmental presence.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate block inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer targeting the ref element instead of appending to document.body, and store the animation loop id for cleanup on unmount. In Next.js mark the component 'use client' and guard with typeof window !== 'undefined'. There are no local asset paths to replace — all data (3D texture, sky gradient) is generated procedurally at runtime. The GUI controls can be omitted or replaced with React state.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 (Data3DTexture and GLSL 'in/out' syntax are ES300 features); not supported on older iOS Safari or Android WebView without WebGL2. The ray-marching loop (controlled by 'steps') is GPU-intensive — high step counts will drop frames on mobile GPUs and integrated graphics. The 128³ texture allocation (~2MB of Uint8Array) plus shader compilation makes initial load slow on low-end devices. Not suitable as a persistent background on battery-sensitive mobile experiences.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and texture.dispose() on unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the canvas container's dimensions breaks layout in embedded or split-panel UIs. Omitting the resize event listener makes the canvas blurry or cropped after window resize. Using too many ray-march steps without a quality setting degrades performance silently. Not setting texture.needsUpdate = true after regenerating the cloud data leaves a blank volume.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static screenshot or CSS gradient fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion, as the continuous slow camera drift and animated cloud frame update cannot be meaningfully paused without extra logic. Add aria-hidden='true' to the canvas element and ensure any overlaid text has sufficient contrast against both light and dark areas of the cloud. The 3D scene has no interactive keyboard targets so no focus management is needed beyond hiding it from screen readers.

technique: HDR environment lighting with switchable tone mapping operators on a 3D model
description: A photorealistic 3D object is lit by an HDR equirectangular environment map (golden-hour sky), with real-time tone mapping (Neutral, ACESFilmic, AgX, Reinhard, etc.) controlling how HDR colors are mapped to the display. Ideal for product configurators, jewelry or luxury goods showcases, digital fashion, or any site section requiring studio-quality 3D presentation.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js, returning a cleanup that calls renderer.dispose() and removes the animation loop. Replace HDR texture path with a URL from your CDN or public folder (e.g. '/textures/venice_sunset_1k.hdr') and replace the GLTF model path with your own hosted .glb URL. Use drei's <Environment> and <OrbitControls> in react-three-fiber for a more idiomatic approach, setting gl.toneMapping and gl.toneMappingExposure on the canvas.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 for full HDR pipeline fidelity; HDR textures can be 2–8 MB so lazy-load them. Moderate GPU cost from environment reflections; lower-end mobile devices may struggle with high-poly GLTF models. Not suitable for very performance-constrained environments without LOD and texture compression. DRACO-compressed models require the DRACO decoder WASM to be hosted separately.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call dracoLoader.dispose() and renderer.dispose() on unmount; not handling the async loading race condition when the component unmounts before promises resolve; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a ResizeObserver on the container element; neglecting to set texture.mapping = THREE.EquirectangularReflectionMapping after loading the HDR; leaving CustomToneMapping shader patch applied globally when switching back to built-in operators.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static high-quality render image as a fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion or when WebGL is unavailable. Disable OrbitControls or lock interaction for motion-sensitive users. Add aria-label to the canvas element describing the product being shown. Ensure any UI controls (tone mapping sliders) are keyboard-navigable with visible focus states.

technique: PBR clearcoat material showcase with HDR environment and orbiting point light
description: Four photorealistic spheres display high-end clearcoat material effects — metallic car paint with flake normals, carbon fiber, a dimpled golf-ball surface, and scratched metallic with water ripple normals — all lit by an HDR panorama and an animated orbiting light. Ideal for product configurators, automotive or luxury goods websites, material/finish selectors, or any hero section that needs to communicate premium quality.
usageNote: Wrap the init logic in a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js, assigning renderer.domElement to the ref. Replace HDRCubeTextureLoader paths (pisaHDR/) and all texture paths (Carbon.png, Water_1_M_Normal.jpg, golfball.jpg, etc.) with URLs served from your /public folder or a CDN. FlakesTexture is procedural and needs no external asset. Use react-three-fiber's <Canvas> with MeshPhysicalMaterial clearcoat props as an alternative.
constraints: Requires WebGPU-capable browser (Chrome 113+ with WebGPU flag, or Edge); falls back to WebGL via WebGLNodesHandler but still needs MeshPhysicalNodeMaterial support. HDR cube loading is network-heavy (6 HDR files). Four shadow-casting meshes plus a point light make this moderate-to-high GPU cost; not recommended as a background element on low-end or mobile devices.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and texture.dispose() on unmount causing GPU memory leaks; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a ResizeObserver on the container element; omitting renderer.setPixelRatio causing blurriness on HiDPI screens; not setting colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace on diffuse maps causing washed-out colors; forgetting to await renderer.compileAsync before adding the group, which can cause frame stutter on first render.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static product image fallback when prefers-reduced-motion is active or when WebGPU/WebGL is unavailable. The 3D canvas has no inherent keyboard focus or screen-reader content; add an aria-label on the canvas element and a visually-hidden text description of the materials shown. Pause the animation loop when the canvas scrolls out of viewport using IntersectionObserver.

technique: instanced mesh rendering with animated TSL shader coloring
description: Hundreds to thousands of identical 3D objects scattered randomly in space, each colored with a continuously shifting sine-wave RGB animation driven by world position and time. Ideal for hero sections, product launch pages, or data visualization backgrounds that need to convey scale, density, and dynamism without sacrificing GPU performance.
usageNote: Wrap the init/animate logic in a useEffect with a canvas ref for React/Next.js, returning a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and removes the DOM element. Replace BufferGeometryLoader path 'models/json/suzanne_buffergeometry.json' with your own hosted geometry (e.g. via /public in Next.js) or swap in a built-in BufferGeometry like THREE.IcosahedronGeometry to avoid the external asset dependency entirely. For react-three-fiber, use <instancedMesh> with a ref and set instance matrices in a useFrame hook.
constraints: Instanced rendering (Method.INSTANCED) is highly performant and the recommended mode — it issues only one GPU draw call regardless of count. NAIVE mode with count > 500 will degrade performance severely on mid-range or mobile GPUs. Requires WebGL 2 (for instancing) and TSL/WebGPU node materials; fallback to standard MeshPhongMaterial is needed for broad compatibility. Not suitable for environments that cannot load WebGL 2.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call geometry.dispose() and material.dispose() when switching methods or unmounting — the clean() function pattern must be preserved. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using a ResizeObserver or container-relative sizing. Leaving the animation loop running after component unmount in React. Keeping the NAIVE method with high counts in production without a cap.
accessibilityNotes: The continuous color animation should be paused or replaced with a static color when the user has prefers-reduced-motion enabled — check window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') and disable the time-based colorNode animation. Provide an aria-hidden='true' attribute on the canvas and a visually hidden text alternative describing the decorative nature of the scene. No keyboard interaction is required for purely decorative use.

technique: real-time shadow mapping with dual lights, procedural noise materials, and soft shadow radius
description: A dark atmospheric 3D scene featuring a slowly rotating torus knot with perforated noise-based shadows, soft spot and directional lighting, and a procedurally textured ground plane. Suits hero sections of creative portfolios, game studio landing pages, or product showcases requiring depth and drama.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer targeting the ref element instead of appending to document.body, store the animation loop ID for cleanup, and call renderer.dispose() on unmount. The WebGLNodesHandler import enables TSL node materials on WebGL — ensure your bundler resolves 'three/webgpu' and 'three/tsl' via an import map or Vite alias. No local assets to replace. In react-three-fiber, this pattern is harder to port due to custom node materials; vanilla Three.js inside useEffect is recommended.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 with nodes support (via WebGLNodesHandler) or a WebGPU-capable browser. Shadow maps at 2048×2048 for two lights are moderately expensive; mobile mid-range GPUs may struggle. Not suitable for use cases requiring more than ~60fps on integrated graphics. The mx_fractal_noise TSL functions require the three/tsl module available in Three.js r160+.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and remove the animation loop on component unmount causes memory leaks in SPAs. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of measuring the container element breaks embedded canvas layouts. Not updating camera.aspect and renderer.setSize on resize causes distortion. Cloning the material without also cloning shadow-related node properties can produce incorrect shadow masks.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a static fallback image for users with prefers-reduced-motion or for browsers lacking WebGL2 support. The canvas has no inherent keyboard or screen reader interface; wrap it in a decorative aria-hidden container. Pause or stop the animation loop when the canvas is not in the viewport using IntersectionObserver to respect reduced-motion preferences and save battery.

technique: animated skinned character with skeletal animation playback
description: A fully rigged 3D humanoid character plays a looping animation in a blue-lit scene, demonstrating smooth skeletal skinning. Suits hero sections for games, fitness apps, fashion brands, avatars, virtual try-on, or any product that benefits from an animated human presence.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect that creates the renderer on a canvas ref and returns a cleanup function calling renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame. Replace the local Michelle.glb with a URL to your own hosted GLTF/GLB file (CDN, public folder, or signed S3 URL). With react-three-fiber use <primitive object={gltf.scene}> and useAnimations() from @react-three/drei for cleaner animation wiring.
constraints: Requires WebGPU-capable browser or falls back to WebGL via WebGLNodesHandler; skeletal animation is GPU-heavy with many bones so limit concurrent animated characters on mobile. High-poly GLB files will hurt load time — use Draco compression. Not suitable for very low-end devices or contexts where a static image suffices.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call mixer.stopAllAction() and mixer.uncacheRoot() on cleanup causing memory leaks; not disposing the GLB scene geometry and textures on unmount; hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using the canvas container dimensions; omitting the resize listener leading to stretched rendering; loading the model inside the animation loop instead of once.
accessibilityNotes: Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or slowing the animation mixer when the media query matches. Provide a static poster image or screenshot as a fallback for browsers without WebGL/WebGPU. The canvas is not keyboard or screen-reader accessible by default — add aria-hidden='true' and describe the character via adjacent text content.

technique: large-scale multi-object scatter with shared GPU uniform buffers
description: Two hundred rotating 3D primitives (tetrahedra and cubes) scattered through space, some solid-colored and some textured, all sharing lighting and camera data via GPU uniform buffer objects for efficiency. Suits hero backgrounds, loading screens, or data-visualization splash pages where high object counts with consistent lighting are needed.
usageNote: Wrap in a React useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer targeting the ref, call animate inside the effect, and return a cleanup that disposes the renderer and cancels the animation loop. In Next.js, guard with typeof window !== 'undefined' or use a dynamic import with ssr:false. Replace 'textures/crate.gif' with an imported asset (e.g., import crateUrl from '/public/textures/crate.gif') or any publicly hosted image URL. The vertex/fragment shaders are stored in script tags with type='x-shader/x-vertex'—move their GLSL source into JS template literal strings instead.
constraints: Requires WebGL 2 for UniformsGroup / UBO support; not available on very old mobile browsers or some WebGL 1-only contexts. Rendering 200 meshes with custom shaders is moderate-to-high GPU cost; reduce mesh count to 50–80 for low-end mobile. Antialias is enabled, which adds cost on high-DPI devices.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to dispose cloned materials and geometries on unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Not updating camera.matrixWorldInverse each frame will break view-space lighting. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of using the container element's dimensions breaks embedded (non-fullscreen) use. Sharing a single material instance without cloning means all meshes share the same per-object uniforms, producing incorrect transforms.
accessibilityNotes: Add a prefers-reduced-motion media query check; if active, stop the animation loop and render a single static frame or replace with a CSS background. Provide an aria-hidden='true' attribute on the canvas and a visually hidden descriptive text element for screen readers. Ensure the page behind the canvas remains keyboard-navigable if used as a background layer.

technique: multi-point-light array with GPU uniform buffer objects on a 3D object grid
description: Hundreds of independently orbiting colored point lights illuminate a grid of spheres and a ground plane, producing a rich, shifting multi-colored lighting environment. Ideal for hero sections of creative agencies, game landing pages, tech product showcases, or any site that needs an impressive, GPU-powered real-time light-show backdrop.
usageNote: Wrap the init/animate logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; attach the renderer to the ref element instead of a hardcoded container id. Use a cleanup function to call renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame. This example uses inline GLSL via script tags — migrate those to template-literal strings or imported .glsl files. UniformsGroup requires WebGL2 context; ensure the WebGLRenderer is created with { antialias: true } and that no local shader assets are needed beyond the inline GLSL. react-three-fiber does not yet expose UniformsGroup natively, so raw Three.js inside useEffect is the recommended path.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 (UniformsGroup / UBO support); will silently fail or throw on WebGL1 contexts. High GPU cost at 200–300 dynamic point lights; not suitable for low-end mobile or integrated graphics without reducing pointLightsMax significantly. Desktop-first pattern. Shader compilation time may cause a visible stall on first load.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to update camera.matrixWorldInverse each frame after OrbitControls move, causing lighting to appear frozen relative to the camera. Not calling renderer.setPixelRatio(window.devicePixelRatio) leads to blurry output on retina displays. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of using the canvas container size breaks layout in embedded/partial-page uses. Forgetting to dispose cloned materials per mesh causes memory leaks when the component unmounts. Leaving pointLightsMax at 300 on mobile will tank frame rate.
accessibilityNotes: Add a prefers-reduced-motion media query check; if matched, stop the animation loop and render a single static frame or replace with a CSS gradient background. The canvas carries no semantic content — add aria-hidden='true' and ensure any overlaid text has sufficient contrast against the dynamic lighting. No keyboard interaction is required for the visual, but OrbitControls should be disabled or provide a skip mechanism for keyboard-only users.

technique: depth-video point cloud with mouse parallax
description: Renders a live video feed as a 3D point cloud using per-pixel depth data, producing a ghostly volumetric particle field that shifts perspective as the user moves the mouse. Suits immersive hero sections, creative agency showcases, interactive art installations, or data-visualization experiences where human presence or spatial depth needs to feel tangible.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, wrap initialization in a useEffect with a canvas ref and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the animation loop. Replace the document.getElementById('video') call with a ref to a <video> element rendered in JSX. The vertex and fragment shaders are currently loaded via script tags with type='x-shader'; move their GLSL source into JS template literal strings or .glsl files imported with a shader loader. No local asset paths need replacing, but you must supply your own depth-video source in the <video> element.
constraints: Requires WebGL with shader support; not suitable for environments where custom ShaderMaterial is unavailable. Processing a 640×480 point cloud (307,200 points) every frame is GPU-heavy; mobile devices with weak GPUs will struggle. Requires a depth-encoded video source (e.g. from a Kinect or synthetic depth camera) to produce meaningful 3D output—a standard RGB video will not produce correct depth displacement. Additive blending and disabled depth test mean layering order may look unexpected over complex backgrounds.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call video.pause() and texture.dispose() on cleanup, causing memory leaks in SPA navigation. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of measuring the container element, breaking layout in non-fullscreen panels. Leaving GUI controls visible in production. Not pausing the animation loop when the component is off-screen, wasting GPU resources. Omitting the resize listener update to camera.aspect, causing distorted perspectives on window resize.
accessibilityNotes: The point cloud is purely decorative and conveys no textual information, so add aria-hidden='true' to the canvas container. Provide a static screenshot or poster image fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion enabled or when WebGL is unavailable. Ensure the underlying video element has aria-hidden or a descriptive track if it carries meaningful content. No keyboard interaction is required since mouse parallax is supplementary; consider disabling the parallax effect for reduced-motion users by checking the media query and keeping the camera static.

technique: interactive equirectangular 360° video panorama with drag-to-look controls
description: A fully immersive 360-degree video sphere the user can drag to look around in any direction, placing them inside a live video environment. Ideal for virtual tours, real estate walkthroughs, event previews, travel/hospitality hero sections, or VR-style product showcases.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, wrap the init logic in a useEffect with a canvas ref: create the renderer targeting the ref element instead of appending to a container div, store the video element in a useRef, and return a cleanup function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancels the animation loop. For the video source, replace the document.getElementById('video') lookup with a <video> element created programmatically or via a ref, setting its src to your hosted equirectangular video URL (ideally an HLS or DASH stream for large files). In react-three-fiber, use a <VideoTexture> abstraction with a useVideoTexture hook from @react-three/drei on an inverted SphereGeometry.
constraints: Requires WebGL renderer; decoding a full 360° video is GPU and CPU intensive, so 4K+ sources will struggle on mid-range mobile. The video must be served with CORS headers if on a different origin. Autoplay requires the video to be muted in most browsers. Works best on desktop; touch drag is supported via pointer events but latency may vary on low-end mobile.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call video.pause() and renderer.dispose() on unmount causes memory leaks and orphaned decode threads. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of measuring the container breaks embedded or partial-page use. Not inverting the sphere geometry (scale -1 on x) causes the video to render inside-out. Failing to set texture.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace produces washed-out colour. Binding pointer events to document instead of the canvas element causes conflicts when embedded in a page with other interactive content.
accessibilityNotes: No keyboard navigation is provided by default; add arrow-key handlers to update lon/lat for keyboard users. Provide a static equirectangular still image fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion or when autoplay is blocked. Add an aria-label to the canvas element describing the panorama content, and expose a text description of the scene for screen readers. Consider a pause/play toggle button for users who find moving video distracting.

technique: volumetric ray-marched 3D cloud rendering with procedural Perlin noise
description: A softly lit, rotating volumetric cloud rendered inside a blue gradient sky sphere using GPU ray-marching through a 3D noise texture. Ideal for atmospheric hero backgrounds on weather apps, nature/travel sites, ambient landing pages, or sci-fi/fantasy product showcases.
usageNote: Wrap the init and animate logic inside a React useEffect that references a canvas via useRef, passing the ref's current element to WebGLRenderer instead of appending to document.body. Tear down renderer, controls, and animation loop in the useEffect cleanup function. No local assets are used — the 3D noise texture is generated procedurally at runtime, so no file paths need replacing. For react-three-fiber, the custom GLSL shaders and Data3DTexture must still be constructed imperatively inside a useEffect or a custom R3F <primitive> component.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 because it uses Data3DTexture (sampler3D) and GLSL ES 3.0 in/out syntax — WebGL1 is not supported. GPU ray-marching is moderately expensive; reduce the 'steps' uniform (default ~100) for mobile or low-end GPUs. Not suitable as a full-page background on battery-sensitive mobile contexts without a quality toggle. Desktop mid-range GPUs handle it well at 60fps.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and texture.dispose() on unmount causing GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of measuring the container element, breaking layout in non-fullscreen contexts. Not cancelling the animation loop (renderer.setAnimationLoop(null)) on cleanup. Skipping unpackAlignment = 1 on the Data3DTexture causes corrupted noise sampling. Forgetting to set texture.needsUpdate = true after creation.
accessibilityNotes: Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or skipping the animation loop entirely and showing a static gradient sky fallback (plain CSS background or a canvas snapshot). The canvas has no semantic content so add aria-hidden='true' and ensure any overlaid text has sufficient contrast against the blue-to-white sky gradient. No keyboard interaction is required unless OrbitControls are exposed to users, in which case provide mouse/touch alternatives.

technique: instanced volumetric ray-marching of 3D voxel data
description: Multiple copies of a voxel-defined fractal solid are rendered using per-instance ray-marching through a 3D texture, producing richly shaded geometric forms that auto-rotate in 3D space. Suits a data visualization platform, architectural or scientific portfolio, generative-art landing page, or a tech product hero section where structural complexity communicates depth and precision.
usageNote: Wrap the entire init/animate block inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React or Next.js; pass the ref's current element to WebGLRenderer instead of appending to document.body. Clean up by returning a dispose function that calls renderer.dispose() and cancelAnimationFrame. Replace the VOX asset path ('models/vox/menger.vox') with a path relative to your public/ folder (Next.js) or a URL imported via a bundler asset plugin; alternatively generate the 3D texture programmatically to avoid the file dependency entirely. React-three-fiber (R3F) can also host this via a custom <primitive> or shaderMaterial, but the raw GLSL and instanced approach maps more cleanly to vanilla useEffect.
constraints: Requires WebGL 2 (sampler3D, in/out GLSL, gl_FragDepth); will not run on WebGL 1 contexts or very old mobile GPUs. Each ray-march loop runs 100 iterations per fragment per instance, making this GPU-heavy; limit instance count and avoid mobile or low-end integrated graphics. Desktop Chrome, Firefox, and Edge with WebGL2 support are the primary targets.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and geometry/material.dispose() on unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/window.innerHeight instead of the container element's dimensions breaks layouts inside cards or split-pane UIs. Neglecting to update camera.aspect and renderer.setSize inside a ResizeObserver causes distortion. Passing the wrong precision qualifier or omitting 'precision highp sampler3D' on some drivers silently breaks volume sampling.
accessibilityNotes: The auto-rotating 3D scene should respect prefers-reduced-motion: pause or eliminate auto-rotation when the media query matches by checking window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') and setting controls.autoRotate = false. Provide a static screenshot fallback image for users with JavaScript disabled or on unsupported devices. The canvas has no inherent keyboard focus or screen-reader content; add aria-hidden='true' and a visually hidden descriptive text element nearby.

technique: 3D volumetric cloud / isosurface ray-marching with Perlin noise
description: A soft, three-dimensional cloud-like solid rendered via GPU ray-marching through a 3D Perlin noise texture, revealing an organic sculpted surface with shaded normals. Suits hero sections for scientific visualisation tools, medical imaging platforms, weather or climate apps, or any product that wants to convey depth and complexity through an abstract 3D form.
usageNote: Wrap renderer creation and the animation loop inside a React useEffect with a canvas ref (or use react-three-fiber with a custom rawShaderMaterial and a Data3DTexture created in a useMemo). The noise data generation is CPU-intensive so move it into a useEffect or a Web Worker to avoid blocking the main thread. There are no local asset paths to replace; all data is generated procedurally at runtime.
constraints: Requires WebGL2 (Data3DTexture and GLSL ES 3.0 are mandatory); will silently fail or show nothing on WebGL1-only contexts. The per-frame GPU ray-march is moderately expensive; reduce the 'steps' uniform (e.g. from 100 to 50) for mobile. Not suitable for very low-end or integrated-GPU mobile devices. The 128³ noise generation allocates ~2 MB of CPU memory at startup.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call texture.dispose() and geometry.dispose() on unmount causes GPU memory leaks. Hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of reading from the canvas container breaks responsive layouts. Not updating the cameraPos uniform each frame breaks the ray-march entirely. Omitting glslVersion: THREE.GLSL3 causes shader compilation failure. Using LinearMipmapLinearFilter without generating mipmaps on a Data3DTexture causes rendering artefacts.
accessibilityNotes: The rotating 3D cloud provides no information to screen readers; add an aria-hidden='true' attribute to the canvas and provide a meaningful text or static image alternative in the surrounding DOM. Honour prefers-reduced-motion by pausing the OrbitControls auto-rotate and freezing the animation loop, replacing it with a single rendered still frame.

technique: photorealistic 3D product viewer with animated camera intro, HDR environment, and bloom post-processing
description: A high-fidelity 3D luxury watch rendered with physically-based materials, HDR environment lighting, soft shadows, and subtle bloom, with a smooth animated camera flyout on load followed by interactive orbit controls. Ideal for premium product pages, e-commerce hero sections, or brand showcases where conveying craftsmanship and materiality is critical.
usageNote: Wrap the init logic inside a useEffect with a canvas ref in React/Next.js; assign renderer.domElement to the ref'd canvas rather than appending to a container div. Replace the HDR texture path (textures/equirectangular/lobe.hdr) and GLTF model path (models/gltf/rolex.glb) with paths to your own assets served from /public or a CDN. For react-three-fiber, use useLoader(GLTFLoader, url) and <Environment files={...}/> from @react-three/drei as a simpler alternative. The TWEEN import must be sourced from the 'tween' package or replaced with a library like GSAP.
constraints: High GPU cost due to HDR environment, shadow maps (2048px), Unreal Bloom, and TAA multi-sampling; not suitable for low-end mobile devices or battery-sensitive contexts. Requires WebGL2 for HalfFloatType render target. Post-processing composer is initialized but the EffectComposer wiring is incomplete in the snippet—agent must add it manually. DRACO-compressed GLTF requires the DRACO decoder wasm files to be served statically.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to call renderer.dispose() and controls.dispose() in the useEffect cleanup; not cancelling the animation loop (setAnimationLoop(null)) on unmount; hardcoding window.innerWidth/innerHeight instead of reading from the container element; omitting the resize observer when the canvas is not full-screen; failing to serve DRACO decoder files from a reachable public path; not replacing the HDR and GLTF asset paths with real hosted URLs.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a high-quality static product image as a fallback for users with prefers-reduced-motion or when WebGL is unavailable. The animated camera intro should be skipped or shortened if the reduced-motion media query is active. Add an aria-label to the canvas element describing the product. Keyboard users cannot interact with OrbitControls—consider adding ARIA-described keyboard shortcuts or a static alternative view.

technique: dual-canvas onscreen/offscreen WebGL rendering with Web Worker thread isolation
description: Renders two 3D canvas panels side by side — one on the main thread and one inside a Web Worker via OffscreenCanvas — demonstrating smooth 3D content even when the main thread is deliberately janked. Ideal for performance-critical product showcases, data dashboards, or hero sections where UI interactions must not stutter background 3D visuals.
usageNote: In React/Next.js, use a useEffect hook with two canvas refs. Dynamically import the worker and scene init logic. Move the Worker instantiation and transferControlToOffscreen call inside useEffect after mount. Replace the Worker path string with a bundler-compatible URL (e.g. new URL('./offscreen.worker.js', import.meta.url) for Vite/Webpack 5). The addons jank.js and scene.js are custom to this demo — you must supply your own scene initializer and optionally your own jank simulator.
constraints: OffscreenCanvas with WebGL is not supported on Safari < 17 or older Android browsers; always implement a graceful fallback to main-thread rendering. The pattern shines for expensive 3D scenes that need to stay smooth while the UI is busy. Requires browser support for transferControlToOffscreen and module Workers. Not suitable for projects targeting broad legacy browser support.
antiPatterns: Forgetting to check transferControlToOffscreen support before transferring control, causing runtime errors; not terminating the Worker on component unmount leading to memory leaks; hardcoding canvas dimensions instead of reading clientWidth/clientHeight dynamically; missing pixelRatio handling causing blurry output on high-DPI screens; assuming the Worker can import from the same paths as the main bundle without adjusting asset base paths.
accessibilityNotes: Canvas elements should have a descriptive aria-label or role='img' with alt text. Provide a static image or CSS fallback when OffscreenCanvas is unsupported (the demo shows a message element; replace with a meaningful fallback image). Respect prefers-reduced-motion by pausing or simplifying animation inside the Worker via a postMessage flag; the Worker has no direct access to matchMedia so the main thread must relay the preference.
